📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christopher Lloyd is celebrating his 10th anniversary with his wife, Lisa Lloyd (née Loiacono).

It has been revealed that in a Monday, November 23, X post, the Back to the Future star, 88, shared a photo of him and his wife decked in all black at a recent charity event in honor of his Back to the Future costar Michael J. Fox’s Parkinson’s research foundation.

Industry observers note that he captioned the post, “Oh Lisa… I love you more than words can simply put. Happy anniversary to us now and always ❤️❤️❤️❤️.”.

Lloyd met Lisa, 56, in 2005 and they tied the knot in 2016.

The actor was previously married four times, first to Catherine Boyd from 1959 until their divorce in 1971, Kay Tornborg from 1974 to 1987, Carol Ann Vanek from 1988 to 1991, and finally Jane Walker Wood, whom he wed in 1992 and divorced in 2005.

Earlier this month, the couple opened up about their marriage ahead of their 10th anniversary together.

In a recent development, “I appreciate his focus and his calmness. Because I’m very outgoing and gregarious. And sometimes he won’t talk. So it’s a balance,” Lisa praised the actor in a joint interview with People.

In a recent development, lloyd added, “Well, Lisa claims I’m kind of calm, even though I may be going crazy inside! But I think I’m pretty easy to live with, get along with.”.

In a recent development, “He reads all day long,” Lisa also shared, noting that Lloyd doesn’t go online. “I’ve been with him almost 22 years. My head’s full with a bunch of stupid stuff that you see on the internet… I watch how contemplative and in control he can be, and I’ve always been more hyper and outgoing than him.”.

In a recent development, lloyd, meanwhile, praised Lisa as being “full of energy and excitement to do this and that. She’s far more naturally social than I am. I’m not a social bug by nature, and it just seems the gel just comes together.”.

In his recent memoir, In My Own Time, Lloyd opened up about his past addiction to cocaine.

“That was all it took. I was hooked almost immediately,” he wrote. “I loved it, and that was where my cocaine abuse began.”.

“I wasn’t asking myself what it meant or what it was doing for me,” he added. “I just knew I liked it, and before long, it had a hold on me.”.

  • According to Kensington Palace, which announced the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal fresh documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.
  • Recent findings suggest that heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton claims, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a public event. Instead, they're the voice-over in a previously unannounced documentary about the Princess of Wales and her life since she disclosed a diagnosis of cancer in 2024.

According to Kensington Palace, which announced the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal fresh documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.

Recent findings suggest that heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer. In less than 24 hours, the princess climbed the three highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales: Ben Nevis (4,413 feet), Scafell Pike (3,209 feet), and Yr Wyddfa–Snowdon (3,559 feet). The undertaking wasn't just a personal effort, as it was also in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization that supports people living with cancer before, during, and after the disease.

The documentary will also support that organization, Kensington Palace notes, saying “All funds received through the documentary's distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and beyond cancer.” The Royal Marsden Hospital, at which Middleton received treatment, is also referenced in the film, as Middleton's brother, James, asks her “Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?”.

But while many patients participate in the bell-ringing ritual at the conclusion of treatment, Middleton states she missed out on that moment. “Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she replies. “So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James responded, suggesting her Three Peaks experience was that symbolic peal.

Sources indicate that while Prince William is no stranger to documentary work, nor are Prince Harry and wife Meghan Markle, this is Kate Middleton's first venture into the format. Perhaps to ease her into the project, Heal's Director of Photography is a face quite familiar to the Princess: Will Warr, the filmmaker behind her video announcement marking the end of her chemotherapy treatments.

It has been revealed that “Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis,” Kensington Palace indicates of Heal, a message underscored by Middleton's words in the trailer. “You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”.

In a recent development, “It’s clear we're not meant to face life’s challenges alone,” the princess says as the trailer concludes. “Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realize that there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that.".

  • Industry observers note that next month marks the second anniversary of Marvel Rivals, and to celebrate, a new Lego set is on the way that lets you build the game's unofficial mascot, Jeff the Land Shark.
  • It has been revealed that the 495-piece set captures the adorable strategist in all his glory, including his substantial eyes, toothy smile, huge tongue, and even his collar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that next month marks the second anniversary of Marvel Rivals, and to celebrate, a new Lego set is on the way that lets you build the game's unofficial mascot, Jeff the Land Shark. While we regularly see Lego Marvel sets roll out, this is the first-ever Marvel Rivals kit, and it'll go on sale starting January 1, 2027, priced at $50. GameSpot can also exclusively reveal the first images of Jeff below, showing the completed build alongside his box art. See at The Lego Store The 495-piece set captures the adorable strategist in all his glory, including his significant eyes, toothy smile, huge tongue, and even his collar. This won't be a static figure either: once fully assembled, Jeff has a movable head, legs, tail, and fins that let builders recreate his joyful trot, swimming, and battle poses. For added touches, his collar includes his signature name tag, his tongue can be removed to close his mouth, and his fin can be detached so builders can replicate Jeff's Hide-and-Seek movement ability from the game. "Jeff brings together everything players love about a breakout gaming character: an unforgettable silhouette, a personality you understand instantly, and the ability to turn any match into a story," Lego Marvel design lead Jesper C. Nielsen noted in a press release. "We wanted this Lego model to capture both sides of him, from the lovable companion fans want beside their screen to the unpredictable strategist they meet in battle." Meanwhile, Jeff and the rest of the Marvel Rivals roster are preparing to cap off an entire year of Avengers-centric events that have been building up to the game's big Avengers: Doomsday tie-in. Season 11.5 kicks off on December 11. Nightcrawler was recently added to the game, bringing mutant energy, swords, and teleportation strategies, and he'll soon be followed by Marvel's unique take on Dracula, who has spent the last few months hibernating and healing for the battles ahead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dancing With The Stars Season 35 finale is here, and it's always bittersweet for the competitors. Losing can be a bummer, but not as painful as it is for some of these celebrities to say goodbye to the pros they've been working with every day for the past couple of months. Tatyana Ali is going to miss Jan Ravnik, and her touching words to him have me in my feels.

It has been revealed that ali shared her goodbye message to Jan on Instagram ahead of the finale's premiere on the 2026 TV schedule, presumably so they can lock in on finale night and wow the judges with their last dances. If it wasn't clear throughout the season, Tatyana confirmed she loved working with her dance partner:.

As I’ve stated before, meeting you and getting to know you has been the best part of this whole thing. I am going to miss seeing you every day. I’m going to miss singing with you. I’m going to miss laughing with you. You are one of the most exceptional people I have ever met in my life.

Industry observers note that the duo is in the midst of a Cinderella run, in which the fan vote helped propel them to the semifinals and the finale after Jenna Dewan and Harry Shum Jr. were voted out instead. She's now in a position to be a Mirrorball winner who had the lowest Week 1 score of all time, assuming she can get the votes over some other fan favorites.

Recent findings suggest that it's a credit not just to her improvement as a dancer, but to Jan Ravnik, who came under fire from former pros last season. Maks Chmerkovskiy took shots at Ravnik for not being a professionally trained ballroom dancer, and said he was unworthy of being a performer on the show. This finale appearance disproved that, and if Ravnik needed any more reminders of that, Tatyana Ali had more words of encouragement:.

Your drive, your hard work, your passion, and your brilliance are astounding. You inspire me. You’re my friend. For life. I just adore you. And there’s nothing I could say in this video that I that you don’t actually know. You have a light that is so bright, and everything you’ve got: The way you carry yourself, the way you handle situations, exactly as it should be. Don’t ever accept any less than you deserve because you deserve it all. You’re a star. In the realest. The realest, most soulful version of that word. I love you.

It's been a long road for both of them, and they've had doubters along the way who questioned whether they'd rise to the occasion. I would reckon those doubters are gone ahead of the finale and ready to see what they have planned for the massive night.

The duo are planning to perform a salsa to “Jamaican (Bam Bam)” by HUGEL & SOLTO, a freestyle dance set to Cab Calloway's "Minnie the Moocher," and will close with Judy Garland's "Somewhere Over the Rainbow." That's quite a lineup, and I'm especially excited to see how she and Jan tackle Calloway's classic tune.

Win or lose, Jan and Tatyana's journey has potentially changed the dancing series forever. Sharna Burgess and others are up in arms about the voting situation and wondering if fans have too much power in dictating who should and shouldn't be in the finals. I'll be interested to see how this conversation evolves in the off-season, and if changes are on the way for fan voting.

#177309. We Played 'Magic: the Gathering’s Most Unhinged Set of All Time and It Was Pure Chaos

We Played 'Magic: the Gathering’s Most Unhinged Set of All Time and It Was Pure Chaos

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, Polygon had the opportunity to open some of the weirdest Magic: The Gathering packs in the game’s 33-year history.
  • It has been revealed that “My goal was that each card would be charming,” principal designer Gavin Verhey told Polygon at MagicCon.
  • Sources indicate that the charm is absolutely there, and it makes it extremely difficult to pass on some of the set’s weirder cards when they don’t fit your deck’s strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, Polygon had the opportunity to open some of the weirdest Magic: The Gathering packs in the game’s 33-year history. Mystery Booster Commander Edition brings the chaos of Mystery Booster to the multiplayer Commander format, and it's exclusively available online through limited Festival in a Box releases or at events like MagicCon. Each pack mixes reprints from across Magic history with experimental playtest cards and 60 latest "Rulebreaker" cards that literally break Commander’s typical deck-building restrictions in strange ways by transforming how other cards work. In some cases, they let you add additional colors to your deck. There's also a sorcery that can be your Commander.

It has been revealed that “My goal was that each card would be charming,” principal designer Gavin Verhey told Polygon at MagicCon. “You should see it and you’d be like, ‘That’s crazy. I’ve never seen that before.’ Or, ‘That’s so funny, made me smile.’”.

Sources indicate that the charm is absolutely there, and it makes it extremely difficult to pass on some of the set’s weirder cards when they don’t fit your deck’s strategy. Polygon participated in a Mystery Booster Commander Edition draft event. Despite pulling from the same pool of cards, Corey Plante and Jake Kleinman walked away with totally different decks: Corey built a rabbit army around Cadira, Caller of the Small. Jake went for flying creatures and graveyard tricks. Here’s how it went for both of us.

Each player is assigned to a pod of eight and given three packs of Mystery Booster Commander Edition, each containing 20 cards. Although each pod has eight players, it's a "Pick 2" draft, meaning you grab two cards out of each pack you see, which speeds up the process and makes it easier to develop your strategy early on.

Industry observers note that jake: I participated in an Unknown event at MagicCon last year, so I was somewhat prepared for this, but it's always overwhelming opening a pack full of chaotic cards from across Magic history and beyond. My first pack had a new legendary creature that was all about Phyrexian synergy, which seemed fun in theory but useless in a draft. Plus I'm not really a Phyrexia guy, so I passed it. I did grab a playtest card called Magus of the Chains as part of an early blue-black graveyard strategy I started developing with lots of discard and mill cards. I also took every flyer in those colors I saw because evasion is extra-powerful in a chaos draft like this one.

Sources indicate that corey: When it came to opening each of the three packs, my primary goal was to claim​​​​​​​ the coolest, rarest cards I could find. I made a few mistakes in prioritizing​​​​​​​ the various playtest cards I came across for their novelty​​​​​​​. Abbot of the Sacred Meeple caught my eye as an unhinged hodgepodge of board game mechanics. But it’s worth almost nothing and is basically unplayable. Massive mistake. Too many of my pulls were defined by grabbing what looked cool.

Jake: I was similarly tempted by a weird little white playtest card called Tax Taker that's not even worth the cardboard it's printed on. At one point, midway through the draft, I also picked up a few powerful white cards and considered pivoting​​​​​​​ to black-white lifegain. My real hope was that I'd find a blue-white-black commander that let me combine all three, but that never happened and I wasn't able to grab much white interaction. In the end I felt like I had a pretty powerful pile of blue and black cards with plenty of card draw and removal to overwhelm my opponents. My two favorite draft picks were Visara the Dreadful and a totally bonkers playtest card called Lich's Duel Mastery (neither of which I ever actually got to play).

Corey: I managed to grab some great, weird cards too! Starting Town NPC is a green creature that gives every creature in your hand a two-cost adventure called Fetch Herbs that gains you two life. And, for some reason, every creature you cast from exile enters with an extra +1/+1 counter on it. My two favorite picks out of the whole draft were Norwood Priestess and Ashaya’s Enduring Bond. For only four mana, Norwood Priestess can tap to put a green creature from your hand onto the battlefield. It feels like the kind of card that can slot into any green deck.

Recent findings suggest that I pulled Ashaya’s Enduring Bond in my third pack. It’s the somewhat infamous new Gruul (red-green) sorcery that can be your Commander. It discovers X where X is the amount of mana spent to cast it, so it actually gets some use out of Commander tax. I pocketed this one so I could build it ASAP.

Jake: I also grabbed one fun card later on purely so I could build a deck around it in the future. Feroz, Ulgrotha's Warden is a Planeswalker that lets you cheat out your own creatures (one of my favorite Commander mechanics) while imposing an extra two-mana tax on everyone else's creature spells. I can't wait to make the rest of my pod suffer.

With the drafting finished, each player had 45 minutes to build a 60 card Commander deck. You could pick one multicolored Commander and grab any two monocolor Commanders​​​​​​​ as if they had Partner. Or, if you somehow only had a Commander in one color, you could just pick a second color for your deck.

Jake: I need to make a confession: I totally misunderstood the rules. In my defense, the event was complicated and could have been better explained by the staff. Then again, nobody else seemed to have any concerns following the rules, so maybe I'm just dumb.

Industry observers note that the Companion app that Wizards uses to organize these ticketed events stated to build a 40-card deck, so that's what I did. I had also assumed, based on the Unknown event I did last year, that we'd be playing one-on-one matches. Instead, this was four-player Commander with 60-card decks. So my deck was totally out of place. Weirdly, this worked to my benefit in game 1 and doomed me in game 2, but more on that later.

Corey: Yeah, I'm not sure where you got that idea, but I'm glad it worked out.

I pulled Norwood Priestess and Emiel the Blessed early, which pushed me toward Selesnya (green-white is a safe space for me). I wound up taking almost all of the green and white cards that came across my playmat.​​​​​​​ Eventually, I breathed a sigh of relief when I picked up Cadira, Caller of the Small. She’s a 3/3 orc that costs three mana (one colorless, one green, and one white)​​​​​​​ with trample that, whenever she deals combat damage to a player, generates a 1/1 white rabbit creature token for each token you control. They quite literally… multiply like rabbits.

In a recent development, I stumbled upon a strong-ish interaction between Emiel the Blessed and Valorous Steed. Emiel can blink your creatures (not good for tokens, actually), but he also lets you pay one green or white mana whenever one of your creatures enters to give them a +1/+1 counter, or two such counters if that creature is a unicorn. Valorous Steed is indeed a unicorn (yay!) that creates a 2/2 white knight when it enters, so in one game I got a strong loop going where Emiel kept blinking Valorous Steed to generate more tokens.

Industry observers note that I also had the flavorful Champions of the Hareish, which depicts an angry-looking rabbit with a carrot sword. He establishes a “Buddy list” where you put a +1/+1 counter on Champion whenever a creature on his Buddy list enters. Creatures entering that don’t qualify allow you to add one of their creature types to the list. The final key piece for me was Intangible Vines.

Jake: My own confusion aside, the deck I built was actually pretty cool. I didn't wind up using any of the weird playtest or Rulebreaker cards as my Commander, though a few made it into the deck. Instead, I paired up Grazilaxx, Illithid Scholar and Rankle, Master of Pranks.

Grazilaxx could get me lots of card draw (especially with all my flyers), while Rankle would let me control the tempo of the game and fill up my graveyard so I could reanimate my scariest creatures later on and swing in for the win. I figured Magus of the Chains would also help with the graveyard strategy, although that card ended up being more trouble than it was worth.

In a recent development, the only thing left to do is shuffle up and play. The Companion app gave everyone a new seating assignment to create a series of four-person groups. (Some people were missing, but the staff worked promptly to make sure everyone had a full pod.) After game 1 the same thing happened again for game 2.

Corey: My first match ended in a stalemate. Everybody mostly built up their board states, but nobody had a powerful win condition.​​​​​​​ This went on until the judges forced us to move on. I was pleased to see that my deck was working as intended here, especially since I was targeted by the table several times.

I was able to play a ramp piece in the early rounds and cast Norwood Priestess on turn three​​​​​​​. The guy to my left literally noted aloud, “Oh that’s gotta go.” Then he destroyed it with some kind of removal. I also got my Commander in ASAP and started building up a modest token army, so she doubled my tokens every time she dealt combat damage to a player. I basically just attacked whoever I could connect with and apologized for it, saying I was just trying to build up some tokens. Those tokens also proved really useful for chump blocking.

Recent findings suggest that what my deck really needed, however, was more token generation and ways to buff and protect Cadira so she could reliably connect in the late-game. My deck kind of stalled over time, but I had enough tokens by then that nobody could touch me. Eventually, the clock just ran out.

Recent findings suggest that jake: My first game went surprisingly well. The archenemy at the table very quickly became a guy who'd built a mono-green deck​​​​​​​ with a pair of squirrels as his partnered Commanders. Meatsqueak, Hoard Lord generated food tokens whenever another creature died, which then buffed all his squirrels, while Toski​​​​​​​, Bearer of Secrets was an indestructible card-draw engine. Toski got even scarier when he played Questing Cosplayer, a playtest card that gives another creature all the abilities of Questing Beast (vigilance, deathtouch, haste, and some other scary stuff). Another guy at my table made a land-focused deck built around Grizzlegom​​​​​​​, Hurloon Hero, which gets lots of cool benefits based on how many lands you have out. It was a cool idea, but he put way too many lands in his deck and got mana flooded.

The squirrel army overwhelmed the rest of us pretty rapidly, and the two other players were quickly knocked out. I thought I was done for​​​​​​​ too, but thanks to my army of flyers and a bunch of removal spells, I was able to clear a path and sneak in for the win. My MVP for that first match was Sigil of Sleep, a one-mana Aura from 1999 that let me bounce his creatures, providing a way to deal with that indestructible Toski​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that corey: In my second match, I fared even better, coming in at a close second thanks entirely to Intangible Vines hitting the battlefield early. It’s a silly little two-mana white enchantment​​​​​​​ playtest card that’s wickedly powerful for Cadira: All creatures are tokens. That wound up pretty absurd since I also had plenty of smaller nontoken creatures that suddenly counted as tokens. This allowed me to protect myself long enough for the significant threat at the table to take out the other two players before she set her sights on me. By this point, Champions of the Hareish (getting rabbit on his buddy list and churning out rabbit tokens is OP here) had gotten big enough that I was becoming the threat. If I’m being perfectly honest, I didn’t stand a chance since she had several big creatures with interesting abilities and some weird Planeswalker that unleashed its ultimate.

Jake: My second game was a ton of fun. This time the problem promptly became another player who built a deck around Nephilim Epochal, a Rulebreaker card designed to finally give the fan-favorite creature type Nephilim​​​​​​​ its own Commander. Nephilim Epochal lets you search for another Nephilim when it enters, and then each one buffs the rest​​​​​​​ while making it so they can't be blocked by monocolor creatures (which is most other creatures in Mystery Booster Commander). The deck didn't actually have any other Nephilim in it, but it did have a few changeling creatures, which accomplished the same thing. The guy piloting the deck was also a competitive-level player, and he quickly outmaneuvered the rest of us.

It has been revealed that I actually might have had a shot at winning again, but my illegal 40-card deck wound up being my demise. The game went long and at one point, I pulled off a fun combat trick by flashing out Illusory Ambusher, a blue creature that lets you draw cards based on how much damage it takes. I drew 12 cards, inadvertently leaving just five left in my library. After that, the Nephilim focused on taking out the other two players, while I slowly decked myself to death.

According to recent reports, corey: For Magic fans who love the sheer randomness of the draft experience, you’d be hard-pressed to find something more exciting than Mystery Booster Commander Edition. So many of the cards just feel weird and delightful, the playtest cards in particular.

According to recent reports, jake: I totally agree, one of my favorite parts of the whole experience was just reading all the bizarre and hilarious cards that got passed my way during the draft. One upcoming Commander card I haven't even mentioned yet is a blue creature card featuring a pair of bug-men called Sash and Wasitcast, Unmen​​​​​​​ that lets everyone at the table manifest the top card of their library into a 2/2 face-down creature and then rewards them for attacking each other. I also just loved seeing which cool old cards were in these packs, some of which made me feel nostalgic for my time playing Magic in the early 2000s.

Industry observers note that the event itself was also a blast. Everyone I met was super-cool and down to just have fun — even when they found out my deck was technically illegal. I do wish the entire thing had been organized slightly better, but considering this was the first official Mystery Booster Commander, I assume Wizards will work out the kinks of the live event soon.

Corey: My one substantial regret is that I didn’t choose one of the newly introduced Mystery Booster Commander Edition cards as my Commander rather than Cadira, who’s originally from 2022’s Battle for Baldur’s Gate. I also pulled a Feroz, Ulgrotha’s Warden! But he came too late to matter to me since I had absolutely zero blue cards.​​​​​​​ I like how his vibe is about oppressing the rest of the table. He was enticing enough to grab, and I might wind up building a deck around him.​​​​​​​.

Jake: I also pulled a Feroz and thought about building it, but it was too late in the draft. Also, that card is mean!

Recent findings suggest that corey: I’m genuinely excited about pulling Ashaya’s Enduring Bond and have already started building a deck with it as my Commander. The first-ever sorcery Commander? Talk about a fun challenge. I’m thinking of emphasizing abilities with inherent randomness to them, more Discover cards, and effects that copy sorceries.

Jake: I've already put a few cards I picked up from the event into my various Commander decks, and I may still build Feroz to play against my friends at home when I'm feeling extra spicy.

One Element Of Avengers: Doomsday Has Me Excited Above All Else

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, "Avengers: Doomsday" is going to be one of the biggest movies of the year, if not ever, that much is certain.
  • Indeed, the worst thing one can say about this film right now is that it looks exactly like what you would expect.
  • In a recent development, that being said, there is one notable reason to be excited about "Doomsday." No, not the X-Men (though their inclusion is certainly cool) or the return of Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, "Avengers: Doomsday" is going to be one of the biggest movies of the year, if not ever, that much is certain. But so far, the movie's marketing has been quite, well, underwhelming. We already had one "Avengers" film (well, two) that relied entirely on gathering lots of known Marvel Cinematic Universe characters on screen at the same time. To do that again feels less special, as exciting as it is to see Cyclops (James Marsden) leading the X-Men into battle here.

Indeed, the worst thing one can say about this film right now is that it looks exactly like what you would expect. It's massive, sure, but it doesn't feel surprising in any way. Marvel announcing Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom in the movie felt desperate, too, as it was obviously the studio's way of trying to win back the fans who'd been disappointed by the MCU's post-"Avengers: Endgame" output. "Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day" aside, Marvel's no longer the reliable hit machine that it once was.

In a recent development, that being said, there is one notable reason to be excited about "Doomsday." No, not the X-Men (though their inclusion is certainly cool) or the return of Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen). Instead, it's the fact that "Doomsday" is technically a direct sequel to "Thunderbolts*," itself by far the best non-"Spider-Man" MCU movie since "Endgame." More specifically, it picks up where that film left off, with the titular team (also known as the West Chesapeake Valley Thunderbolts sponsored by Shane's Tire Organization) now officially being known as the New Avengers.

Sure enough, the final "Doomsday" trailer features a few shots of the Newly introduced Avengers amidst all the new footage of Chris Evans as Steve Rogers, and it's enough to finally get me hyped for this film.

For the most part, the visuals in the final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer look horrendously muted and dull, save for a single brief shot of David Harbour's Alexei Shostakov dressed in a horrendous New Avengers tracksuit staring in awe as Shang-Chi (Simu Liu) arrives at Avengers Tower. Immediately, the image both brightens the trailer and reminds you that as serious as "Doomsday" may be (with the old Avengers looking more tired and beaten up than ever), the New Avengers bring a whole different vibe to the table. After all, they're silly, not great at teamwork, and don't consider themselves to be gods. Instead, they talk through their psychological complications and even hug it out like something out of "Neon Genesis Evangelion.".

As the final trailer makes clear, "Doomsday" is all about different superhero groups coming together. You have the remnants of the original Avengers team, the X-Men, the Thunderbolts/New Avengers, and the Fantastic Four — plus the stragglers from various MCU titles that we collectively kind of forgot about. Each brings a different dynamic to the film, with the New Avengers specifically being a group of loser superheroes and criminals not unlike the Guardians of the Galaxy ... with the major difference being that the former have to save themselves before they can save anyone else. It's why "Thunderbolts*" makes for such an emotional gut punch, especially when its leads come together as a team, and the idea of seeing them interact with the MCU at large does more to make "Doomsday" feel interesting than any number of cameos could.

"Avengers: Doomsday" will see the Newly introduced Avengers suit up alongside their companions when it hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

In GTA 6, you can teach one loud-mouthed hunter that Lucia (or Jason) is the deadliest game, as this secret mission will require cunning and sharp shooting to survive. It's Hard Target meets SAW, and the victor gets a pretty sizable stack of cash. Here's how you can be the most elusive of quarry. Go to Hyde Island Located north of Lummox County and the Moreau River, Hyde Island is where you can start this mission. All you have to do is land on the island, and after a few steps, a dart will hit you and knock you out. Listen to your captor's speech Now for the boring part. You'll wake up inside of a shipping container, with a fashionable explosive necklace locked in place. Once your captor finishes his rant, the game begins, and you'll want to move. Run to the tent directly in front of you You'll have 10 seconds to reach a tent in front of you, where you'll find a gun and a paltry two rounds for the sidearm. After the count is up, a hunter on a quad bike will show up, and he'll be gunning for you. To make things worse, he also has a dog with him that'll track you throughout the island. Don't engage him; he's heavily armored, and two bullets aren't nearly enough to stop him—besides, you'll need those rounds for his dog, Caesar. Sorry, animal lovers. Search for more outposts You can find more ammo, adrenaline, and a shotgun at nearby outposts. Each one is lit up, so be fast, be sneaky, and try not to get caught. The hunter is going to be tracking you constantly, even without his dog, and he has a sniper rifle that can take you out in just a few shots if he catches you. Prepare for a showdown Get as much ammo as you can, and choose your spot for the last stand. The hunter's dog will be a pest, so deal with it first. It's easy to spot, with a red light on its collar. Trees also make for good cover against the hunter, so once he's in range, start nailing him with shots to critical areas. Once he stumbles, unload a few shotgun rounds and finish him off. Collect your rewards Once the hunter is down, search his body for the Island-Poacher FF-50 sniper rifle and ammo for it. Head west to the boathouse to reclaim your personal items and $15,000 in cash. Not a bad haul for a deadly night's work. What happens if you fail? If the hunter does kill you, you'll lose a chunk of cash and wake up near one of your safehouses. The good news is you can retry the mission by heading back to Hyde Island, but the bad news is you'll have to listen to the hunter's speech again. Breaking: Steven Spielberg's Next Movie Is A Star-Studded Western Written By Another Legendary Filmmaker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, Steven Spielberg confirmed that his next movie as a director would be a Western.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, Deadline has revealed that the movie, an adaptation of Kevin Barry's novel "The Heart in Winter," will star Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley and Mark Rylance, and it's hard not to be elated.
  • No one's more enthused than Spielberg, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Steven Spielberg confirmed that his next movie as a director would be a Western. This will be his first official crack at the most American of film genres, and that's reason enough for cinephiles to get excited.

Recent findings suggest that now, Deadline has revealed that the movie, an adaptation of Kevin Barry's novel "The Heart in Winter," will star Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley and Mark Rylance, and it's hard not to be elated. Factor in that Barry's book is being adapted into a script by Oscar-winner Paul Thomas Anderson, and there isn't a word in the English language to capture the utter exhilaration movie fans are feeling at this moment.

No one's more enthused than Spielberg, though. As he told Deadline:.

"It's really the excitement for me to get to work together with my dear friend and colleague Paul Thomas Anderson on a genre, but more particularly, the genre notwithstanding, a story that quite promptly became close to both our hearts and we felt that we could do as a team.".

Sources indicate that murphy will play Tom Rourke, an Irish immigrant eking out a living in Butte, Montana. He works as an assistant to a photographer and supplements his income by penning letters for illiterate miners seeking potential brides from the east. He needs the extra scratch, too, due to his alcohol and opium addictions. Tom is spiritually adrift until mail-order bride Polly Gillespie arrives in Butte. They fall fast in love, steal some money, and set what proves to be an eventful course for San Francisco.

Overall, Barry's book has echoes of Spielberg's theatrical directing debut on "The Sugarland Express," as it's about two lovers on the run from the law. But this being the late 1800s, and the pair being challenged as horseback riders, their journey isn't quite as fast-paced.

Industry observers note that kevin Barry's "The Heart in Winter" has been described as "a tragedy written as farce" (per The Guardian). Critics found it hilarious and wildly entertaining, and after his excellent work on "One Battle After Another," I can't imagine anyone more suited to a tale about a character with an opium addiction stealing a mail-order bride and heading to San Francisco than Paul Thomas Anderson. But what's most interesting to me is that this will be the first time Anderson has written an entire script for another filmmaker. He previously did rewrites on the Apple-backed "Killers of the Flower Moon" and "Napoleon" for Martin Scorsese and Ridley Scott, but he's the primary writer here.

Recent findings suggest that as for Steven Spielberg, no filmmaker alive knows more about Western conventions than him, and you can rest assured he will aggressively avoid cliché. I mean, he'll be sure to keep the horizon line out of the middle of the frame, lest John Ford's eye-patched ghost haunt him for the rest of his days, but don't expect traditional Western violence of the shootout and saloon brawl variety. I haven't read the book yet, so I don't know if such scenes exist in Barry's novel, but if they do, they'll look unlike any shootout or brawl you've ever seen.

Sources indicate that what's curious is that Spielberg went with the Montana-set "The Heart in Winter," given that he'd been talking about making a Texas Western. Texas is not Montana by a long shot, which makes me wonder if he might change the location of Barry's novel. I doubt he'd do that, so now he's cheesed off everyone in Texas who was hoping he'd make their state look sensationally epic. He'll have to make it up to them somehow.

“H3 Podcast” host Hila Klein is stepping away from the popular podcast after filing for divorce from husband cohost Ethan Klein, whom she publicly accused of cheating on her.

“I will miss you all more than I can put into words. Thank you for all the love and support over the years,” she concluded.

Hila accused Ethan, 41, of having a six-month affair in a shocking Instagram post on October 23, which led to the “H3 Podcast” going on an “indefinite hiatus.”.

At the time, Ethan mentioned he was “working with Hila to urgently remove my ownership and financial stakes in any podcasts” and other joint ventures created through their production firm, h3h3 Productions.

On November 13, Hila and some of the “H3 Podcast” crew shared a photo on Instagram from a team meeting, suggesting that they were planning to get a new version of the podcast — sans Ethan — back on track.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the biggest YA franchise in the game is back on top.
  • Industry observers note that directed once again by franchise shepherd Franchise Lawrence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" opened to a massive $120 million domestically.
  • Recent findings suggest that "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" looked like it was going to be a bigger hit than people realized, which proved true.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the biggest YA franchise in the game is back on top. Lionsgate released "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters over the weekend, and to say that the franchise's latest prequel film did well would be an understatement. This movie is already a huge hit for the studio and has brought the property back to its former, $100 million-plus opening weekend glory.

Industry observers note that directed once again by franchise shepherd Franchise Lawrence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" opened to a massive $120 million domestically. Internationally, the prequel bowed to $105 million, giving it a gigantic $225 million global start. It's now Lionsgate's biggest opening of 2026 overall. "Michael" ruled the box office with a $218 million global opening earlier this year, but "Sunrise on the Reaping" even managed to best the King of Pop. Now, whether or not this movie gets to the $1 billion mark like "Michael" in the long run is another question entirely, but it illustrates just how big this opening was.

Recent findings suggest that "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" looked like it was going to be a bigger hit than people realized, which proved true. It arrived right in line with bullish estimates, which climbed through the roof in the weeks leading up to its arrival. As such, it's now poised to become one of the biggest hits of the year overall.

Industry observers note that so, what went right here? How did Lionsgate manage to make such a substantial bet and have it pay off so spectacularly well? We're going to look at the biggest reasons why "Sunrise on the Reaping" ruled the box office on its opening weekend. Let's get into it.

In a recent development, the biggest thing that this movie had going for it is that it wasn't just another "Hunger Games" film or a prequel for the sake of a prequel. It was a story that hardcore fans of the franchise have been waiting a long time to see. Specifically, one involving the famed games where Haymitch Abernathy, the character played by Woody Harrelson in the previous "Hunger Games" movies, won.

According to recent reports, "Sunrise on the Reaping" pits a young Haymitch (Joseph Zada) against President Snow (Ralph Fiennes), to put it in the simplest possible terms. "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins wrote the book the movie is based on and, rather crucially, the novel was received very well by fans. And by most accounts, Francis Lawrence, with the help of Collins, delivered one heck of an adaptation. All of this to say, the movie promised something fans had been wanting for a hot minute and delivered the goods when the time arrived.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, Jennifer Lawrence also broke her silence on her "Hunger Games" return in "Sunrise on the Reaping" ahead of the film's release, assuring that this movie was getting the original gang back together. That undoubtedly helped get more casual viewers on board who perhaps were only more interested in the original set of "Hunger Games" films. Overall, Lionsgate made the most of what this story had to offer, turning it into not just another movie but a true event within one of the biggest franchises of the last 20 years — one that demanded to be seen on the biggest screen available as soon as possible.

According to recent reports, this is the kind of movie that hardcore fans were always going to be in the bag for, no matter what. That having been remarked, positive word of mouth never hurts. And while critics were, more or less, on this film's side, it worked like gangbusters for the intended audience. In the case of a long-running, beloved franchise, that is always more important.

According to recent reports, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" holds a decent 69% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, as of this writing. However, it carries a stellar 94% audience score, which is near-universal praise from actual ticket buying fans. It also earned a damn good A- CinemaScore, which means word of mouth is going to be great in the weeks to come. Even though "Focker In-Law" could be a rare comedy box office hit over Thanksgiving, with Disney's "Hexed" opening as well, there should be more than enough room for this prequel to have a stellar second frame over the holiday weekend.

In a recent development, /Film's Nina Starner wrote that "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is a prequel that "delivers" in her review. Certain critics may have been a bit softer on it, but enough of them liked it to prevent the needle from being pushed down. More importantly, fans are loudly proclaiming their love for this film, which is going to do way more to motivate viewers who might have been on the fence to check it out in the coming weeks.

Lionsgate doesn't always have a lot of success when playing in the massive-budget realm, but this franchise has generally been the exception to that rule. All of "The Hunger Games" movies have been hits at the box office and, save for the very first film, they've all benefited from November releases. This ended up being an "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" situation. All the same, the studio wisely picked the perfect spot on the calendar for this prequel to thrive.

Industry observers note that word of mouth can't be predicted, but getting in on an otherwise fairly dead pre-Thanksgiving weekend was very wise. "Sunrise on the Reaping" got one totally unimpeded weekend to do its thing and will now benefit from a long, five-day holiday weekend over Thanksgiving. It's basically going to have nine full days of ruling the box office before taking any sort of meaningful hit.

Sources indicate that "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2" ruled the box office in 2015, also in November, delivering a $102 million opening weekend en route to $653 million worldwide. This latest prequel had an even bigger opening, meaning it could eclipse that global figure when all's said and done. Not to get too ahead of ourselves, but it may wind up closer to "Mockingjay — Part 1" ($766 million worldwide), if all goes well.

Wherever the chips fall at the end of the day, it's going to be in large part because this movie wasn't competing with a slew of other blockbusters in the midst of a crowded summer. This is the big cinematic event of choice right now and will be for at least a couple of weeks.

It certainly doesn't happen too often, but if a franchise gets it right, the breakout sequel effect can come into play. One of the best examples in history is "The Dark Knight." While Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" was actually a bit of a box office disappointment, pulling in a so-so $373 million worldwide, "The Dark Knight" was simply too good to be ignored and made $1 billion at a time when movies rarely ever hit that milestone.

Other examples include "John Wick"/"John Wick: Chapter 2" and "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse/"Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse." A very good first movie happened, people caught up with it after the fact, and that resulted in a much larger audience for the sequel. That brings us back to "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Despite being the sixth entry in this property, it benefited like a breakout sequel would have.

It has been revealed that 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" was a surprise victor at the Thanksgiving box office, ultimately pulling in nearly $350 million worldwide on a $100 million budget. A solid result, but it wasn't nearly what the first four movies in the "Hunger Games" franchise made. However, audiences and fans caught up with it and ended up enjoying it. So, after an eight-year break, Lionsgate kind of used that first prequel to prime the pumps on this franchise, even if that wasn't the intention.

Industry observers note that the end result is that "Songbirds & Snakes" teed up the ball for "Sunrise on the Reaping," paving the way for the film to enjoy a much, much bigger opening than its predecessor. It's not a traditional breakout sequel, but it's a breakout sequel to a prequel people enjoyed.

Perhaps the most key factor when it comes to playing Monday morning quarterback with the success of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" has to do with how massive franchises are typically handled in Hollywood these days. Spin-offs. TV indicates. Animated entries. Theme parks. More merchandise than anyone knows what to do with.

Sources indicate that that never really happened with "The Hunger Games." That's in no small part because author Suzanne Collins has a lot of say over how those affairs are handled. Even so, there was an eight-year gap between movies by the time "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" came around and another three years before "Sunrise on the Reaping." Neither Lionsgate nor Collins ever allowed for overexposure to get the best of this franchise. That allowed for people to be legitimately excited about this film.

Industry observers note that former Disney CEO Bob Iger even admitted that multiple Marvel demonstrates and Pixar movies going to streaming hurt those brands. The Marvel Cinematic Universe is mighty, but even fans grew tired of that. Likewise, Pixar is as good as cinema gets, yet audiences learned that they could just watch those movies at home. Meanwhile, Lionsgate has maintained discipline with the "Hunger Games" films and ensured that they remained cinematic events. Short-term gains and overdoing it would have potentially kneecapped what is now one of the studio's biggest hits in years. Hollywood could stand to learn a thing or two from this sort of execution.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a balmy late-September day in London, and Dolly Alderton is explaining to a befuddled Emma Frost what “iPhone face” means. Frost has never heard the term; her fellow showrunners Alderton and Zoe Kazan have.

According to recent reports, “You know [how] you look at some faces, like Rosamund Pike’s face—it looks like it’s never seen an iPhone? It looks like it’s seen a lute and a loom,” Alderton tells Frost.

In a recent development, “So actors who look like they’re comfortable in a period show, rather than feeling inherently modern,” says Frost, as understanding dawns. Alderton and Kazan affirm her: “Yes, yes. Exactly.”.

Now that Frost gets it, she turns back to the group’s Zoom screen. “Sorry, what was the question?”.

Kazan began her career as an actor, while Alderton started out as a dating columnist and Frost was a sculptor and painter. Now all three are overseeing vastly different but comparable Netflix period dramas, each based on a classic work of literature: East of Eden (Kazan’s, which was released October 1), Pride and Prejudice (Alderton’s, out December 3), and The Age of Innocence (Frost’s, coming February 18). They’ve gathered in a London conference room at Netflix headquarters for a roundtable discussion about art, work, the unique experience of adapting a beloved book—and, apparently, iPhone face.

Sources indicate that though this is the first time the trio has met face to face, their conversation flows so easily and naturally that interrupting them with questions sometimes feels impolite. Early on, I note that all three of these novels are, on some level, about unconventional women. Alderton, Frost, and Kazan pause for a moment, considering this Lit 101–level observation.

“That’s true, I think,” agrees Frost.

And then they’re off to more interesting topics.

Vanity Fair: Have you read each other’s books?

Dolly Alderton: No, I haven’t read either of your books.

Alderton: Did you read them at school, or did you read them for fun?

According to recent reports, frost: Pride and Prejudice I read when I was a teenager at school. East of Eden I read first about 15 years ago, I think.

Alderton: So Em already wins the round table.

Frost: And for both of you, was it the thing you most wanted to adapt?

Alderton: I would never have dared to dream to. I was so overwhelmed when I was first approached. I just thought, it’s such a precious IP. It would be way too much, and I wouldn’t be the right person. But then when I was asked to pitch for it, at that point there’s no other answer but yes.

Kazan: First of all, was it the Austen you liked the most?

According to recent reports, alderton: Yes. It was the one that I’ve always loved because of Lizzie Bennet. I’ve always been obsessed with Lizzie Bennet. She was my hook. But how about you two? Did you ever dream of adapting these texts?

Frost: I was at a place where I mentioned, “I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period.” Netflix asked me to do The Age of Innocence, and it was, I think at that moment, the one book that made me just go, “Oh my God, okay, let me go back and revisit it.” Because I know I love it, but you have to know what the reason is [to adapt it again]. And the thing that totally blew me away on a reread was how relevant and resonant it is. It is about the freedom of the individual versus the conformity of the pack. It has so many themes in it that are really resonant with social media, the bullying of the group.

Recent findings suggest that alderton [turning to Kazan]: Tackling Cathy, how did you begin? What was your way into that?

Sources indicate that kazan: I think of adaptation as an advanced form of reading. For me, everything I’ve ever written has come from a feeling of “I have to write this specific thing.” When I was 15 and I read the book for the first time, I felt like it literally grabbed me by the throat and wouldn’t let go. And then I just kept coming back to it. And specifically her character, I felt like I had never read anyone like that before or since.

[to Alderton] The BBC’s Pride and Prejudice—is that the one that you—.

Alderton: No, that wasn’t my Pride and Prejudice.

Sources indicate that alderton: Yeah, the Joe Wright one was the one that I was more familiar with. But I’m so interested in what you were saying about getting to know Cathy. I was kind of nervous about doing press for a book that’s so beloved, and I’m finding it’s actually been really easy so far because I just know the people so well. So much of it has been basically like, putting Mr. Darcy and Elizabeth, all the Bennet family and Bingley through therapy. That psychological interrogation of these very well-known characters has been the thing I’ve just really, really enjoyed.

Frost: Have you both had to change points of view from the novel? Do you feel like you’ve had to make a specific choice about who you are foregrounding? I think I know the answer in your case, Zoe.

Kazan: No, I actually don’t. I’m aware that the way that I read a book is different from the way that anyone else reads that book. When I read East of Eden, I feel like I see Steinbeck becoming enthralled by this character, finding her as curious as I do. I think he starts out a real place of judgment and over the course of the book, really moves towards love and understanding.

According to recent reports, alderton: I have a similar thing in that for the majority of the book, one of the lead characters is completely unknowable. Not just to Elizabeth, but to the audience as well. So you have to honor that to make it satisfying. That’s kind of frustrating when you’re writing a romantic lead for the first three and a half episodes. None of us, least of all the female protagonist, can see who he is, and we misunderstand him. There is no other option I think than staying with Lizzie.

Frost: It’s very different because the book is entirely from Newland’s point of view. The thing that I wanted to do, and that Netflix were really excited for me to do, was to open it up to find out who the women were.

I think in the book—rightly, because she’s writing from Newland’s point of view—both May and Ellen are sort of constructed as his other. One is the thing to be won, and one is effectively the antagonist. It’s so interesting, because it’s a female author—and [Wharton herself], she’s part Newland. That's who she was growing up. And she’s part Ellen, this woman who now lives in Europe, who's become really cosmopolitan, who is even based on her own love triangle.

The impossibility of that love triangle is the thing I want people to feel. It’s not like one of them is wrong. They're all just feeling what they’re feeling.

Alderton: And how do you feel about bringing that new perspective and analysis to the story? For a book that's so beloved, did you feel excited by that? Or did you feel kind of daunted by it?

It has been revealed that frost: Maybe I should have felt daunted. I didn’t. I think Edith Wharton—it’s so based on her own personal experience of when she was 45, she had this sexual awakening. She was in this really dull marriage. She’d never had an orgasm. When she was 45, she fell in love with this journalist and had this passionate affair.

Frost: She had this big affair, then he ghosted her. But she was trying to make sense of it through this love triangle. When she wrote it, she couldn’t possibly have written herself as a female character in the center of an illicit love triangle because we were still in time of censorship, and she was being published in a very commercial magazine. So she had to make herself the man that has more agency.

Sources indicate that alderton: With any script, you have a relationship with the characters. But with what we are doing, you have this relationship with the writer.

Kazan to Alderton: You’re also a novelist. How are you thinking about bisecting yourself—using both parts of your brain, the novelist part and the dramatist part?

According to recent reports, alderton: I’ll tell you how I felt about it. I’ve written two novels, both of which I’ve tried to adapt. I found it really, really hard. I found adapting Pride and Prejudice incredibly effortless. When I went from Pride and Prejudice to my novel, I was like, "Why is this so much harder? I hate this novelist. Jane Austen is so much easier.".

What amazed me is just, it’s like she wrote it to be adapted. It’s like her agent had noted to her, “I know you’re going to write this novel about this family of five women, but remember, we could get a great movie deal off the back of it. So try and make it as adaptable as possible.” It has literally been written for TV in this totally perfect six-part structure. I just wish she was around to have written screenplays.

Kazan: This is how I feel about Tolstoy too. When I read War and Peace, I’m like, “Oh, he’s seeing it as if it’s a movie.” It’s very strange to read that so far ahead of the technology to make that possible.

It has been revealed that where was each of your point of entry? What was the first scene that you wrote?

Frost: I always break the whole thing in quite a lot of detail to feel like I understand where the story's going. I think when I actually started writing, I probably wrote from the beginning.

Kazan: So you outlined her therapy?

Alderton: I do the same. It’s the only thing that gives me freedom and confidence to write.

Kazan: And did you know how many episodes you wanted from the start, or did that change?

Frost: At one point it was longer, and at one point it was shorter. It’s eight in the end. What about you?

Recent findings suggest that kazan: I wanted eight originally, and then for budget and logistical reasons, I had to boil it down to seven quite late in the process. I had been four years into adapting it.

Kazan: Yeah. And we were a month away from production, and I had to restructure everything quite late in the game.

Recent findings suggest that kazan: Yeah, but you know what? It was actually this enormous gift. I had this writing teacher in college, a poetry teacher who talked a lot about constraints. And I don’t know if you've ever seen the... What’s his name? He’s a nightmare, but forgive me—the guy who directed Melancholia.

Kazan: There’s this beautiful Lars Von Trier film called The Five Obstructions, a documentary. He challenges his filmmaking teacher to remake this perfect short film that he made in the 1960s with five sets of obstructions to help him break open his creative process again. And that, combined with what my poetry teacher was always saying—which is the form gives you freedom.

Kazan: I feel like having to... Every time I’ve received, “Okay, we don’t have the money for X, or we don’t have the location for Y, or you have to boil eight episodes down to seven,” that it made me think again about, okay, what’s key here? 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that not even porn is immune to the GTA 6 effect, as it's just one of several forms of entertainment that has seen a decline in viewership since the massive open-world game released. It's not surprising, given the game's record-breaking start, with 32.5 million sales from preorders alone. On PS5, GTA 6 is the "biggest launch" in PlayStation history, and players spent an average of 17.4 hours playing in its first few days--which probably didn't leave much time for a quick browse of after-hours material. According to Mashable, US traffic on Pornhub--which I've been told is one of the largest pornography websites, by traffic--dipped by as much as 15.5% an hour after GTA 6 launched. Paradoxically, Pornhub traffic had actually been up by 16.5% compared to average days, likely indicating that people were bored and randy. Pornhub traffic started to fluctuate after the GTA 6 launch and reached an average peak a few days later. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7l7Lu69V_c Thanks to the game's massive success, we're also seeing the Rule 34 effect on GTA 6, as Mashable's research noted a 16,196% spike in GTA-related searches. Up to 15 million search queries were made on November 18 alone, with people searching for GTA 6, the GTA 6 strip club, and content depicting the co-protagonist Lucia specifically. The fan-favorite stalker--and possible serial killer--Mandy also appeared in search results, while Lucia's partner-in-crime Jason ranked low. Thursday Night Football also saw a substantial dip last week, with the lowest viewership of the season so far for a TNF game. While Rockstar's new open-world adventure can't be blamed entirely for that dip, it certainly must have had an impact, given that the football game was held on GTA 6's launch day. That effect didn't extend to the box office, as The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to a massive $120 million in the US, almost triple that of the last film in the series, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. For more GTA 6 news, you can read up on how modders are attempting to make an unofficial PC port, how to fix GTA 6's broken HDR, and you can check out our list of walkthroughs in the GTA 6 guides hub.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fortnite Treasure Hunters ends on Dec. 5, which means all treasure, including the Pirate Shop Access token, which grants players up to four weeks of free Item Shop goodies, will be vaulted soon. With less than two weeks to go, a large portion of the community fears that they will not be able to get their hands on the Pirate Shop Access token at all.

In a recent development, after opening thousands of chests in hopes of finding the token this season, next week will be the final stretch. Epic Games is giving players a bit of hope by hosting a Golden Week with improved treasure spawns. Treasure Hour odds will also be especially boosted during Golden Week, but unfortunately, not for the Pirate Shop Access token.

With Chapter 8 fast approaching, Epic Games has added all previous treasure hunt rewards to the loot pool. This means that gamers will be able to find previous weekly rewards — Solid Gold skins, vehicles, pickaxes, and more — as treasure in Fortnite. To give more players a chance to claim these limited-time rewards, Epic is hosting a Golden Week event.

According to recent reports, golden Week begins on Nov. 28 at 9 a.m. ET and lasts until the end of the season. The odds of finding treasure will be set to 1 in 21, instead of the current 1 in 62. While Pirate Shop Access token odds won't go up per se, gamers will be much more likely to come across a chest that spawns treasures and could get them the token.

It has been revealed that golden Week Treasure Hours will be the final Treasure Hours of the season, meaning the last time that the Pirate Shop Access token will have increased odds. Unfortunately for fans strictly trying to find the token, Epic Games has confirmed that Pirate Shop Access token odds will only be boosted to 1.5x on Nov. 28. The event focuses on Solid Gold skins, which is why they will be 15x more likely to drop rather than 7x.

According to recent reports, the latest "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer highlights MCU heroes assembling for their biggest battle yet. It will also surely be one of their most profitable, given the hype around this movie. Despite Marvel Studios' well-publicized troubles of late, the Avengers' return remains highly anticipated. As such, any new revelations Marvel is willing to provide about the team-up movie are significant to say the least.

In a recent development, the final "Doomsday" trailer doesn't actually feature any major reveals, which is a good thing for those who prefer to keep their theater experience as pure as possible. For those who like to know as much as they can ahead of a Marvel Cinematic Universe release, however, it means much of the movie remains a mystery. (We're still no clearer on whether Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom is actually a Tony Stark variant or not, despite Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige's recent comments.) That mentioned, the latest tease did contain several notable moments that have only served to increase the already significant hype.

The newly introduced "Doomsday" trailer finally gives Cyclops the X-Men line fans were waiting for, when Marsden's hero delivers his "To me, my X-Men" rallying cry to assemble his mutants, the Avengers, Fantastic Four, and several other heroes. But beyond that tantalizing glimpse at the film's big showdown, there are several other notable moments, and lucky for you, we've gone and rounded 'em up.

The precise plot of "Avengers: Doomsday" remains under wraps for now, but at this point, we can pretty much piece together the major beats. Previously, co-director Joe Russo told Empire that Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he "lost a child." That lined up with what we've seen in previous trailers, wherein Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman talked about how Doom "used to be different" before "everything he loved was taken from him." Now, the latest "Doomsday" trailer has confirmed that the Avengers themselves are responsible for it all.

In the upcoming trailer, Chris Evans' Steve Rogers can be heard saying, "Years ago, we did what was needed to make the world right," in reference to the events of 2019's "Avengers: Endgame." He continues: "But we didn't know those choices would have consequences." It seems that Steve's choice to travel back through time to be with his lover, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell) — and whatever the Avengers did to defeat Josh Brolin's Thanos — caused some sort of multiversal upheaval in which Doom's daughter met her, well, doom.

According to recent reports, this is why RDJ's villain tells the heroes of "Doomsday" that they've been living "stolen lives." With Steve's speech in the new trailer, it's all but certain he and the Avengers are responsible for whatever killed Doom's daughter, and likely the multiversal collapse referenced in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" TVA scene. Turns out, Doom is the "consequence" to which Steve refers.

Thanks to what seemed like a hasty casting announcement prior to the final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer, we knew Hailee Steinfeld's Kate Bishop would be appearing in the movie. Now, the trailer has given us our first look at the heir to the Hawkeye mantle in a very quick shot that shows her looking up at something that's clearly got her very worried. But Kate might be just one of the Young Avengers to appear in the film.

We know Scott Lang's (Paul Rudd) daughter, Cassie Lang (Kathryn Newton), is also part of "Doomsday." She shows up briefly in the upcoming trailer, too, looking as concerned as Kate. Interestingly enough, both characters are in their superhero suits, which suggests they'll be joining the big fight against Doctor Doom. That means two members of the Young Avengers will be involved in "Doomsday." Marvel Studios has yet to officially introduce these heroes as the superhero group from the comics, but has been slowly building up this new generation of Avengers over the past few years.

The only likely member of the Young Avengers who hasn't appeared in trailers and is yet to be confirmed as being involved with "Doomsday" is Iman Vellani's Ms. Marvel. According to Andy Serkis, Ms. Marvel will appear in "Doomsday," but Marvel hasn't made that official. Otherwise, there are a handful of other young heroes that could show up and potentially form the Young Avengers proper in the movie itself, including Riri Williams/Ironheart (Dominique Thorne) and America Chavez (Xochitl Gomez). For now, it looks more likely than ever we'll see an official Young Avengers group unite in "Doomsday.".

It has been revealed that the new "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer shows Chris Hemsworth's Thor rising from the floor surrounded by yellow lightning as opposed to his typical blue lightning. That's significant, as it all but confirms he'll be wielding a powerful new force known as the Odinforce. This power, created by the Kings of Asgard, is a major upgrade for the character, and the latest trailer appears to have shown it in action.

In a recent development, one of the most frequently showcased "Doomsday" scenes thus far has been the moment in which Thor launches himself at Doctor Doom, only to be stopped mid-air and flung backwards by the villain's formidable force (which, as it happens, involves a Jacky Kirby-inspired energy blast from Doom). Clearly, the God of Thunder is as outmatched as the rest of his cohorts.

But back when the first four teaser trailers for "Doomsday" dropped, we saw Hemsworth's hero begging his father for the "strength of the All-Fathers." Since then we've seen concept art and a "Doomsday" billboard that seemingly spoiled the fact Thor was getting a major upgrade in the form of the Odinforce. It's this force that turns his lightning yellow, and the final "Doomsday" trailer is the first time we see footage of it in action. The brief shot reveals Thor ascending in a forest, which looks to be the same forest in which he begged for the strength of the All-Fathers in the original teaser. Looks like he got his wish. Whether it will prove effective against Doom, however, remains to be seen.

Recent findings suggest that we got our first look at the X-Men in "Avengers: Doomsday" courtesy of the X-Men-heavy trailer back in January 2026. Since then, we've learned how the mutants might find their way to the Avengers. The film will take place during the collapse of the multiverse, whereby several "incursions" will see planets and timelines collide. These collisions are likely to be the reason for the film's major crossovers, i.e. the Fox-era X-Men and the Fantastic Four arriving on the Avengers' Earth 616. But it seems when the X-Men and Avengers first come face to face they initially clash, as evidenced by footage from prior trailers in which Yelena Belova/Black Widow (Florence Pugh) takes on Mystique (Rebecca Romijn) and Shang-Chi (Simu Liu) battles Gambit (Channing Tatum).

According to recent reports, now, however, the final "Doomsday" trailer has confirmed that Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson/Captain America will face off against James Marsden's Scott Summers/Cyclops. The trailer shows the pair going toe-to-toe in what looks to be a pretty brutal clash, with Wilson holding Cyclops by the neck as he unleashes an optic blast. Clearly, the X-Men and Avengers ultimately manage to, as Thor puts it, "put aside their petty squabbles." But for at least a moment, the two superhero teams will be at odds in the movie, and Sam Wilson's showdown with Scott Summers looks set to be a major highlight.

Industry observers note that the final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer reminds us of the main threat facing Earth 616 in the movie. While Doctor Doom is the big bad, the entire multiverse is collapsing, and in the latest trailer we see a brief shot that shows two planets in the sky above Fresh York City. The trailer also features several shots of heroes looking up at the sky, or out of windows and reacting with shock and dismay, and it's likely this planetary incursion is what has them so upset.

We've known that the heroes of "Doomsday" would be dealing with multiversal collapse in the film for some time. But this is the first shot we've seen in an official trailer that shows planets on a collision course with Earth. Previously, a Dunkin' Donuts commercial gave us our best look at the threat the Avengers face in "Doomsday," with a shot showing a planet looming in the sky over Avengers Tower. But it looks as though multiple timelines/planets are set to collide with Earth based on the brief scene from this latest trailer.

Exactly which planets these are remains unclear. One may in fact be the Fox-era X-Men's world, and this cityscape view could be giving us a glimpse of their arrival in the Avengers' timeline. Either way, clearly the stakes have never been higher, as failure means the complete and utter destruction of the multiverse.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

Pastries—from the merrymaking gentry presumably, though who can say for certain—were distributed, with an assist from a cop in uniform and gear.

If you listened carefully then to the sounds of the city—not for any semantic meaning, but if you were to really pitch your ears to the utopic promise of music—you might have heard the determined whoosh of a weighted blade dropping, dropping, dropping, the ax of public opinion falling in downward demotic motion.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Serling wrote 92 of the 156 "Twilight Zone" episodes that aired during the show's five season run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, no TV writer is as synonymous with their creation as Rod Serling is with "The Twilight Zone." As the show's host, he was the face of the series. In an anthology series, you can't expect to see the same actors and characters every time you tune in, so the only familiar sound to welcome you into the twilight zone was Serling's calm, sardonic voice.

Serling wrote 92 of the 156 "Twilight Zone" episodes that aired during the show's five season run. The first episode that did not come from a Serling script is the series' ninth episode, "Perchance to Dream," with writer Charles Beaumont self-adapting a short story he originally wrote for publication in Playboy magazine. (Now, technically, the beloved eighth "Twilight Zone" episode "Time Enough At Last," boasting one of the show's most depressing endings, was based on a short story by Lynn Venable. However, Serling wrote the teleplay.).

"Perchance to Dream" stars Richard Conte (nowadays most remembered for playing Don Barzini in "The Godfather") as Edward Hall, a man who hasn't slept for days — because he's convinced if he falls asleep, he'll die. But his insomnia is born of a different medical condition. Hall has a weak heart, so much so that if he experiences a significant enough shock, even in his dreams, it might literally kill him. The episode sees Hall visiting a psychiatrist, Dr. Eliot Rathmann (John Larch), and recalling how his own mind seems to be trying to knock him off a ledge with terrifying dreams.

The title "Perchance to Dream" comes from a soliloquy in "Hamlet," when the eponymous prince muses: "To sleep, perchance to dream." But Hamlet is talking about the sleep of death and his temptation to suicide. That makes the line a fitting, though flipped-on-its-head, title for a story about a man terrified he'll die if he falls asleep. ("Batman: The Animated Series" would later use "Perchance to Dream" as the title for star Kevin Conroy's favorite episode.).

The episode is primarily set in Dr. Rathmann's skyscraper office, but peeks inside Hall's dreams to let us see his terror. The second half cuts between the office and Hall recounting his dreams of a carnival, where "everything [is] warped and twisted out of shape," and the nightmare that came closest to killing him. A cat-eyed woman named Maya (Suzanne Lloyd) leads Hall down a haunted trail, packed with monstrous animatronics, and then onto a roller coaster.

In a recent development, maya's feline coding marks her as a predator, toying with Hall like a terrified mouse trying to escape her claws. Watching the episode now, it feels like "A Nightmare on Elm Street" with a femme fatale instead of a knife-handed slasher. The carnival scenes use Dutch angles and foggy camera filters feel extra unnerving and wrong. Combined with the Halloween aesthetic and Maya's cutting laughter, the dream lives up to the nightmare that Hall described.

According to recent reports, charles Beaumont remained one of most prolific "Twilight Zone" writers. During the second season, he self-adapted his spooky short story "The Howling Man," helping turn it into one of the scariest "Twilight Zone" episodes ever. But "Perchance to Dream" first proved that Beaumont could makes trips to the Twilight Zone genuinely terror-inducing.
