📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the best sci-fi stories work because they reflect society's current state or predict what's to come. The Twilight Zone featured many episodes in which aliens and the supernatural served as metaphors for societal issues like racism or fascism. Minority Report still resonates thanks to its unflinching look at how predicting the future can go horribly wrong. 15 years ago, CBS delivered a television series that blends the best of a long-running sci-fi saga with the network's procedural formula. That series has grown even more timely as technology like Flock cameras and generative AI become the subject of fierce debate.

Sources indicate that that series is Person of Interest. Created by Jonathan Nolan (The Dark Knight) and produced by J.J. Abrams (Lost), Person of Interest centers on the unorthodox team of former CIA operative John Reese (Jim Caviezel) and reclusive billionaire Harold Finch (Michael Emerson). In the wake of September 11th, Finch developed a machine for the government that can identify potential terrorist attacks; he hires Reese to prevent potential crimes using the information the Machine provides. This premise carried Person of Interest for five seasons, and like any good sci-fi, it raised more than its share of time.

Anyone who has watched J.J. Abrams' previous work on Lost or Fringe knows he tends to back series with a labyrinthine plot, a great hook, or both. Person of Interest is such a series, as it begins to reveal what caused Reese to drop off the grid after his CIA days and how Finch created the Machine. It also introduces a number of threats, like Decima Technologies, a organization that wants the Machine for its own nefarious ends, and Samaritan, another source of technology like the Machine that's willing to go to extreme lengths to eliminate potential threats. Like Minority Report before it, Person of Interest digs into the dark side of government surveillance and what can happen when that technology falls into the wrong hands.

Perhaps the most interesting sci-fi elements in Person of Interest come with the introduction of former Marine Sameen Shaw (Sarah Shahi) and the brilliant hacker "Root" (Amy Acker). Both women have their lives radically reshaped by the Machine: Shaw worked for a government program that used its intelligence to root out threats, while Root becomes its living avatar after growing obsessed with it. They also serve as foils to Reese and Finch, creating a great dynamic in Person of Interest's later seasons. Another great dynamic is the unorthodox partnership between Reese and NYPD detective Joss Carter (Taraji P. Henson), as Carter goes from wanting to arrest Reese to seekinghis help on certain cases.

In a recent development, person of Interest was a massive success for CBS, earning some of the network's highest ratings and critical acclaim throughout its run. However, its biggest legacy remains the questions it raised about artificial intelligence, especially in a landscape where AI is debated across the entertainment industry. Jonathan Nolan discussed these themes in an interview, noting that Person of Interest grew out of his work on The Dark Knight and Interstellar—both movies that tackle surveillance and artificial intelligence, respectively.

"More than almost anything I’ve done, people talk to me about Person of Interest...I wouldn’t credit us with any particular gift for prophecy. The pieces of it were right there if you cared to look at them.".

The dangers of unchecked technology are a theme Nolan has returned to in his current projects, particularly those he's developed with his wife, Lisa Joy. At its peak, Westworld added upcoming layers to the age-old story of artificial intelligence run amok, while Fallout builds on the video games that inspired it by showing the lengths those in power will go totest new technologies. None of it would have been possible without the success of Person of Interest, and now that the series is streaming on Peacock, it's worth a watch.

  • According to recent reports, the trailer begins on Dec.
  • The preview then moves into the investigation and the attention that followed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I've sat through Ryan Murphy's takes on Jeffrey Dahmer and Lizzie Borden, so I'm no stranger to true-crime dramas that seem determined to make audiences uncomfortable. But after watching the trailer for Netflix's upcoming The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey, which premieres as part of the 2026 TV schedule, I felt more uneasy than I ever did watching either of those productions. The trailer itself is surprisingly restrained, and Melissa McCarthy looks terrific as Patsy Ramsey, alongside Clive Owen as her husband, John. Nothing in the footage is particularly shocking, at least by the standards we've come to expect from the genre. Yet I finished watching it with a sinking feeling I haven't quite been able to shake.

According to recent reports, the trailer begins on Dec. 26, 1996, with McCarthy's Patsy making the frantic 911 call reporting that her daughter is missing. Police arrive at the Boulder, Colorado, house, and the family indicates them a ransom note. We know how the search ends: JonBenét is found dead in the basement. Watching actors retrace those hours, even briefly, made me uncomfortable. The sequence feels eerily familiar because so many of us have heard the details repeated for decades.

The preview then moves into the investigation and the attention that followed. Officers question what happened inside the home, reporters crowd the family, and suspicion increasingly falls on the parents. McCarthy's Patsy breaks down, insisting, "I didn't kill my baby." There's also a chilling moment when the district attorney, played by Shea Whigham, acknowledges that even the facts investigators can establish may never satisfy a public desperate for an explanation. It's a trailer built around grief and accusation, with no resolution waiting at the end.

According to recent reports, I think a lot of that comes down to remembering that JonBenét Ramsey was just 6 years old when she was murdered in 1996. Nearly 30 years later, her killing remains unsolved; nobody has been convicted, and her mother died in 2006 without ever seeing someone brought to justice for her daughter's death. In the decades since, JonBenét's murder has become the subject of countless documentaries, television specials, and endless speculation. Netflix itself released another docuseries about the case in 2024.

I understand that this new production may be trying to examine the media circus surrounding her death, and perhaps it will handle that responsibly. But watching the trailer, I couldn't stop thinking about how much entertainment we've already made out of this little girl's murder. Hasn't JonBenét Ramsey's death made enough money for other people?

The people making this series seem aware of that problem. McCarthy has spoken about how the public fascination with the mystery overshadowed the fact that parents lost their child, and Netflix notes the drama examines the consequences of the media frenzy. I appreciate that intention. Richard LaGravenese, the showrunner, is telling a story that cannot provide the ending audiences have spent years demanding. Boulder police still describe JonBenét's murder as an active investigation.

Maybe the full series will find a thoughtful way to reckon with all of that. I'm certainly not questioning McCarthy's performance based on the footage we've seen. I just keep thinking about the difference between watching a fictional horror story and revisiting a real child's death for entertainment. The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey premieres on Netflix Dec. 10 for everyone with a Netflix subscription. I'm not sure yet whether I'll be able to watch it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Denis Villeneuve brought on seasoned casting director Francine Maisler for the first Dune movie, they were starting from scratch.
  • Sources indicate that luckily, the pair had already worked together on Villeneuve’s three previous films, Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, and Arrival.
  • In a recent development, when they were casting the first installment, Maisler was aware that it was possible that these actors might play these characters for more than just one film.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Denis Villeneuve brought on seasoned casting director Francine Maisler for the first Dune movie, they were starting from scratch. For the ambitious adaptation of Frank Herbert’s 1965 sci-fi novel, they had to cast not only the lead character, Paul Atreides, but dozens of other main characters—powerful warriors, scheming royals, shape-shifting conspirators—to inhabit the world.

Sources indicate that luckily, the pair had already worked together on Villeneuve’s three previous films, Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, and Arrival. “Denis’s vision is my compass,” Maisler tells Vanity Fair. “His passion [for Dune] since he was a teen was all I needed to follow.”.

In a recent development, when they were casting the first installment, Maisler was aware that it was possible that these actors might play these characters for more than just one film. “I did have an idea that they would have to have the presence and the acting talent to be able to carry this potentially for three movies,” she states.

In a recent development, dune (2021), starring Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides and Zendaya as Chani, was just the first step. Maisler returned to cast Dune: Part Two (2024), and Dune: Part Three, which will wrap up Villeneuve’s trilogy when it hits theaters on December 18.

Maisler is a titan of casting, having worked on hundreds of films with filmmakers such as Luca Guadagnino, Greta Gerwig, Aaron Sorkin, Paul Greengrass, Adam McKay, and Terrence Malick, and she was nominated for the first casting Oscar in 2026 for her work on Ryan Coogler’s Sinners.

Recent findings suggest that the casting Oscar didn’t exist when she began working on the Dune franchise, but this installment is likely to draw attention from the Academy. Over the three films, the cast has grown into an incredible ensemble, packed with many of today’s biggest movie stars, along with well-known veterans and a few unexpected choices. “One thing about Denis is if ever I bring him a name and he likes it, and I’ll say, ‘Well, do you want to hire that actor?’ He states to me something I think is so poetic,” says Maisler. “He says, ‘Francine, let me get back to you tomorrow. I need to dream about it.’”.

Ahead of the release of Dune: Part Three, Maisler looks back at casting the trilogy’s most important roles, including the exciting upcoming additions to the upcoming film—and the possibility of more Dune in the future.

In a recent development, in Herbert’s book, Atreides is a slender 15-year-old with dark hair. “To find a 15-year-old who had that talent to carry this whole movie, we weren’t sure was out there,” remembers Maisler. The name that came up was then 22-year-old Chalamet, whom Maisler had previously cast in Hostiles, Beautiful Boy, The King, and Little Women. Chalamet, who didn’t have to audition but did meet with Villeneuve, would have to play Atreides from a young man who then begins to amass power in the second film and, after a 12-year time jump, is burdened with the choices he’s made waging a galactic war in the third. Though Chalamet hadn’t led a big blockbuster before, Maisler saw the depth of his talent. “I do think Beautiful Boy showed me the depth of Timothée as an actor, as a young man, and that this was the next step in his progression as an actor, that he was able to hold a franchise in his hand,” notes Maisler.

There was a worldwide search for Chani, the skilled Fremen warrior from Arrakis who falls in love with Atreides. At the time, Zendaya was in the middle of filming the first season of Euphoria, and her graduation from Disney star to movie star had not yet happened. Zendaya screen tested with Chalamet, which sealed it for Maisler and Villeneuve. “She came in with five other incredibly talented actresses, but the minute you saw her with Timothée in a room, you just knew that there’s something special happening,” she claims. “She has such power when she walks in the room, and she’s breathtaking in the most interesting way.”.

Of course, Paul Atreides’s parents, Duke Leto Atreides and Lady Jessica, needed to look like Chalamet, but Maisler started with the characters’ essences when casting. Duke Leto Atreides was considered a fair and devoted leader as the noble head of House Atreides. Maisler saw that gravitas in Oscar Isaac. Lady Jessica becomes a force in the story because of her heightened physical and mental control as a trained member of the Bene Gesserit sisterhood. “Rebecca is so powerful, isn’t she?” says Maisler. “She really, I have to say, surprised me. I always knew how talented she was, but she just owned that part.”.

In a recent development, villeneuve and Maisler had worked with Brolin on the 2015 crime thriller Sicario. Maisler, who calls Brolin “one of our greatest actors,” was excited to have him back, this time playing Gurney Halleck, the Warmaster of House Atreides and a mentor to Paul Atreides. The character is described in the book as a warrior-poet, requiring strength and depth. “He’s so charismatic, so masculine,” claims Maisler of Brolin. “He’s kind of a throwback from other generations.”.

When Momoa’s agent brought up Momoa’s name, Maisler wasn’t quite sure about the idea because at the time he was known for starring in the DC movie franchise as Aquaman. “I was a bit skeptical, I have to admit, because I knew he had this incredible presence on screen, but I didn’t know, truly, his talent, and that’s taught me a lot about being open to people who come from different types of films,” she indicates. Villeneuve was more open to the idea at the start, and met with him about playing Duncan Idaho, a fierce fighter and protector of Paul Atreides. He returns in the third movie as a ghola—a sort of clone—named Hayt, which demands a more complicated performance from Momoa. “Jason’s an incredible artist, and I’ve come to just love him,” says Maisler. “He’s so funny. I want to put him in a romantic comedy next, because he really is one of the big surprises in the ensemble.”.

Industry observers note that taylor-Joy had already risen in stardom by the time she joined the franchise for the second film. Her breakout was in The Witch, and she starred in hit series The Queen's Gambit, which earned her a Golden Globe and a SAG Award. This made it slightly surprising that Alia Atreides, Paul’s volatile sister, makes a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it appearance in the second film. “I give her a lot of credit for not counting lines in the second one,” claims Maisler, who says Taylor-Joy signed on for the second because of the potential of the third installment. Indeed, in Dune: Part Three, Alia is a loyal sister and vengeful force who is not afraid to get blood on her hands. Taylor-Joy’s charisma and intensity will jump off the screen, says Maisler. “Actors are very smart, and they know when to trust a director like Denis,” she says. “When he says there is going to be something in the third film and he describes it, he will make it happen.”.

A tribal leader of the desert-dwelling Fremen, Stilgar is a seasoned warrior and becomes a devout follower of Paul Atreides as Muad’Dib. The role required a level of intensity. “Oh, I think we all just prayed that Javier would do it,” indicates Maisler. “I think every actor wants to work with Javier, and he’s one of probably a handful of actors I think can do anything.”.

In a recent development, pugh joined for the second film as well, but like Taylor-Joy, she didn’t have a ton to do. But Princess Irulan, who marries Paul Atreides as a political union, is a key part of the plot in Dune: Part Three, joining a conspiracy against Paul. Maisler first saw Pugh in the 2016 film Lady Macbeth, and then cast her as Amy March in Gerwig’s Little Women. “You saw on that what an intelligent actress she is, and singular,” she states. “She knows no boundaries, and she’s confident and bold.” She says Pugh has always reminded her of Debra Winger, the star of An Officer and a Gentleman (1982), and Terms of Endearment (1983). “She’s just commanding, and she has this energy, and everything she does is fascinating,” says Maisler. “You can’t take your eyes off of her.”.

In a recent development, the third installment brings in yet another major star with Pattinson, who plays Scytale, a shape-shifter who is conspiring to dethrone Paul Atreides. Maisler, who also worked with Pattinson in Primetime, which also came out this year, describes him as “one of the versatile actors in his choices.” She had also worked with Pattinson on Mickey 17, which proved that he could play many different versions of a character—a skill that would be required of him in this third Dune movie. “Robert's a tremendous actor, and I think he takes these really bold chances,” indicates Maisler. As for his recent announcement as the next James Bond, Maisler has faith he and Villeneuve will deliver. “I think the way Denis and Rob created the character in Dune: Part Three together speaks to the surprises that we will see in Bond,” she says.

For Dune: Part Three, Maisler and Villeneuve had to find two actors who looked like twins and also looked like the offspring of Chalamet and Zendaya. They initially hoped to cast real twins, but didn’t find the right pair. In the end, they found their Ghanima and Leto II in Ida Brooke and Nakoa-Wolf Momoa. Brooke, who looks strikingly like Zendaya, is a relative newcomer who previously appeared on Apple’s sci-fi drama Silo (which stars Rebecca Ferguson). And Nakoa-Wolf Momoa, who makes his feature acting debut in Dune: Part Three, is Jason Momoa’s son—though Maisler didn’t know that when she first watched his audition tape. “Then came this tape of this young man who had incredible presence, and—we didn’t ask for this—he added some combat footage to his tape,” she claims. Maisler says sometimes actors will call in a favor to get their child an audition, but Wolf, as she calls him, got this on his own. This casting was the most key for the third film because of what might be to come. “It was almost like casting the first one where these two young actors could go on to potentially, if there’s another movie where they’re leads,” says Maisler. There have been no official announcements of any future Dune movies, but for those mourning the end of the Villeneuve trilogy, Maisler is planting a small seed of hope here. The third Dune book, Children of Dune, centers on Leto and Ghanima, which means the two young actors Maisler found may have more story ahead of them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 1959, Gregory Peck starred in a surprisingly bleak dystopian sci-fi movie about the end of the world. Perhaps unsurprisingly, given its subject matter, "On the Beach" was a box office disappointment, despite the fact it also starred Ava Gardner, Fred Astaire, and a pre-"Psycho" Anthony Perkins. But as Turner Classic Movies notes, "the film struck a chord with the public and for decades remained the definitive dramatic portrayal of the aftermath of a nuclear attack.".

In a recent development, peck made his film debut in 1944's "Days of Glory" and, amazingly, earned an Oscar nomination for his work in John M. Stahl's "The Keys of the Kingdom" that same year. While that film proved to be his breakthrough, it wasn't until the 1950s that he truly ascended to megastardom, becoming one of the biggest leading men in Hollywood. He started the decade by irritating 20th Century Fox chief Darryl F. Zanuck, who wanted Peck to shave his mustache for the 1950 Western "The Gunfighter," before going on to star alongside Audrey Hepburn in the romance classic and one of the best movies of the '50s, "Roman Holiday.".

He also appeared alongside Ava Gardner in 1952's "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," before reuniting with her for 1959's "On the Beach." While their prior collaboration had been a romantic adventure outing, "On the Beach" was a decidedly more gloomy affair in which humanity was wiped out almost entirely, while the survivors waited to be killed off by radioactive winds. Not exactly, "Roman Holiday," then. Still, the film has its share of romance and adventure, even if it does end on a fairly dreary note.

Recent findings suggest that "On the Beach" isn't always cited as one of the best Gregory Peck movies, and is a bit of an underrated entry in his filmography that deserves more attention. For one thing, the film is directed by Stanley Kramer, the legendary filmmaker who also oversaw "The Defiant Ones," "Guess Who's Coming to Dinner," and "It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World." All of Kramer's movies tackled social complications, and with "On the Beach" the glitch was nuclear war. The film arrived in an era in which such a thing was an ever-present threat and like many other filmmakers after him, Kramer wanted to hammer home the absurdity, horror, and tragedy of it all.

Sources indicate that he did so by adapting Nevil Shute's 1957 novel "On the Beach," in which nuclear war erupts, wiping out most of the major nations and leaving clouds of radiation across the northern hemisphere, which begin to drift South towards Australia. Kramer's movie version uses the same premise, though unlike in the book, we never learn who actually dropped the bombs that wiped out life in the Northern hemisphere. Instead, we simply learn that Gregory Peck's Capt. Dwight Towers and the crew of his American nuclear submarine USS Sawfish are arriving in Melbourne to escape the nuclear fallout in their homeland.

Industry observers note that towers is greeted by Australian naval officer Peter Holmes (Anthony Perkins), who invites him to a party. There, Towers meets regretful nuclear scientist Julian Osborn (Fred Astaire) and Ava Gardner's Moira Davidson, with whom Towers falls in love. Soon, it transpires that the nuclear fallout everyone expected to float down to Australia might not make it that far south, and Towers sets out with his submarine crew to investigate.

Recent findings suggest that without giving away the ending, "On the Beach" doesn't wrap up on all that happy a note. Stanley Kramer remind viewers that there's "still time" via a banner that literally says as much. But it happens to be flapping away in a deserted Melbourne in a way that calls to mind the end of "Oppenheimer," in which the titular scientist ponders how the nuclear destruction of our species is inevitable regardless of how long we stave it off.

That might have something to do with the film's disappointing box office. After all, it couldn't have been a lack of star power. "On the Beach" was also shot on-location in Melbourne and was, as The Sydney Morning Herald noted in 2019, "the biggest film ever made" in the city. Stanley Kramer, meanwhile, was on a roll following the success of 1958's "The Defiant Ones," and "On the Beach" earned positive reviews. It should have been a bigger hit and should definitely be more widely remembered than it is today.

Recent findings suggest that many films designed to remind audiences of the devastating threat posed by nuclear weapons have come in the wake of "On the Beach." In 1966, the BBC released the horrific mockumentary "The War Game," which was summarily banned by the Government of the United Kingdom for its disturbing depiction of nuclear attack and the ensuing fallout. Then there was 1983's "The Day After" and 1984's "Threads," the apocalyptic TV movie that shook Britain to its core. More recently we've seen movies like "House of Dynamite" provide a realistic look at how a nuclear attack might unfold. But Gregory Peck's 1959 film was one of the first to really deal head-on with the threat of nuclear annihilation and deserves to be remembered for it.

Canceled Mass Effect Addressed Squad Members’ Fates, Writer Reveals

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the cancellation of the fifth mainline Mass Effect game, Mass Effect: Universe, fans can't help but wonder what could have been.
  • It has been revealed that while Valente was clear that she had to avoid certain specifics when discussing the canceled Mass Effect: Universe to avoid breaking NDAs, she hinted at which characters from previous Mass Effect titles would likely have appeared in the game.
  • “I think the best way to answer your question is to say that any character who physically *could* survive, we considered allowing to survive into the new game and made decisions on them,” Valente stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the cancellation of the fifth mainline Mass Effect game, Mass Effect: Universe, fans can't help but wonder what could have been. In a recent Reddit AMA, Universe writer Cat Valente answered questions about the sequel, including how it would have addressed squad mates’ fates and Mass Effect 3’s controversial endings. Valente is an award-winning sci-fi and fantasy author and a Mass Effect series veteran, having previously written the 2018 novel Mass Effect: Annihilation. She worked on Universe for three years.

It has been revealed that while Valente was clear that she had to avoid certain specifics when discussing the canceled Mass Effect: Universe to avoid breaking NDAs, she hinted at which characters from previous Mass Effect titles would likely have appeared in the game. Universe would have been set 600 years after the original Mass Effect trilogy, but since certain species, like Asari and Krogan, can live 1,000 years or more, many characters from Mass Effect 3 could still be alive. Based on a leaked trailer, we already knew Liara T’Soni would appear in the game, but Valente hinted that other characters likely would as well.

“I think the best way to answer your question is to say that any character who physically *could* survive, we considered allowing to survive into the new game and made decisions on them,” Valente stated. “We thought about all the things you’d have wanted us to think about, and I hope you do believe that, because it’s the truth. Everyone in that room loved those characters, or loved to hate them, as much as any fan. We took each and every one of them and their fates very seriously.”.

It has been revealed that humans, Salarians, Turians, and Quarians don’t live long enough to survive for 600 years, so these characters were out of contention for a return. Beyond Liara, Grunt could certainly have appeared in Universe, as Krogan can live for centuries, and he was “only” a few hundred years old. Wrex is much less likely, given that he was implied to be close to a thousand years old already, and the same goes for the Asari Samara, but it's still possible in both cases. It’s unclear how the game would have handled synthetics like EDI, given how the ending of Mass Effect 3 hinges on the player’s choice about how to handle coexistence between organics and machine life.

When asked if the writers had considered what would happen to other squad members who wouldn’t have survived until Universe, like Garrus, Tali, and Wrex, she said, “You would have been able to know everything you wanted to know about them.”.

“I don’t have headcanons about those fates, I have canon-canons," Valente added. “I know you’d have been able to find out about them because one of my jobs was to write all those fates and their possible variations (all then submitted to the room, workshopped with everyone, and sent to higher-ups for approval...).”.

Recent findings suggest that beyond squad mates, Valente addressed how Universe would have handled the ending(s) of the Mass Effect trilogy, which she described as one of the game’s biggest writing challenges. She and the team “worked specifically, and for a very long and laborious time, on handling the endings in a way that wouldn’t piss everyone off, at least not piss them off completely, that wouldn’t make them feel like nothing mattered, wouldn’t privilege any one kind of player over another, but also allow us, somehow, to actually write a coherent story going forward, within the limits of having to do it in a playable mainstream video game and not a post-modern 3000 page novel.”.

Recent findings suggest that “But we did our best, and I think we landed in a good place. There wasn’t one single solution, but several working together, and unfortunately I can’t say any more than that.” She added that “There was an answer, yes, I know it, as [sic] least inasmuch as I know what it was when I was working there, because part of it was my job, and we tried our damnedest to do right by the story and the fandom. That room was *full* of ambition and enthusiasm, and I don’t think it could have been in better hands. We knew all the discourse on the endings, of course we did, and I do think as a fan I would have been happy with the solution (at least what it was when I left) if I booted up the game having had nothing to do with it.”.

Mass Effect 3 infamously ended with a choice about future coexistence between humanity and synthetic life: destroy all intelligent machines, “control” them, or create a synthesis between organic and synthetic life.

Valente also teased that the game would address lingering questions from Mass Effect: Andromeda, including the identity of The Benefactor, and introduce entirely upcoming alien species. “I don’t think there’s a problem with saying of course there were going to be new aliens?” Valente added. “We all pitched new species and some were accepted and moved along to art etc and some weren’t. Same with the squad. All of us pitched squad members and our directors chose between the pitches. I can’t give you any more than that.”.

Although a tiny glimmer of hope remains that BioWare and Mass Effect: Universe could be revived — a politician alluded to the possibility of the Canadian government helping BioWare buy itself back from EA — a comeback still seems like a long shot. If nothing else, we now have a slightly better idea of where Universe would have gone next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that terrifier has grown quite a bit since 2016. While modern horror icon Art the Clown technically got his start in the indie horror movie All Hallow's Eve in 2013, he was reintroduced to the world in earnest in 2016's Terrifier, which put the supernatural killer clown into the spotlight.

Recent findings suggest that now, Terrifier has hosted two sequels, both of which well exceeded their thrifty budgets. Now, Art is appearing in multiple forms of media, including as a skin in Fortnite. It was time to sit down with the creator and get the scoop on how all this feels, given the relatively short lifespan of the series.

We spoke to Damien Leone, creator of Terrifier, and Dave Richard Senior Creative Director at Behaviour Interactive, to get a sense of what these two were cooking up with the latest Art the Clown collab.

Our exclusive image for the Dead by Daylight collab is at the end of the article, and it contains disturbing imagery reminiscent of the Terrifier series.

Recent findings suggest that as of today, fans can test out the Terrifier collaboration in Dead by Daylight, which brings both Art the Clown and Sienna into the mix. Decidedly a modern-day franchise, Art joins a ton of cult-classic slashers and villains, but he does it in a unique way. The main gimmick this time around is the Bag of Toys, providing access to weapons like flails and even a gun.

According to recent reports, sienna sports multiple passive abilities, including one that impacts the entire team of survivors. I asked Damien about how he was able to link up to bring Art to yet another game, and he was happy to oblige:.

For us personally, the most requested collaboration, I think, above all, all areas - video games, you know, apparel - probably since I'd say sometime around the production of Terrifier 2, I started hearing about Dead by Daylight, and fans were like, 'You got to get Art in that game; it's the greatest game, you know? Perhaps we had to, you know, we were still really in our infancy back then, and maybe we had to prove ourselves a little bit.

But you know, I'm just thrilled that this finally happened, and our fan base, especially, is beyond thrilled. And these guys did such an incredible job bringing art and Sienna to life in this game. So I'm really, really excited. It's going to be a good one.

Damien recalls the wheels really turning around when Terrifier 2 was released in theaters:.

Yeah, that was a crazy time, the theatrical window of Terrifier 2, which I think was supposed to play for a weekend, and it just blew up, exceeded everybody's expectations. And then the whole next Monday to Friday, I remember the team scrambling like, 'Oh no, we gotta, we gotta keep this, we gotta get more screens here. Like, this is crazy.'.

And that whole week was, you know, talk shows and Stephen King tweeting about us, and then we got it back into the theater, and it was like a very rare movie where it was like spiked, took a massive dip that week, and then we got it back into the theaters. It spiked again, and then it just kept growing for the next couple of weeks. Just unbelievable.

Damien was delighted to talk about the Terrifier franchise, and I even got an enhancement on Terrifier 4, and how he sees the movie as more than just a sequel:.

Writing Terrifier 4. You know, if I really didn't care, I would have written it a year ago. It's like, but I just put so much into it. You know, there really is a lot. There's a lot more that goes into these scripts. Especially when you care for the audience, and you don't want to let them down, and when they've been so loyal and dedicated, you know. Especially for us, we've never had marketing.

Sources indicate that I've been saying this for years, but we've never had, like, a big marketing push with these movies. We've never had a Hollywood-movie budget to really get the word out. It's always just been sort of an organic, you know, grassroots movement, and it's all been fans just talking about it and coming to horror conventions and spreading the word and making videos, you know. So we never, you know, that's really special to us, and especially to me. So I never want to let them down. I always want to deliver something to exceed their expectations.

Sienna's inclusion feels natural given how big of a role she's had in Terrifier since the second movie, and according to Richard:.

Sources indicate that I mean, for us, it was a no-brainer. Like, as you know, I did watch the Terrifier movies in order when I saw Sienna for the first time on screen, I was like, 'Wow, this is like the final girl reinvented with some vulnerabilities, more approachable, but also like superpowers, and she could be the Ash William of the world as well.' So I thought she was so interesting.

So it was the right off the bat part of the package for us. Like Sienna needs to come in Dead by Daylight, and the package of abilities she brings with her are unique to our character. Like you know all of the characters we integrate, but she has some angles are really interesting from the survivor side that we can see in movies out there.

Damien couldn't have been happier with how Sienna turned out, and the sheer charisma that actor Lauren LaVera brought to the role:.

Industry observers note that when I created Sienna, my idea with that character was to really sort of pay tribute to the final girl, and not that that's not done, but the final girl is the star of the movie every time, right? Even though the slasher takes the spotlight, when you break the movie down, it's about the final girl. That's the lead character. That's the character that your audience is investing in.

But I wanted to try and now put Sienna on the same sort of pedestal as Art The Clown, even from a visually striking standpoint, like, you know, he jumps off the screen. I wanted her to jump off the screen as well, like, and turn her into a character that could jump off the page of a comic book. And I really wanted to, you know, pay her that respect. So you know, I think that's one of the main reasons why she really gravitates toward a lot of people, and she leans, you know, she lends herself, you know, to a video game for sure because of, yeah.

Damien also had great things to say about LaVera:.

But I mean, a lot of it is also, like Dave remarked, vulnerability. It's what Lauren, of course, brings to that character that makes her so relatable, and why people really gravitate toward that character, and I just love that Lauren got to really be a part of this game as well. I mean, that's a dream come true for her. I know that for sure.

Recent findings suggest that so, you know, especially the first two Terrifier movies, you can't really get you know they're they're so low budget. They're so outside the studio system, you know. We're just like these amateur filmmakers making these films, and to just see them now, we get to this level where, you know, we are incorporated in video games, and it's sort of this, you know, it's touched upon in pop culture. It's really a dream come true for us. Pretty amazing.

Digging further into Terrifier as a whole, I also got some insight into how Damien prepped LaVera for the role in the film series, which is paying off substantial time years later in this collab:.

I gave Lauren a whole playlist, even though a lot of the songs weren't in the movie. But just to get her in the mindset of who I thought Sienna would be. I mean, there was a lot of synthwave. There were a lot of Fleetwood Mac songs on there. So that was a fun process.

Of course, translating anything across different mediums is going to have some complications, and Richard explained how tough that can be:.

Right, mixing and matching all of these characters together creates all of these emergent scenarios that are quite interesting. But obviously, there comes unique gameplay with them as well. Art a clown comes with such a unique kit that we wanted to show how creative he can be with all of these different tools, how cruel he can be with all of these different tools. So you know he's gonna bring his garbage bag along, and all of these tools are, you know, we internally we compared it when building it in a prototype to Mario Kart, right? And where you get these question mark box, and then you get a tool, and you have to do something with it. So we guide the player toward being tactical and being creative with the tool they get, you know, it can be the acid bottle, it can be the gun.

Sources indicate that you know, for the first time we have an end gun with a bullet, which, by the way, Damian, I thought was super brilliant to add to a slasher movie. You know, when you just get that gun out and become super serious, you're like, holy shit, what just happened? It's like a taboo. You can't use that. So, so we had to integrate it, and the cool thing is that the more creative you are, like the player, the most creative they are with that, they get the chance to unlock a kill animation that is unique to that tool they're using, and that's something we're calling them Moris in DBD, like Memento Mori, and art is the character that has the most because of all of these different tools will have a different animation related to them, and players go crazy with that usually, and they will.

I asked how Art's license differs from big ones that have been added in the past, and the answer that Richard gave us made perfect sense:.

It's interesting what you're saying about Freddy, for example. But really, you can't expect anything. Like, every license we've worked with has been very different. And even though a character has a lot of history, it doesn't mean that we, as a developer, have access to this history either legally in the partnership or, like, the people who actually worked on it. Maybe they didn't track anything, and we don't have access to it, right?

You know, here we could work with Damien and his team directly. You know, it's so precious when we do something contemporary like that. Also, the character, even though is quite fresh, is really well-defined. Like we know what this character stands for. We know we understand how it was built and what is great about him, and Sienna too, right? So, I'd say yeah, the history or the veteranhood of a character doesn't mean it's going to be easier or harder.

Damien states that he would have linked up sooner if he could, as soon as he started noticing more and more people digging Art:.

Yeah, yeah. Oh, as soon as an opportunity arises, I love it. I love it. I would have. I would have put him in this game years ago for sure. But you know, it's all sort of gradual baby steps. And you know, people ask, when did you know it was sort of, you know, you've arrived, or when did you know that you had a hit on your hands? And you never really think there's a particular moment, but you start seeing things over time that sort of make you know the light bulb goes on a little bit.

And I think originally it was, you know, you start seeing tattoos on a lot of people. It's one tattoo, and then it's like, then you start losing count of how many. Tattoos you're getting tagged in on Instagram. You're like, oh wow, you know, people really like this character, right? And then, you know, action figures and then things like that. So, I mean, I love those opportunities. Like I was saying before, it's really a unique and special position to be in.

Damien had nothing but nice things to say about Richard and his team translating Art, and how the process was very collaborative, but also respectful:.

I mean, you. Well, you guys. Just did such an incredible job of bringing sort of David's performance to life in this game, all right. And one reason people really gravitate toward this character is that he has so much fun doing what he does and being this sadistic killer clown. And you took so many of his really, you know, idiosyncratic sort of attributes and really injected them into this game. And I think, you know, hardcore horror fans who love, especially Terrifier, would just love to be in his, you know, clown shoes, you know, so to speak, a little bit.

According to recent reports, and like you mentioned, I mean, you really, you know, and when it comes to something like this, collaborating with this team, I trust them, right? I really don't want to step on their toes. You know, this is their wheelhouse, so I really just let them go. And of course, I mean, you know, they want me to be involved every step of the way. But for the most part, my main concern is: Are you capturing Art the Clown's likeness? Are you capturing his gestures, his mannerisms, his weapons? So that's really my concern.

Other than that, I mean, these guys know exactly what they're doing and exactly what their fan base is expecting, and you know what, a latest, sort of fresh approach they could take with Art that maybe they haven't quite gotten yet with another character. And I think that for me personally, as a fan, I think they knocked it out of the park, and I saw the care that they put into really capturing Art. So I'm thrilled.

Damien continues, talking about his fondness for Art, and how he fits the idea of a video game perfectly:.

It has been revealed that I think you nailed it. I think you know, aside from the video games, just for the films themselves, it's Art the Clown's charm that sort of allows us to get away with some of the really despicable things that we do. But that's by design, right? It's like, ultimately, I want the audience to have fun with the films, and, you know, ironically, I mean, Art the Clown is sort of the character that, even though he's the one doing the horrible things, he's sort of the one that breaks the fourth wall and kind of like always winks at the audience and reminds them that you know this is fantasy.

According to recent reports, we are just having fun here, and we're, you know, it's a callback to, you know, my generation of, you know, 80s slashers, that kind of void that's been missing. Right, they didn't take themselves too seriously. You know, we know we're in like part seven right now. You know, we know what this is. You know, those kinds of films.

With our time coming to a close, I really wanted to know how far the teams pushed to get all of Art's sadistic kills into the game, and whether there was any internal pushback. Richard gave us a thoughtful and interesting answer:.

It's an interesting question. Thanks for asking. Like, if we're going to do Terrifier, I mean, we can't sugarcoat it. It's expected it needs to be in there, right? And also, we have a 10-year-old game, so there are, you know, things in there that are difficult to do when compared to newer games, for example, like technology-wise and stuff like that.

Sources indicate that so there's a there was like a finesse here to see how we can make something creative in the kill, cruel that kind of makes you laugh, you know, with art, but at the same time make you, you know, cringe, without having access to realistic gore on screen. So I think the team did marvelous here.

DBD has been for a long time saying we are an accessible horror game. But there is a higher demand for more gore and more violence in media, but also from our fans. They're like, yeah, you can crank it up.

In the end, Terrifier seems to be changing Dead by Daylight going forward, and has already left its mark: "This was a great opportunity to test the waters, crank it up a little bit, you know, and maybe we'll crank it up even a little bit more in the future of Dead by Daylight when we get to that huge graphical rework that we've talked about during our anniversary.".

Marshals Season 2 Forces Kayce To Relive One Of His Most Controversial Yellowstone Storylines

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Marshals" Season 2, Episode 7, "Under the Influence," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Arielle Kebbel's Belle Skinner go undercover in an off-grid cult.
  • Kayce Dutton has been haunted by his "Yellowstone" experience since the very beginning of "Marshals." The youngest Dutton scion has seen it all (including the worst things the Dutton family ever did on "Yellowstone") and has been trying to put it all behind him since Taylor Sheridan's neo-Western series wrapped up back in 2024.
  • "Under the Influence" sees ATF agent Sam Colby (Adam Joel) go missing after embedding himself in Moonstone Farm, a homesteading cult led by the mysterious and intense Eric Savard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 7, "Under the Influence," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Arielle Kebbel's Belle Skinner go undercover in an off-grid cult. During their time there, Kayce is confronted by the cult's charismatic leader, who forces him to relive the loss of his infant child — a moment from "Yellowstone" that was both tragic and, in the eyes of many fans, ridiculous.

Kayce Dutton has been haunted by his "Yellowstone" experience since the very beginning of "Marshals." The youngest Dutton scion has seen it all (including the worst things the Dutton family ever did on "Yellowstone") and has been trying to put it all behind him since Taylor Sheridan's neo-Western series wrapped up back in 2024. Unfortunately, as Brett Cullen's Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Harry Gifford observed in "Marshals" Season 1, "Duttons are born with dysfunction in their blood," and "Under the Influence" forces Kayce to confront one of his most painful memories. That memory just so happens to be linked to one of the most controversial storylines in "Yellowstone" history.

"Under the Influence" sees ATF agent Sam Colby (Adam Joel) go missing after embedding himself in Moonstone Farm, a homesteading cult led by the mysterious and intense Eric Savard. This character is played by Beau Knapp, who delivers a surprisingly compelling performance as the Moonstone figurehead. (The show should bring him back ASAP.) After Kayce and Belle infiltrate the farm, Savard emerges to welcome them at a community meeting that promptly turns sinister when the cult leader forces Kayce to relive the trauma of losing his infant son. It's clearly a rough time for both the Dutton boy and for fans, who have to be reminded of this contentious "Yellowstone" moment.

It has been revealed that in "Under the Influence," Eric Savard confronts Kayce Dutton and asks him what he's lost. After a few lies, Savard pushes Kayce, and he's left with no choice but to draw from his real-life experience. "My son," he states. "He was barely an hour old. I wasn't even there." This is a reference to "Yellowstone" Season 5, in which a pregnant Monica Dutton (Kelsey Asbille) decides to drive herself to the hospital during early labor. Why? Well, that remains one of the biggest points of contention, as it seems she and Kayce had no birth proposal whatsoever. Meanwhile, Tate Dutton (Brecken Merrill) could have driven her but didn't, and for some reason, calling an ambulance was completely out of the question. All of this led to Monica driving herself, almost hitting a buffalo, swerving, and crashing head-on into an oncoming truck.

It has been revealed that the result was the loss of baby Dutton, who was set to be named in honor of Kayce's father, John Dutton (Kevin Costner), who himself suffered a terrible and controversial death in "Yellowstone" Season 5. Baby John passed away roughly an hour after the crash, which is what Kayce references in "Under the Influence.".

Baby John remains one of many "Yellowstone" characters who should never have died. His passing not only seemed avoidable but like a quick way to get some drama out of the show's final season and nothing more. Fans have since criticized the whole thing (check out Reddit to get a sense of their distaste), and it stands as one of the show's least effective storylines. Now, "Marshals" has tried to revisit it for some drama of its own. But like most things in this CBS spin-off, there's not really much beyond a surface-level reference.

Earlier in "Marshals" Season 2, we saw a flashback in which a young Kayce Dutton looked in the mirror at a fresh Yellowstone brand on his chest. This is the brand his father, John, used to bring relatives and ranch hands into the "Yellowstone" brotherhood, forever tying them to the ranch. That same brand is shown in "Under the Influence," wherein Kayce is pulled off a man he's fighting only for his shirt to open, revealing the unmistakable Yellowstone mark.

It has been revealed that "Marshals" Season 1 had trouble figuring out what it was about, juggling storylines and never seeming to explore any one of them in too much depth. That's mostly remained the case for Season 2, but there does seem to be a bit more of a focus on Kayce reckoning with his past. The second season of "Marshals" began by putting a twist on a "Yellowstone" tradition, namely by using animal imagery to evoke Kayce's inner emotional state. The character would encounter a Buffalo on his property at times when he was trying and failing to mentor Tate Dutton and steer him away from embracing what Tate calls "the Dutton way." Since then, we've seen a small but noticeable increase in scenes showing Kayce reflecting on his family's past.

"Under the Influence" might be the most significant in that respect, as it ends with Tate moving out of East Camp and Kayce drinking again after having abstained for years. What's more, Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz asks Logan Marshall-Green's Pete Calvin about Kayce's story, to which Pete replies it's not his place to tell. At this point, it seems as though the show's writers might actually be interested in going a little deeper into Kayce's Yellowstone trauma, and that's a good thing.

When Kate Middleton stepped out on the green carpet at the Earthshot Awards ceremony in Mumbai this week, it was “an absolute princess moment,” claims British designer Amanda Wakeley.

“Catherine has really come into her own. She has found her stride and a latest confidence, and you see that in this dazzling but also practical ‘tourdrobe,’’’ Wakeley, who has previously dressed the Princess of Wales and used to dress Princess Diana, tells Vanity Fair.

According to recent reports, it has been 10 years since Princess Kate last visited India. Her fashion choices are more sophisticated now than on her visit in 2016, and the speech she delivered at the Earthshot Prize ceremony on November 17 reveals a upcoming confidence. With her elevated look, there’s no trace of High Street labels. Kate’s flared floral dresses and the wedge shoes she used to love (but the late Queen Elizabeth apparently disliked) have been replaced by Manolo Blahnik pumps, couture power suits, and clothes by some of her favorite designers, such as Emilia Wickstead.

Prince William and Princess Kate attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

Kate’s decision to wear a striking vermilion dress made from handwoven silk by Upcoming Delhi–based designer Mahima Mahajan to the Earthshot Prize ceremony spoke volumes. The eye-catching dress, which she paired with a burgundy Prada velvet clutch, was chosen after Kate had selected a special suite of emeralds from the royal gem collection. The green stones on the dress perfectly matched her jewels, which served as an homage to both Queen Elizabeth II and India, as the green of the Indian flag represents growth and prosperity.

In a recent development, the dazzling stones known as the “emerald tassel suite” were worn frequently by the late Queen Elizabeth II, and while Kate has previously worn the earrings, this marked the first time she wore the set. The effect was dramatic.

“Never has Catherine looked more like a queen in waiting,” Wakeley notes of the look.

Wearing the suite ensured that Kate, who has free rein of the royal jewels, looked more regal than ever. “What was fascinating was seeing Catherine wear these incredible family heirlooms along with more relaxed collections from some of her favorite modern jewelry designers like Kiki McDonough and Astley Clarke,” remarks Wakeley.

Kate’s carefully curated wardrobe for the trip wasn’t just about power dressing—it was also about showing she can be sustainable as well as on trend.

“It was good to see Catherine making a proper nod to sustainability by rewearing her Roksanda dress,” Wakeley notes. “It’s clear a lot of thought has gone into her outfit choices. Her wardrobe has to be practical, and her clothes have to work harder than most people consider for their clothing; she needs weight in the hem of the floaty dresses. She has learned lessons the hard way. She is often seen bending down, talking to children, so she’s conscious of how low a neckline is, how short a skirt is.”.

Princess Kate visits the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital, on November 18, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

Industry observers note that for her visit to Mumbai’s Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital on November 18, Catherine chose a striking red tailored Emilia Wickstead skirt suit with Manolo Blahnik pumps. On November 16, she opted for a pistachio blazer by designer Veronica Beard, paired with white Alexander McQueen trousers and pearl-buckled Camilla Elphick flats, a relaxed and accessible look for when she picked up a cricket bat.

Princess Kate plays cricket on November 16, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

Industry observers note that as Princess of Wales, Catherine is often compared to Princess Diana. “The main difference is Diana was a fashion icon. Catherine has become a style icon,” Wakeley says. “There’s a significant difference. Diana played into the fashion of the day and was finding her style. During the time she resigned from public life, she worked out her style DNA. Catherine has had to do that on the job. Very wisely, she has worked out her style and doesn’t get too impacted by fashion and trends. She goes for what she likes. What works for her rather than trends. She really knows now what works for her.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I put out a public plea to Amazon and James Bond producers and all but begged them to cast Kristen Stewart as a Bond villain during Robert Pattinson's forthcoming run as the legendary British spy, I admitted that I'm not exactly a Bond superfan. Still, I'm excited that Pattinson is bringing his gifts as an actor — and, hopefully, his predilection for silly little voices — to this storied role. In the wake of this casting announcement, people have been fan-casting 007's standard array of supporting characters.

I do know, from the Daniel Craig run of Bond films, that Moneypenny — portrayed by Naomie Harris in those movies — works as the secretary to M, the head of MI6 and Bond's boss. (That role has been played, most recently, by Dame Judi Dench and Ralph Fiennes.) Harris' modern Moneypenny was sometimes found in the field alongside Bond, and there's a simmer of flirtation between them throughout their interactions ... so ideally, we're looking for a British actress who can flirt and hold her own against Pattinson's 007. Who should play Moneypenny in the Robert Pattinson Bond era? I have some ideas.

Since her breakout role on the sci-fi series "Humans," Gemma Chan has done a little bit of everything. She appeared in one of the most successful romantic comedies ever made, "Crazy Rich Asians," and left an impression as the wealthy but big-hearted Astrid. In "Eternals," she joined the Marvel Cinematic Universe (for the second time) as the deeply empathetic superhuman Sersi, who's in love with her fellow Eternal Ikaris (Richard Madden) despite hiding as a human on Earth and dating a guy named Dane Whitman (Madden's "Game of Thrones" brother Kit Harington). In "Mary Queen of Scots," she starred alongside Margot Robbie and Saoirse Ronan as Elizabeth of Hardwick, a close friend of Queen Elizabeth I (Robbie) who helps her capture the ill-fated Queen of Scots, Mary (Ronan). Chan is versatile; we know that. She's also one of the most beautiful people I've ever seen, and she'd make a great Moneypenny.

Seriously: imagine the feline, stunning Chan flirting up a storm with Robert Pattinson's Bond in one of his (hopefully many) movies in the franchise. The only knock against Chan is that she might be a little too serious — even in comedic projects like "Crazy Rich Asians," "The Afterparty," and "The Five-Star Weekend," she tends to play the straight man — but still, she'd be an excellent pick.

Sources indicate that if you don't read the name "Natalie Dormer" and immediately think about how she'd make a great Moneypenny, let me educate you. Dormer, an English actress who's been uniformly excellent for decades now, has played three notably flirtatious roles that have all helped define her career: the original temptress Anne Boleyn in "The Tudors"; Irene Adler (and Jamie Moriarty) in "Elementary"; and Margaery Tyrell on "Game of Thrones." In all three of these projects, Dormer's characters seduce and entrance the guy in charge — Jonathan Rhys-Meyers' King Henry VIII, Jonny Lee Miller's Sherlock Holmes, and brothers Joffrey and Tommen Baratheon, played by Jack Gleeson and Dean Charles Chapman, respectively — and have an ulterior motive simmering just below the surface.

Sources indicate that I stand ten toes down behind all of the picks on this list, but the more that I think about Dormer's particular brand of flirting opposite Robert Pattinson, the more I want to see it. Dormer doesn't get enough play for my liking. Not only would she make an unbelievable Moneypenny in future Bond movies, it would put her name back on the map ... and hopefully lead to some other fun projects where she gets to smirk and wink her way through the role. I know I begged for Kristen Stewart to be the villain; now I'm begging for Dormer to play Moneypenny.

It has been revealed that on some level, Anya Taylor-Joy is an obvious choice to play Moneypenny opposite Robert Pattinson as James Bond. She's gorgeous, has a British-adjacent accent (she was born in Miami but grew up in London), and she's one of the most popular actors working today. In fact, she's set to appear in the highly anticipated "Dune: Part Three" alongside Pattinson this coming December. Still, sometimes the obvious choice is the right one.

Taylor-Joy, who won a Golden Globe for her turn in the miniseries "The Queen's Gambit" and blew audiences away in movies like "The Witch," "The Menu," and "Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga," is one of the most interesting performers working today. In some ways, playing a "side" character like Moneypenny would be a downgrade for Taylor-Joy, who typically enjoys top billing on her projects. Still, I think she'd be a deeply fun addition to Pattinson's Bond franchise, and I have zero doubt, thanks in part to her work in Autumn de Wilde's stunning 2020 "Emma" adaptation and her turn in the fun but flawed "Last Night in Soho," that Taylor-Joy can flirt and banter with the best of them. Honestly, there's very little Taylor-Joy can't do as an actress, based on her body of work. If she has the time and the energy, I think it would be really lovely to see her pop up in Bond movies as Moneypenny.

Yes, I'm bringing another Westerosi royal into the Moneypenny conversation — but hear me out! Olivia Cooke, like Natalie Dormer, has been a reliable on-screen player for over a decade now. After making a name for herself in the dark indie movie "Thoroughbreds" — where she starred alongside Anya Taylor-Joy — Cooke appeared in "Ready Player One" and Oscar darling "The Sound of Metal" before booking a leading role in the first major "Game of Thrones" spin-off and prequel, "House of the Dragon.".

Industry observers note that on that series, Cooke plays the conniving and deeply flawed leader of the Green faction, Alicent Hightower, who betrays her childhood best friend Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D'arcy) by marrying Rhaenyra's ailing father, becoming the queen, and trying to supplant Rhaenyra with a younger male heir. Then, on the dishy Amazon Prime series "The Girlfriend" that aired in 2025, Cooke starred alongside Robin Wright as the absurdly named Cherry Laine, a flirtatious and openly sex-positive woman who starts dating a man with an overprotective mother (Wright).

According to recent reports, cooke is a versatile actress, and like Dormer, she's able to wield her beauty like a sharp weapon, which would make for an extremely fun performance as Moneypenny. "House of the Dragon" is set to wrap up after its fourth season, so Cooke will be free from that particular commitment. Amazon would be wise to snap her up for their next Bond era.

According to recent reports, michaela Coel is probably the most offbeat choice to play Moneypenny in a future James Bond project, but do me a favor and walk with me here. Ever since her breakout role in "Chewing Gum" and her heartbreaking work as a writer and star on her HBO masterpiece "I May Destroy You," Coel's profile has risen significantly, but I would selfishly like to see it rise further. The actress has popped up in everything from the "U.S.S. Callister" episode of "Black Mirror" to the psychosexual A24 drama "Mother Mary" alongside Anne Hathaway, and she's uniformly excellent in every single one of her performances.

Coel, who also has an Emmy for her guest performance on the Amazon Prime series "Mr. & Mrs. Smith" (and should have several for "I May Destroy You"), is a truly formidable actress who can hold her own against A-listers like Hathaway and Ian McKellen in 2025's "The Christophers," and I think she'd add a serious edge to Moneypenny that would just elevate this role. We don't know what future Bond movies will do with the character after Naomie Harris brought her into modern times, but after Harris, Coel is certainly a worthy actor to pick up the mantle and deliver her own sly, cunning take on Moneypenny. Seriously, if you have any doubt, go watch Coel in "Mother Mary" and tell me you wouldn't love to see her defiantly flirt with Pattinson's James Bond.

In a recent development, robert Pattinson's James Bond film, as of this writing, will release some time in 2028 with Denis Villeneuve as its director. Hopefully, we'll see one of these five astounding women play Moneypenny.

He might've produced some of the most acclaimed performances of all time, including winning two Academy Awards for Best Actor out of six total nominations (Philadelphia and Forrest Gump), but Tom Hanks might be best known to many as the voice of one of Pixar's best characters. Over three decades, Hanks' rootin'-est, tootin'-est cowboy has brought joy to theaters and homes around the world, and this year, he, Buzz (Tim Allen), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and the rest of the gang returned for their latest adventure.

According to recent reports, toy Story 5 debuted in June this year, immediately becoming the must-see movie of early summer. The film earned more than $1.1 billion in an impressive box office run, against a reported production budget of $250 million, which is right now enough to rank it as the third-highest-grossing film of the year. It was also a massive hit with critics, shaking off the mixed response to the previous installment. "The impressive fifth installment not only justifies its existence but feels like a necessary response to how much the world has changed in the past three decades," Taylor Gates wrote, giving the movie an 8/10 rating in her review.

Industry observers note that for Tory Story fans, 2026 has been another great year. But the last month comes with a sting in its tail, or rather a snake in its boot. On December 23, 2026, Toy Story 2 is officially leaving Hulu. Considered one of the greatest animated sequels of all time, this second installment debuted in 1999 and blew away both critics and audiences, managing the unthinkable by outperforming its groundbreaking predecessor. The film was directed by John Lasseter and written by Andrew Stanton.

In a recent development, toy Story 5 isn't the only franchise entry to be the third-highest-grossing film of its year. So was Toy Story 2, finishing behind The Sixth Sense and Star Wars Ep. 1: The Phantom Menace in the final rankings for 1999. The film scored a total haul of $511 million against a reported budget of $90 million, which was made up of $246 million in domestic revenue and a further $265 million from overseas markets.

In a recent development, toy Story 2 is leaving Hulu on December 23. Make sure to stay tuned to Collider for the latest stories.

One Variant Of Marvel's Doctor Doom Is A Descendant Of A Brutal Historical Villain

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the 2000s, Marvel Comics launched "Ultimate Marvel," a reboot that brought its lead characters into the 21st century.
  • "Ultimate Fantastic Four" also reimagined the FF's nemesis, Doctor Doom.
  • "Ultimate Fantastic Four" #7 (by Warren Ellis and Stuart Immonen) depicts Victor's childhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the 2000s, Marvel Comics launched "Ultimate Marvel," a reboot that brought its lead characters into the 21st century. "Ultimate Fantastic Four" pivoted from from the classic "astronauts bathed in cosmic rays" origin (which is so 1960s). Instead, the "Ultimate" FF were teen geniuses transformed in a teleportation experiment.

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" also reimagined the FF's nemesis, Doctor Doom. Renamed Victor Van Damme, this Doom was part of the Baxter Building think tank and was also transformed in the Four's accident. This Doom has no armor, but literal metal skin. (You can see that both the 2005 and 2015 "Fantastic Four" films took from "Ultimate Fantastic Four" for their Dooms, to their detriment.).

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" #7 (by Warren Ellis and Stuart Immonen) depicts Victor's childhood. On his tenth birthday, Victor's father revealed to him that they are descendants of Vlad Țepeș, or Vlad the Impaler/Vlad Dracula, the infamous 15th century king of Wallachia. Van Damme Sr. explains to his boy:.

According to recent reports, "Vlad Dracula understood that truth is inborn. That men of greatness must bend an ignorant world to their truth by any means necessary. And so he bent Wallachia to his will. He was cruel, but cruelty is no vice. It is a tool of necessity.".

In a recent development, from that moment, Victor was told he must be a man who bends the world to his will. His father instructs him to memorize his family line from Vlad down, beating him whenever he fails. Doom being the descendant of royalty, coming from money, and being imparted from childhood with lessons that a great leader is a ruthless one are all massive changes to his character. Victor von Doom acts like an aristocrat, but unlike Victor Van Damme, he came from nothing.

Doctor Doom is an Eastern European king, beloved by his own people but seen as monstrous by outsiders. He's a monarch in Vlad the Impaler's image, so making Doom a literal descendant of Vlad fits. But "Ultimate" Doom does not live up to his family legacy.

His first "kingdom" is a camp of squatters in Copenhagen. Clad in green rags (instead of a regal cloak), Doom compares his new skin to "Wallachian armor," but he didn't forge it himself. His metal body can form sharp spikes, like the kind on which Vlad impaled his enemies. Reed Richards, much pettier and hotheaded than his classic self, scratches Victor with one of those spikes and leaves a scar: "Impaled on your own sword, Victor.".

Vlad is associated with dragons; his father, Vlad II, was a member of the Order of the Dragon knighthood, and known as Vlad Dracul, or "Vlad the Dragon." (Vlad III's infamous moniker can mean "son of the dragon.") "Ultimate" Doom brands his followers with dragon tattoos made up of mind-controlling microfibers.

Dracula can also mean "son of the Devil." Doom's metallic body has cloven hoof legs, echoing goatlike depictions of Satan. But "Dracula" or not, Doom doesn't drink blood — and neither did the real Vlad the Impaler. Pop culture has reforged Vlad into the historical basis for Bram Stoker's "Dracula" and its vampiric villain. Later "Dracula" adaptations like Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 "Dracula" film or the action-horror manga "Hellsing" explicitly depict Dracula as the same person as the historical Vlad.

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" indulges this, too. Victor's father tells his son that Vlad let his enemies believe he drank blood. As Doom, Victor brands his subjects on their necks, and controls them like vampires do familiars.

Dotor Doom echoes both the historical Vlad and the literary Dracula; his fictional nation, Latveria, is a pastiche of the gothic Transylvania seen in "Dracula" movies. (Many "Fantastic Four" adaptations also insert Doom having an infatuation with Sue Storm that he never has had in the comics, like how many "Dracula" films make the Count and Mina Harker lovers, not monster and victim.).

"Dracula" is often paired with Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," especially thanks to Universal and Hammer's films of both. Doom melds "Dracula" with "Frankenstein." He shares Dr. Frankenstein's name, Victor, and both men's lives are defined by the death of their respective mothers. Victor Frankenstein tried to create life in grief over his mother's death, while the machine that blew up in Doom's face was an attempt to contact the "nether world" and his mother's soul.

As the classic Doom stands in the shadow of these villains, historical and literary, Victor Van Damme in "Ultimate Fantastic Four" stands in Doom's. "Ultimate Doom" almost feels like a purposefully-inverted villain, taking Doom down a peg yet only highlighting the strengths of the original.

Classic Doom was born into a poor Roma tribe. The world told him he was lesser and he made himself into a king to prove it wrong. "Ultimate" Doom was taught from childhood that the world was his birthright, but he isn't strong enough to carry it — like Kendall Roy if he was a Eurotrash super-villain. Classic Doom created an armored second skin to hide himself and his supposedly scarred face from the world. "Ultimate" Doom's flesh hardened like a chrysalis, turned brittle, and cracked off, leaving only metal — as if a heartless tin man with the features of the Devil is all he ever was.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nintendo Switch Online's expansive library of retro games is a treasure trove of nostalgic experiences, and it just got a little bit better.
  • Recent findings suggest that while I often think of Wave Race as a series that got its start on the Nintendo 64, the first Wave Race actually came out all the way back in 1992 for the Game Boy.
  • It has been revealed that blue Storm has an eclectic mix of courses too, like a Venice-inspired city, a frosty blue glacier, and a jungle river surrounded by ancient ruins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nintendo Switch Online's expansive library of retro games is a treasure trove of nostalgic experiences, and it just got a little bit better. That's because the 2001 GameCube racing game Wave Race: Blue Storm has just been added to the Nintendo Switch Online Plus Expansion Pack library. With the chilly season fast approaching, it's the perfect excuse for a little tropical getaway from the comfort of your couch.

Recent findings suggest that while I often think of Wave Race as a series that got its start on the Nintendo 64, the first Wave Race actually came out all the way back in 1992 for the Game Boy. The N64 version marked a significant leap forward with fully 3D environments, and Wave Race: Blue Storm goes a step further, thanks to the addition of unique weather conditions to mix up the action. Wave heights and visibility will vary depending on conditions, which can be sunny, foggy, rainy, or choppy. In addition to the weather, there are also hazards to keep an eye out for on each course, like leaping killer whales or trees falling into your path after being struck by lightning.

It has been revealed that blue Storm has an eclectic mix of courses too, like a Venice-inspired city, a frosty blue glacier, and a jungle river surrounded by ancient ruins. There's even one level where you bust through an intricate stained-glass window. Take that, church!

Blue Storm includes five modes for your sporting pleasure. Championship mode is the core single-player experience, where you'll go head-to-head with seven other riders across four courses, doing three laps on each one. Time Attack mode is exactly what it sounds like: a way to familiarize yourself with one course and winnow down your lap times. In Stunt Mode, you'll need to perform sick tricks and jumps across courses full of ramps and rings instead of simply getting to the finish fastest. Multiplayer provides couch co-op fun for up to four players, while Free Roam lets you explore the courses without any time pressure.

November marks the 25th anniversary of the GameCube's 2001 debut, and Wave Race: Blue Storm was one of its launch titles. It was the third-best-selling launch title for the platform in North America, behind Luigi's Mansion and Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader. Sadly, Nintendo hasn't revisited the series since, scrapping plans for a Wii installment that would have used both the Wiimote and the Balance Board peripheral. It's not too likely we'll see another Wave Race anytime soon, but it's definitely worth taking Blue Storm for a test-drive if you're a Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack member.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or-winning, Sebastian Stan-starring film "Fjord" will be available to rent on digital platforms beginning November 24, 2026. Given that this is a few days before Thanksgiving, "Fjord" will be the perfect film to watch with the extended family, and won't inspire any kind of snippy, angry political discussions whatsoever.

That, of course, is sarcasm. "Fjord" is, in fact, very, very political. According to /Film's review, "Fjord" is a clumsy, one-sided, and very ideologically weighted drama that is presented as unbiased through its efficient visuals and realistic style, but which is very biased indeed. Even in a room of people who are politically aligned, either to the left or the right, "Fjord" will inspire discussion. Or an argument. Watch it with your politically opposed family members, and let the sparks fly.

"Fjord" tells the story of the Gheorghiu family, which consists of stern Romanian father Mihai (not listed as one of Stan's best roles on /Film's countdown of them) and Norwegian mother Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), along with their two teens, two elementary-school-age kids, and an infant, who move from their long-term Romanian home to the small Norwegian town where Lisbet grew up. The Gheorghius are conservative Christians, which is very different from the local community, mostly made up of non-adherents.

When the Gheorghiu parents are unexpectedly accused of physically abusing their children, Norwegian Child Protective Services immediately takes the kids away (like, in an afternoon), leaving the Gheorghius having to find any kind of legal recourse to get them back. They will eventually have to explain themselves in court. The Gheorghius aren't wholly innocent, confessing to spanking their kids from time to time.

The progressive government of Norway is presented as being full of harridans and busybodies who are hellbent on removing children from their well-meaning parents. "Fjord" presents a political conflict between conservative and liberal ideologies. The Gheorghius attempt to gin up support for their cause by calling in conservative protestors and staging their legal struggle as a bias against Christians. By Romanian social norms, a light spanking is seen as socially appropriate, but the Norwegian government is determined to keep the Gheorghiu kids away from Mihai and Lisbet. The movie sides with the conservative characters, making the entire film feel like light social propaganda.

Recent findings suggest that "Fjord," however, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, as well as the François Chalais Prize, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury, and the Prix de la Citoyenneté. It is also beloved by most critics, racking up a 91% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 165 reviews. Justin Chang's review in The Fresh Yorker noted that some of the villains in "Fjord" are unrealistically larger-than-life, but that it was ultimately subtle. He wrote:.

It has been revealed that "Is 'Fjord' guilty, as some have charged, of stacking the moral decks in the Gheorghius' favor? We are presented with a few potentially hissable villains ... Yet Mungiu has an uncommon ability to temper bluntness with nuance.".

According to recent reports, as soon as it's easily available to rent online, one can watch "Fjord" for themselves and see if it's politically charged, naturally neutral, or morally complex. Cristian Mungiu tends to handle politically difficult concerns with frankness and directness; he reminded us of the necessity of abortion with his 2007 drama "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days." You, however, are the one can must decide if "Fjord" is as powerful.
