Recent findings suggest that this film deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps as recently as September signed a fresh overall TV deal with Disney’s 20th Television, with him exiting his Netflix deal. That pact doesn’t begin until October 2027.

Levy is reuniting with Sony’s leadership Tom Rothman and Sanford Panitch after he previously directed the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” and “Date Night” for them while they were all at Fox.

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman remarked in a statement. “His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative firm around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm. I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy mentioned in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a bighearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful. 21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”.

While just about everyone else in Hollywood has taken a victory lap with the success of “Backrooms,” you may have forgotten that Levy and 21 Laps were producers on the A24 horror movie, and he of course directed and produced Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” which concluded at the end of last year. Up next for Levy is “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which is a “Star Wars” spinoff starring Ryan Gosling and which opens May 28, 2027. And he’s also teaming with Gosling and Disney yet again on Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which opens July 28, 2028. His last feature he directed was “Deadpool & Wolverine,” which made $1.3 billion worldwide.

On the 21 Laps side, the banner is producing a rom-com with Emma Stone and Chris Pine set at Universal called “The Catch;” Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons;” Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

Ever since the project was first announced, "Whalefall" remained a fixture in our most anticipated film of 2026 ... and the movie adaptation most definitely lived up to the hype, at least according to, uh, myself. Who wouldn't be interested in the story of a scuba diver with some serious daddy issues getting caught up in a life-or-death struggle between a sperm whale and a squid, ending up swallowed whole by the aforementioned whale, and needing to find a way to escape before his oxygen supply runs out? Though the original Daniel Kraus novel was previously considered an unadaptable work, writer/director Brian Duffield found a way, and the results speak for themselves.

Of course, that was the experience of watching "Whalefall" on the big screen. What about at home? Fans who found themselves gasping for breath, shielding their eyes, and otherwise staving off panic attacks in theaters (or was that just me?) can now see if the experience translates to the comforting confines of your own living room. 20th Century Studios has unveiled that "Whalefall" will swim towards a digital PVOD release on December 1, 2026. Those who rent or purchase a digital copy from the online retailer of their choice will also get an exclusive bonus feature (a terrible home media trend we've spoken out on before) in the form of a "Creature Design Audio Commentary" featuring production designer Ramsey Avery and VFX supervisor Guillaume Rocheron.

Fortunately, viewers can look forward to the film's upcoming release on physical media early in the new year as well.

In a recent development, if you ended up asking yourself "How the heck did they even do that?" every five minutes while watching "Whalefall," we have some excellent news. The ambitious film that once again puts poor Austin Abrams through the wringer after this year's "Resident Evil" won't just be available to watch at home in less time than it takes to be digested by a whale (don't quote me on that fact), it will also come loaded with extras, bonus features, and other goodies for the eager film enthusiast. We need only wait until January 12, 2027, for the official 4K UHD, Blu-ray, and DVD release, which boasts the following behind-the-scenes treats:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that don’t let the title fool you: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” might offer up a breezy, very fun-to-watch new entry into the life and times of titular (and fictitious) Hollywood stuntman, but co-star Elizabeth Debicki steals the show in David Fincher’s film (in addition to stealing the heart of Brad Pitt’s Cliff). Is it time to greenlight “The New Adventures of Karen Crosby”? We think so.

According to recent reports, the much-anticipated sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon in Hollywood” picks up nearly a decade after the Oscar-winning antics of the previous film, finding Cliff pursuing new professional endeavors (film projecting! bartending! contract killing, kind of!). Stunt work? Eh, only when he feels like, and he certainly feels like after taking an unexpected meeting with Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), whose grace and good humor instantly delight both Cliff and the audience. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie.

It has been revealed that tossed together by the wacky demands of Karen’s marquee client, actor Charlie Nelson (Scott Caan), the shaggy, Tarantino-penned “Cliff Booth” meanders its way through every corner of Hollywood, finding real emotional ballast and crackling chemistry every time Pitt and Debicki share the screen. Characteristically wordy and dense, we learn plenty about Karen along the way (including her early forays into film criticism and her current feelings about movies), and she wins Cliff’s heart by, well, literally and physically slapping the crap out of him.

Ahead, IndieWire catches up with the Aussie star (who gets to use her real accent this time) about Fincher’s film, from slapping her co-star to some serious ruminations on the instantly iconic “pig monologue speech.” No wonder Cliff went so crazy for Karen; she’s a delight.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: What was your relationship with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” when the film came out in 2019?

Sources indicate that elizabeth Debicki: I went to see it in the cinema. I think I went by myself, which makes me think I must have been on a job. I was definitely in the States, maybe I was in L.A., and I went one afternoon. I went and sat in the cinema, and I loved it. It’s really vivid in my memory.

It has been revealed that I didn’t watch it again before we made this for performance reasons. In a way, I realized I didn’t really need to because, [there’s] something about Quentin’s movies, they just kind of wedge themselves in your brain. I can literally see the Playboy Mansion scene. I can see the Manson kids driving up to the house. I can see Margaret Qualley’s feet on the dashboard. I can see everything.

So it sounds like you came into this as a Tarantino fan.

Sources indicate that absolutely. Yeah. I mean, he’s seminal.

And to get Tarantino and Fincher is this incredible two-for-one.

It’s funny, because obviously in the making of this, I had to sort of normalize that. And they helped me do that because they were, from the second I got onto set — which was a two-week rehearsal period where we really worked through the script — we had Quentin for that whole period. [It was] very, very collaborative.

Recent findings suggest that A part of me wonders whether it was that thing where they have sat with the material for so long and had their full body relationship to it, and then I was fresh. I had my own thoughts and feelings. My memories of those rehearsal periods were really all three of them [Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt] just turning to me and saying, “What do you think? What do you think?” The first time it happened, I was like, “Oh my God, what do I think?” After a little while, I started to actually say what I thought, which was great.

What was your audition process like?

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t audition for this. David emailed me and asked me if I would be interested in playing a part. I remember he phrased it in an email as he hoped that I would consider playing a very tricky part in a film he was hoping to make in July. It was a very David-ism kind of email. I think it mentioned something like, “I hope you understand the seriousness of this conundrum,” or something. And I called him up and yeah, I was obviously ready to say, “I’ll do it.”.

He was very, very insistent. He was like, “Wait, wait, wait. I really want to tell you everything about it.” Because at that point he and Quentin were doing a massive edit of the script. He couldn’t send it to me there and then.

Industry observers note that karen is so singular, but she is in a familiar position if you’re working in Hollywood. Did you base any part of your performance on any agents or managers or publicists that you know or have encountered?

It has been revealed that when I first read the script, there were things that just rang so true to me, and might seem outrageous for anyone or slightly absurd maybe for anyone who doesn’t work in this industry. The incredible pig scene where Cliff talks about killing a pig, and then the scene in the car where Karen notes, “Now because of you, I now have to spend my entire morning finding a pig. That is not a joke, that is literally what I have to get up and do. And you know what? I had a lot of things I had to do, and it wasn’t find a pig. And now I have to drive your ass all the way to Marina del Rey because I have to just deliver you because that’s what my client needed.”.

It’s kind of this absurd ask, but it’s folded into “that’s what I need for my process.” Quentin and David, they’re so fascinating because they are Hollywood. They are Hollywood, and also they sit outside it, and they observe it from these very, very unique vantage points. Quentin, in particular, his love affair with L.A. is so profound, and with Hollywood. Part of the thing I loved about her too is that she’s sort of accidentally an agent, which is not frequently do you come across that. One of the things too that feels very human about her is that she sort of had this other dream, but she took one really bad knock, and it broke her heart, and she just buried it deep inside and then made decisions based off that.

When we get to that scene with Karen and Cliff when you’re talking about how Karen had this other career as a film critic, I how much of that was lifted from what would’ve been Quentin’s movie, “The Movie Critic”?

I don’t know. I don’t actually know the answer to that question in terms of the parallel there. But I do love that in the middle of this film about 1977 in Hollywood, that there’s a really notable moment where we think about Pauline Kael, and we think about her and she lives in this film. I’m so glad that there’s this moment where my character gets to say, “Pauline Kael is my god,” because she was. She was incredible.

Sources indicate that as Karen, you have this great monologue explaining to Cliff who you used to be, what had happened with that career path, how wonderful it was that Pauline supported you, and then it didn’t work out. And then you have another monologue about seeing movies as hamburgers. It’s a really funny tension for Karen, because the audience likely assumes she loves movies and does see them as art.

It has been revealed that that’s right, there is a tension there. I feel like one of the things that Quentin can do so well, and kind of totally unique to his own brain, is that he sort of plucks an idea out of the zeitgeist, something that we’re all thinking about, and he feeds it through his characters in a way that feels very organic. This is a big conversation that people are having as the industry shifts and changes. It also was a huge conversation that was happening in 1977. There was this big question of, “Is that art still if it’s commercial, if its box office success equates to this?” I think that the dichotomy of what she believes in her heart and wants to be true and what she spouts in front of people, I sort of think both things are true at once, and I think that’s just the kind of human element.

But I also think that it’s crucial to remember in that monologue that Charlie really pulls it out of her. She really doesn’t want to do the dance, the dancing monkey, or what did she say? “There’s a dancing bear aspect to your request,” I think is such a great line. But yeah, I think both things are true for her.

You have the sense she’s remarked this speech before, and again, maybe she doesn’t totally believe it, but Charlie just loves it and so she has to do it.

According to recent reports, david and I spoke about it a lot, and we sort of landed on we feel like she did it once off the cuff, like at a table at the Emmys or the Globes, and everyone went, “Gee, Karen, that’s genius.” And Charlie heard it and went, “Yeah, that’s genius. She’s my agent, look how smart she is. She’s so great.” Then she’s done it one other time at a dinner. So, by the time we get to the pool, she’s like, “Oh, my God.” It’s becoming a routine against her will, which was also a really fun element to play with in terms of how much she does or doesn’t enjoy it, and finding that balance.

Do you personally read reviews of your work?

Has that always been the case for you?

Has it always been the case? [Smiles] I’m sure anyone who doesn’t read a review once read a bad review.

It doesn’t even have to be a bad one. What I learned is, you can read a review that is seemingly positive, but it might not be what you were trying to do, and then you feel heartbroken about that too. So yes, I really avoid it. Yeah.

You get to slap Brad Pitt a lot in this film. Was that hard to do?

It’s a very beautiful face, and we had to do it. We had to do it. And Brad is a very good sport and a very good stuntman. I think that Brad was very, very comfortable, and I was very nervous. We shot the dialogue for two days, that we were just in almost this sort of trance of the two of them, and of the very unusual power dynamic that [they have]. One of the best things about that scene to me, which I didn’t analyze at the time, it’s so intricate the way that Quentin wrote it. It’s this moment where, in revealing what he wants, he becomes so vulnerable that the power dynamic kind of very subtly shifts in this kind of core foundational way between these two characters.

So, we shot that for two days and then all of a sudden it was like, “Oh, my God, it ends, and I need to figure out how to do this.” We had an amazing stunt coordinator on that job.

We had to do extremely complex things with people, but with me, I was like, “Hey Dave, could we just pop out the back there and have a little chat about the slap…?”.

Everyone knows that David likes to do a lot of takes. How many takes was the actual slapping?

Industry observers note that not so many! It was probably the least amount of takes we did. We probably did a couple, five, maybe six. And then I do remember that Brad sort of went, “OK, I think we got it. I think we’re good now,” and we moved on. But we did the inside [slap] first. It was such a joy to do. It’s such a happy memory. We filmed it, and then we all ran around to the monitor, and we watched it in playback, and we’re like, “Oh, my God, it’s so good.” And then we filmed it again. We were so pleased with ourselves. [Laughs].

What scenes did David ask for the most takes?

The thing about the takes is, it’s coverage-dependent. So, if you have four actors in a scene, like the hamburger monologue, let’s say there’s four setups on each actor, you do 10 takes per setup. So, that becomes a lot.

In a recent development, I will say that in the pig speech monologue, I don’t have a lot of lines, but we did just as much coverage on me as we did on Brad and Scott. That was one of my first days on set, and I remember thinking, “This is so, so unusual. Why is he doing this?” And then a couple weeks later, he showed me a kind of rough edit, and I thought, “Oh, my God, that’s why he did it.” He is using Karen as the kind of go-between. As David would always say, at least there’s one grown-up in the room, and it’s Karen.

So I do have this really funny memory too of doing that during the pig monologue scene. I was off-camera, or we were catching just the side of me; I was very much out of focus, and I took a drag of the cigarette, and I remember he gave me a note for that, something about the speed of it or the intention of it. And I remember thinking ….

Industry observers note that exactly! I was like, “You saw that?” And he was right, he was absolutely right, but I thought, “OK, this is not a set where we get away with anything.”.

It has been revealed that especially in that scene, you have these facial expressions where you are having the appropriate reaction to what we’re hearing, but in such a beautiful way. I think that’s when we all fall in love with Karen. We’re like, “She gets it. She knows how ridiculous this is,” but she is part of this world.

In a recent development, I’m particularly proud of the Tic Tac crunch; that was my prop idea, and I just thought we should end with her crunching down on something, because she’s so pissed about having to then go and spend her entire morning looking for a hog in Malibu Colony or something. Where is she even going to find that pig?

Industry observers note that she did it. I mean, David and I would talk about that too. I’m like, “Do you think she did it or she sent Mallory, her assistant, to go do it?” Either way, someone did it, someone paid for it.

Speaking of falling in love with Karen, there’s been this sentiment circulating as people see the film that there is a real rom-com built into it with Cliff and Karen. Do you see it that way?

I don’t think it’s a rom-com, but I think it’s romantic, and I think they’re funny. Don’t get me wrong, rom-coms are my religion. Yesterday I was walking through Latest York, and I literally felt like I was in “You’ve Got Mail.” I was like, “This fall day, I need a bunch of sharpened pencils.” But I don’t think that this necessarily falls into that category. It’s sort of undefinable, indefinable, but I do think it’s really romantic. I felt that when we were playing it, and we really enjoyed that together.

Sources indicate that the romance of it is kind of surprising, because it surprises her. It’s sort of best case scenario romance, that you think you have it all together, and this person walks in that you absolutely dismiss in terms of that, and then little by little they just sort of reveal this thing. More beautifully, they pull something out of you. I didn’t necessarily intellectualize any of this while we were shooting it, it’s just that I can see that now retrospectively. Not that I read anything, but I am curious what people will make of them.

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

IMAX will screen everything from the pregame and postgame coverage, the full four-hour presentation of the game itself, and of course the Halftime Show headlined by Jay-Z, all beginning at 6 pm ET. ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast team of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters, and Laura Rutledge will be the ones you hear in the theater, so no luck if you’re a Peyton and Eli or Pat McAfee fan. The only thing we don’t know is who’s playing in the game just yet, but this Chicago Bears fan is feeling pretty good about his team’s chances. Sources indicate that tickets are expected to go on sale in January. Specific theater locations and ticketing information will be declared in the coming weeks.

This is the first time IMAX is screening something as substantial as the Super Bowl, but it’s not the first time IMAX has played live sporting events in its theaters. IMAX also screened the opening ceremony for the Paris Olympics, it this year did a series of F1 races in partnership with Apple TV, and events like NHL games and even the NBA Finals have played internationally. This is on a much bigger scale as well, as this will be available in hundreds of IMAX screens across the country.

Recent findings suggest that ABC, Disney, and ESPN hadn’t been in the rotation for the Super Bowl for a long time, so they’ve been going all out for their first go around. Disney is making the game available via broadcast on ABC, as well as on ESPN and Univision, and also for streaming on Disney+. ESPN is also doing an alternate telecast on ESPN 2 with Peyton and Eli Manning as they do for “Monday Night Football” throughout the regular season. And it was previously announced that “The Pat McAfee Show” is getting in on the fun with its own Super Bowl show on ESPNU and “Playbook with Next Gen Stats” on NFL Network.

This is really a boon for theaters to do added business on a day and weekend when most theaters are pretty empty and the latest movie options are few and far between. We’ll see though how the box office responds and how many people relocate their Super Bowl parties to their local multiplex.

Sources indicate that “Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic new scale,” stated Ken Potrock, President, Major Event Integration for The Walt Disney Tech giant. “With ESPN’s first Super Bowl, we’re reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be, with unique moments that only Disney and ESPN can deliver.”.

Industry observers note that “The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great IMAX experience,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of IMAX. “This is a milestone for IMAX that further elevates our standing as a premier global platform for entertainment and events, and we’re excited to work in partnership with Disney, ESPN and the NFL to give football fans an unforgettable night.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for Tracker Season 4, Episode 7.

Sources indicate that although Tracker has a strong, confident, and irreplaceable leading man in Justin Hartley's Colter Shaw — seriously, we wouldn't want our favorite reward seeker to ride into the sunset any time soon — this week's "That's The Job" suggests that perhaps the CBS drama could share its top billing. In this case, the episode introduced us to Luke Kelso, a bounty hunter played by Josh Holloway, who offers some real charisma and potential for narrative growth and development. Could Tracker be hoping to introduce another rewardist with a heart of gold? If "That's The Job" proved anything, it's that there's certainly room for such a recurring force.

Like Colter Shaw, Luke Kelso has a somewhat tragic past that has led him to the world of bounty hunting. He may not have had a father who trained him to be a lone wolf survivalist, but his time in the foster system taught him resilience, and he acquired other skills in the following years that led to becoming a bail bondsman before venturing into his seedier chosen profession. But perhaps the most interesting thing about Luke is that he has often found himself on the wrong side of not just the law, but his own moral code — and it takes meeting Colter and seeing a job through to finally realize that. It's not until Luke sees those errors in his ways, the outcome of his "take the money and run" mentality, that he then understands the value in what Colter does. By the time we leave him in "That's The Job," Luke is a changed man — one who could easily find himself back on Tracker at any given time.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it notes about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

In a recent development, you would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

You know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

You are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

In a recent development, tracker has had a good track record with recurring allies that come back into Colter's life at just the right times. Jensen Ackles has been a presence as Colter's brother Russell (who remains perfect spin-off material) since the first season, as has rival reward-collector and thief Billie Matalon (Sofia Pernas). Likewise, former detective John Keaton (played by Brett Sexton) has made himself a welcome recurring presence since the second season. But unlike the rest of these leading characters, who all have their own things going, John Holloway's Luke Kelso feels so seamless in Colter's world that we could easily see him as either a co-lead or a rotating leading man who tackles select cases throughout the season. Indeed, we've suggested previously that Russell could fill that role in Tracker if the CBS program were to take notes from the classic Western series Maverick, which famously alternated its leading men and occasionally brought them together.

According to recent reports, again, this isn't to say we'd ever want Colter totally replaced with someone else — far from it. Arguably the show's biggest draw is Justin Hartley himself, who continues to use his on-screen charisma to charm his way into the hearts and minds of viewers each week. If not for the Yellowstone-adjacent Marshals, he may very well still be the most popular leading man currently on network television. However, the show is called Tracker, not Colter Shaw (or even Shaw, for that matter). It could be interesting if the occasional episode or two were headlined now and then by someone like Luke. Now that Colter has inspired him to look at the job differently, his weekly routine may not look all too different from our main hero's, and it might give Hartley the chance to enjoy some R&R while not sacrificing what makes the show engaging in the first place, namely the weekly caseload and twisty one-and-done mysteries.

At the very least, it's clear that Holloway (billed as a "special guest star," like Ackles) deserves some additional Tracker screen time. Not only would we adore a team-up between Luke and Russell, but finding ways to further challenge this character as he now seeks a more righteous path would be a great way to bring him back. Perhaps there are other cases that haunt Luke that he now cannot get out of his head? Maybe he looks back on previous jobs and discovers he has been on the wrong side of the conflict on other occasions as well? Finding ways for Luke to further explore his failures and seek to make them right would certainly be enough cause for his return — or even another idea for a spin-off.

Not only does "That's The Job" wrestle with Luke's failures, but Colter's as well. Because of Luke's interference, Colter failed at his own task and was unable to bring a good man home to those he loved. It's the tragedy of the work that, sometimes, things don't all turn out happy in the end. While this is not the first time that Tracker has explored such failures, the arrival of Luke gives Colter (and the audience) an interesting glimpse of the type of man he might have become if he had any less integrity than he does now.

Tracker airs on Sundays on CBS and is available for streaming the next day on Paramount+.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that few actors have left as significant a mark on television and film as Patrick Stewart. Throughout his extraordinary career, the classically trained British actor became synonymous with some of entertainment's most recognizable characters, including Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men. However, his talents extended far beyond the dramatic performances that made him a household name.

It has been revealed that stewart possessed a remarkable ability to command attention regardless of how much screen time he received. While his leading roles demonstrated his dramatic range, his guest appearances frequently revealed another side of his abilities. From outrageous comedic performances to unexpected celebrity cameos, Stewart proved that even the smallest roles could leave lasting impressions.

Sources indicate that following Stewart's death on October 28, 2026, at the age of 86, his extensive body of work offers myriad reminders of his versatility. Although audiences will undoubtedly remember his contributions to major franchises, some of his most entertaining performances came when he stepped outside those familiar characters and embraced opportunities to showcase his comedic timing and willingness to poke fun at himself.

Recent findings suggest that across several decades, Stewart delivered unforgettable guest appearances that occasionally overshadowed the shows themselves. Whether portraying eccentric characters or exaggerated versions of himself, these five performances show why his presence could elevate practically any project, no matter how briefly he appeared.

Stewart's appearance in Frasier remains one of the sitcom's most entertaining celebrity cameos. In the season 11 episode "The Doctor Is Out," Stewart portrays Alistair Burke, a renowned opera director who mistakenly believes Frasier Crane is gay. Rather than immediately correcting the misunderstanding, Frasier lets Alistair continue pursuing him because he enjoys the exclusive social opportunities that come with their supposed relationship.

It has been revealed that stewart's performance is particularly memorable because he so effortlessly embraces Alistair's extravagance. His character showers Frasier with attention, lavish experiences, and the promise of a glamorous lifestyle, leaving the psychiatrist increasingly reluctant to admit the truth. The resulting comedy becomes even more effective because Stewart plays Alistair with complete sincerity rather than treating him as a caricature.

While Frasier was already known for its guest stars, Stewart's chemistry with Kelsey Grammer makes this appearance particularly remarkable. His sophisticated demeanor complements Frasier's personality, while Alistair's romantic confidence creates increasingly uncomfortable situations for the show's central character. Stewart's performance even earned him an Emmy nomination, demonstrating how thoroughly he could steal the spotlight in a single episode.

Few Stewart guest appearances demonstrate his willingness to ridicule his distinguished reputation quite like his performance in Ricky Gervais' Extras. Appearing as a fictionalized version of himself in the first season's finale, Stewart encounters aspiring actor Andy Millman, who hopes the established star might help advance his career. However, their conversation quickly takes an unexpected turn when Stewart begins enthusiastically describing a screenplay he's developing.

Recent findings suggest that rather than presenting himself as the sophisticated actor audiences recognize, Stewart portrays an absurdly immature version of himself whose screenplay revolves around increasingly ridiculous scenarios involving women's clothes mysteriously disappearing. His unwavering enthusiasm for these juvenile ideas becomes the centerpiece of the scene, especially as Andy struggles to understand how such an accomplished performer could find them so entertaining.

What makes Stewart's appearance particularly effective is his refusal to acknowledge the absurdity of his character's behavior. His theatrical delivery and seemingly genuine excitement transform an outrageous conversation into one of the show's funniest celebrity encounters. By enthusiastically undermining his own public image, Stewart demonstrates a remarkable sense of humor that makes his brief appearance unforgettable.

It has been revealed that one of Stewart's final television performances also ranks among his most unconventional. In Prime Video's Bait, Stewart lends his unmistakable voice to a severed pig's head that begins speaking to struggling actor Shah Latif, played by Riz Ahmed. The surreal character emerges as Shah faces intense scrutiny after becoming a potential candidate to play James Bond, forcing him to confront questions surrounding his identity and career.

Stewart's involvement becomes particularly memorable when the series initially presents him as an interviewer questioning Shah about his ambitions. However, the conversation takes a disturbing turn when the audience discovers that Shah is actually speaking to the pig's head, which embodies his internalized insecurities and criticism. Stewart's authoritative delivery makes the character both intimidating and unexpectedly humorous.

According to recent reports, although the premise sounds ridiculous, Stewart's performance reinforces the series' exploration of prejudice, ambition, and belonging. His recognizable voice gives Shah's internal conflict an almost overwhelming presence, demonstrating how effectively Stewart could command attention without physically appearing on screen. Bait stands as a fitting reminder that Stewart remained willing to embrace unusual creative opportunities throughout his career.

Recent findings suggest that long before celebrity voice appearances became commonplace in animated television, Stewart delivered one of The Simpsons' most memorable guest performances. In the season 6 episode "Homer the Great," Stewart voices Number One, the mysterious leader of the Stonecutters, a secret society whose members enjoy considerable influence throughout Springfield. When Homer Simpson discovers the organization's existence, his attempts to join inevitably threaten its carefully maintained traditions.

According to recent reports, stewart's distinctive voice proves particularly effective in portraying Number One, whose commanding presence makes the Stonecutters appear far more vital than their ridiculous activities suggest. His character initially struggles with Homer's disruptive behavior, only to discover that Homer possesses a birthmark identifying him as the organization's prophesied Chosen One.

The humor largely comes from the contrast between Stewart's dignified delivery and the increasingly absurd circumstances surrounding the Stonecutters. Rather than exaggerating his performance to match the show's chaotic energy, Stewart approaches Number One with the seriousness audiences associate with his dramatic roles. This contrast makes his character especially entertaining and highlights why his recognizable voice was such an asset to animated comedy. Even surrounded by The Simpsons' established characters, Stewart makes Number One an unforgettable addition to the episode.

It has been revealed that patrick Stewart voiced several characters in Family Guy, but his best performance was as himself, as the cameo offered a different opportunity to revisit his Star Trek: The Next Generation legacy. In season 7's "Not All Dogs Go to Heaven," Stewart reunites with several former TNG castmates, including Jonathan Frakes, LeVar Burton, and Wil Wheaton, for an animated storyline that takes their established reputations in an unexpectedly ridiculous direction.

After attending a Star Trek convention, Stewie Griffin becomes frustrated when he cannot ask the actors his questions. Naturally, his solution is to kidnap the entire cast and force them to spend time with him. Rather than behaving like the sophisticated professionals audiences might expect, the actors become increasingly childish and difficult for Stewie to manage, turning his dream encounter into an exhausting experience.

Stewart's willingness to play along makes the reunion especially entertaining. Having spent years portraying one of science fiction's most respected leaders, he embraces the opportunity to portray a comically exaggerated version of himself alongside his former colleagues. Although the ensemble shares the spotlight, Patrick Stewart's involvement reinforces his ability to laugh at his own legacy. The episode also serves as an amusing reminder that his chemistry with the TNG cast extended well beyond their original series.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note: This article contains spoilers for “Minotaur.”.
  • Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.
  • In a recent development, seriously, spoilers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: This article contains spoilers for “Minotaur.”.

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.

In a recent development, seriously, spoilers. This is never more true than in the absurdly sad and funny, then suddenly murderous confrontation between cuckolded husband Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) and his wife’s lover Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk) at the hinge point of “Minotaur.” Related Stories 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’ Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer.

Zvyagintsev and Dergachev generally strive to preserve as much authentic production sound from performances as possible. “On my third movie, ‘Elena,’ we recorded the live sound from shooting, and it’s maybe two or three phrases we had to rerecord, but otherwise the whole sound that you hear is fully recorded during the shooting,” Zvyagintsev told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “Our main purpose is to keep as much sound from the shooting as possible and not to add anything extra, and it was the same for ‘Minotaur.’”.

Industry observers note that but for the moment that Gleb attacks Anton, and its aftermath, it was important to Zvyagintsev that the world beyond the apartment start intruding on Gleb — that even though he wants desperately to cover up what he’s done and make sure no one sees or learns about it, we hear dozens of ways in which he isn’t alone. That required a lot of work outside of the studio to record the background noises Zvyagintsev and Dergachev could then layer into the scene.

“We were creating [background] sounds of the kids playing football in the backyard. We would spend the whole day recording the kids, how they’re speaking, the way they’re playing, people passing by on the street,” Zvyagintsev stated. They also recorded different sound layers from Gleb’s luxury SUV, which they could deploy to create maximum panic in both Gleb and the audience.

“The car signals, the leaves on the street, the birds — they all pronounced, and [emphasized] something. So we were modulating all those layers that we recorded, and then we combined them to create the atmosphere and to put it all in one place for the scene,” Zvyagintsev remarked.

There’s atmosphere from outside and from inside, as Zvyagintsev and Dergachev refused to let Gleb have a moment of peace on the soundtrack — until, as with all the cruel jokes of “Minotaur’s” filmmaking, he gets it in the worst way, at the worst possible moment. There’s a terrible silence once he’s struck Anton on the head with his own camera. And then the world comes rushing back in, even louder than before.

“We were trying to create this volume of sounds right after the hit. And then, when Anton is falling, there is this complete silence. And then somewhere far away we hear the car alarm and even more sounds that create this volume. This is what we were looking for,” Zvyagintsev mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that it was key to finesse the sound design of the sequence so as not to overplay it. Zvyagintsev initially wanted to add music to the moment, but had to hold himself back. “It was really tempting,” Zvyagintsev stated. “My composer Evgueni Galperine even wrote the music, which we added. But when we saw the result, we realized, and I understood that no, no, it has to be completely silent.”.

In a recent development, silent as the grave, one might say. But it’s the sound design, the modulation between loudness and silence, that makes the moment so horrifying. Zvyagintsev and Dergachev did it by hand, just to make sure of it.

“Minotaur” is now playing in select theaters.

Published: 14:59 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 15:01 EST, 18 November 2026.

Bayern Munich's chief executive has confirmed Vincent Kompany is expected to return to the dugout on Friday, less than a month after collapsing at the club's training ground.

Kompany collapsed on October 23 while watching Bayern's Under-23 side and reportedly suffered from seizures.

The 40-year-old, who suffered a dislocated shoulder in the fall, underwent tests in hospital which determined that a 'meningeal irritation' had been the cause of his collapse.

If left untreated meningeal irritation can become meningitis. The meninges are the membranes around the brain and spinal cord.

Kompany was discharged from hospital the following week to continue his recovery at home.

The Belgian coach is now set to return to the dugout when Bayern face Cologne on Friday, with Kompany due to also address the media tomorrow morning.

Vincent Kompany is set to return to the Bayern Munich dugout for their Bundesliga match on Friday.

Kompany's return was officially confirmed by Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen.

According to recent reports, 'Yes, Vincent is in pretty good spirits. I ran into him today,' Dreesen told German outlet Abendzeitung.

Recent findings suggest that 'The meningeal irritation has healed. He has already undergone shoulder surgery.'.

Kompany had led training for the first time since his collapse earlier this week, with his arm reportedly in a sling following his shoulder injury.

He had missed five matches during his recovery with Bayern winning two and drawing against Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga.

The German champions also beat Atletico Madrid in the Champions League in his absence, as well as progressing in the DFB Cup.

Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks had overseen the first team during his recovery.

Danks previously worked as Kompany's assistant at Anderlecht before deputising for Dean Smith and Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa and Michael Carrick at Middlesbrough.

Kompany has missed five matches following his collapse at Bayern's training ground on October 23.

Bayern had stressed they wanted to give Kompany as much time as required to recover before returning to work.

The German giants play eight matches in the next month, including two matches in the Champions League, before the Bundesliga takes its winter break.

Reports had emerged after Kompany's collapse that club officials had been concerned by his irregular eating habits, as well as barely exercising, drinking excessive amounts of coffee, and taking on too much work.

Bayern sporting director Max Eberl dismissed the claims last month, reiterating that Kompany's illness had been the cause of his collapse rather than his workload.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that marathon's major Symbiosis update has been teased for weeks, but now it's almost here. Developer Bungie is set to release the major overhaul of its extraction shooter on Dec. 8, bringing plenty of fresh features such as dedicated PvE. One of the biggest additions, however, is an entirely new shell (think of these as Marathon's character classes) called Bishop. Now Bungie has shared our best look at Bishop yet.

According to recent reports, the studio posted a cinematic trailer for the shell on its official X account. The caption for the trailer simply reads: "Bishop Shell // Hunter Killer. Strike once, Strike fast." The video itself, although it isn't gameplay footage, offers a look at the shell's visual design and hints at how it will play. As the description suggests, Bishop seems to be a fast and lethal option for players. We see a Bishop shell taking on another group of Runners (other players) and utilizing some of the game's typical weaponry alongside what appear to be unique skills.

Bungie previously described Bishop as "a new Runner shell built around the fantasy of a fast, surgical blade-wielding robot." That appears to be true. Bishop has an extendable blade in one arm and boosters on its legs, which together should let players move promptly, close large gaps, and get within striking distance of enemies for a lethal strike. More details will be shared closer to Symbiosis' release.

Recent findings suggest that symbiosis will be the culmination of Bungie's months-long work to revitalize Marathon after what was perceived as a poor launch​​​​​​​. While the update includes the addition of latest weapons and the Bishop shell, it also focuses on tweaking the core experience of the extraction shooter to make it more generally appealing. That will mostly be accomplished by giving players a way to engage with the game outside PvP.

According to recent reports, marathon will get​​​​​​​ a handful of features that echo the social features and PvE systems in Bungie's Destiny games​​​​​​​. A social space called Limbo will let Runners connect and challenge each other in low-stakes duels. Expedition will be a roguelite PvE-only mode. Deathmatch, which will pit two teams of three against each other in bite-sized matches​​​​​​​, will be introduced in beta. You'll also be able to play Marathon for free from Dec. 8 to 15​​​​​​​ to celebrate the release of Symbiosis.

#177231. Tech Report: From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2635 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Stewart once said that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.
  • Emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography.
  • Clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jimmy Stewart once said that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.

Emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography. (We spoke on Zoom.).

Clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama. So far, Blunt has notched one Oscar nomination, for Supporting Actress in Christopher Nolan’s bio-drama “Oppenheimer.” Sci-fi thriller “Disclosure Day” could score Blunt’s first Best Actress nod. (More below.) Related Stories How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens.

Sources indicate that 1. “My Summer of Love” (2005, Pawel Pawlikowski) was Blunt’s first movie role. “I remember the wildness of that Edith Piaf dance [‘La Foule’], where I have the cigarette dangling out of my mouth, and she’s trying to romanticize this girl from the wrong side of town and sophisticate her. I remember the scene with Paddy Considine where she tries to seduce him and then she laughs at him. I will never forget the energy in that room and how Paddy was in that scene. I have taken what Pawel taught me about ambiguity and reality on camera, and I have used it throughout my career. I am an untrained actor. I don’t have anything technical to fall back on, but the aliveness that he created on ‘My Summer of Love’ was informative for how I moved forward: what lies beneath the character. You know what the front foot is, and what is the shadow of that person? What’s really going on?”.

In a recent development, 2. “The Devil Wears Prada“ (2006, David Frankel) marked Blunt’s Hollywood breakout as Miranda Priestley’s beleaguered first assistant Emily Charlton. After she gets hit by a taxi, second assistant Andy Sachs (Anne Hathaway) visits her hospital room. Charlton is angry and tearful at everything she is missing. “The hospital scene makes me laugh because that’s really who she is: this completely broken down, vulnerable, insecure person.”.

3. “The Young Victoria” (2010, Jean-Marc Vallée) gave Blunt a queen to embody. “I remember the scene where she asks [Prince] Albert to marry her, because he was not allowed to ask her. She is the monarch, and had to be the one to ask. That scene was so vulnerable and beautifully twinkly, how Jean-Marc shot that.”.

Sources indicate that 4. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a romantic sci-fi thriller, co-starred Matt Damon. “I remember never being able to get through a scene with Matt Damon without laughing. But I did love the scene in the bathroom where they meet. That scene had to sparkle because otherwise you don’t care about them, and you don’t care about them using their magical fedoras to get back to each other. Matt Damon doesn’t know how to be bad. That’s the truth. He doesn’t know how to play a false note. There is something about what Matt does, and he’s so dexterous in his humanity, but I don’t feel it’s technical with Matt. He’s like a laser beam of truth, and I feel myself, anyone who watches him, they ease back and they go, ‘Oh, thank God, Matt Damon’s here.’ He just leads with the truth. He’s like Josh Brolin. They only know how to be honest, and so they have such humanity to them. That’s why you can’t take your eyes off them. John [Krasinski] and I were so proud of what Matt did [with “The Odyssey”]. It’s obviously the most Herculean undertaking, but he grounded everything with that performance.”.

5. “Edge of Tomorrow” (2014, Doug Liman) co-starred Tom Cruise and thrust Blunt into action mode for the first time. Her moment was a war scene set on a beach. “It was the beach set, and we started calling it ‘the bitch’ because it was such a nightmare. That set was always flooded. You were always exposed to terrible elements of the weather, freezing, and we shot that beach scene for a month. Tom Cruise gave me a lot of flowers on that one. He was so good to me, and he revealed halfway through the shoot that this was the deep end of action for him— this was the most challenging action movie that he had ever done, and it was my first action movie, so I was flung in at the deep end of action. But we held each other through that. I loved athletics when I was a kid, and then couldn’t be bothered to work out, and then thought I knew what working out was, and then I realized I didn’t know what working out was until I started training for ‘Edge of Tomorrow,’ and that was a transformational thing to my body. She needed to look lethal, absolutely lethal. And so it helped me a lot, doing all of that physicality.”.

In a recent development, 6. “Into the Woods” (2014, Rob Marshall), adapted from Stephen Sondheim’s stage musical, boasted a huge ensemble cast; Blunt played the baker’s wife opposite James Corden. “‘Moments in the Woods,’ that big song she has right before she gets squished by the giant. She’s weighing up the duality of life, whether she goes for this poetic interlude in her prosaic life or if she goes back to the prosaic life. That kind of agony that she’s going through in the song was cool. I had I’d never sung in front of anyone before, really, other than one small TV thing years ago. I didn’t even want to audition for it, and Rob Marshall mentioned, ‘Look, I’m not looking for singers who can kind of act. I’m looking for actors who can kind of sing,’ and that was great advice. I said it to my 12-year-old this morning as she went off to her musical audition at school. I said, ‘Don’t worry about the notes; just tell us a story. That’s it. That’s what the song should be, and that’s what will make it sound amazing.'”.

According to recent reports, 7. “Sicario” (2015, Denis Villeneuve) plops Blunt’s straight-arrow FBI agent into a violent Mexican border scenario. “The scene that stands out for me is a spellbinding one, when Benicio del Toro comes to my apartment, and he puts the gun to my face and forces me to sign the contract. It’s right at the end of the movie, and I think that scene holds a special place for me because we were not sure about the scene that was written by Taylor Sheridan. It didn’t feel like it belonged in what we were trying to achieve between the characters. We wanted to change it a little bit. It was an idea that Benicio had. We were racking our brains as to how to finish this scene and this moment between the two characters. He always has so many crazy ideas, and he will have some absolute bangers in there. And he called me at about 11 o’clock the night before, and he goes, ‘I think I have it. What about this?’ And I remarked, ‘That is a great idea, because you’ve got this very idealistic FBI agent who’s pulled into this incoherent, amoral world. And she’s being forced to sign a contract that indicates everything they did was aboveboard, and that’s like a death to a character like that.’ We rehearsed that scene for two hours. Denis loved it, and then we all turned to [cinematographer] Roger Deakins: “Roger, what do you think?” And he gave his slow nod of approval, and then we shot it, and it was so.”.

8. “A Quiet Place” (2018, John Krasinski) was Blunt’s first experience being directed by her husband. The memorable moment: giving birth in the bathtub as a killer monster hovers nearby, listening for any noise. “We shot that whole sequence from the water breaking in the bathtub in order, which I was grateful to John for. It took four days. We did two takes of that bathtub scene because he shot it mainly as a oner. It starts as the blood’s trickling out, and it comes up, and you see the creature, and then it goes into that scream, and then the fireworks go off, but yeah, it’s a wild scene. It’s really smart to have a baby in a silent world. Every woman I’ve spoken to about that scene, they go: ‘Oh my God, that scene made me cross my legs.” And I was: ‘Okay, all right.'”.

Industry observers note that 9. “Oppenheimer” (2023, Christopher Nolan) offered Blunt a constrained role as Kitty, the recessive wife of the great physicist (Cillian Murphy). Blunt agreed that the scene that earned her the Oscar nomination was in the courtroom where she is badgered by the formidable Jason Clarke. “I knew that was the monster scene. When I read the script, I thought, ‘What an extraordinary scene, that you have this person staggering in, looking like a liability,’ and Chris had written that she almost chokes, and you think she’s going to blow it. When I talked to him about it after I read the script, I said, ‘What a reclamation that scene is of that extraordinary brain coming back to life.’ The brain that had gone crazy at the ironing board, probably meant for bigger things than being someone’s wife and someone’s mummy, and I had a great deal of empathy for her and a lot of women who went crazy at the ironing board. She owns Jason Clarke in a way, and you realize she could probably run circles around him. He played such a wonderful bully in that film, but we saw what Meryl [Streep] did with Miranda Priestley: There’s such power in quiet, great, great power and great dignity.”.

10. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” (2026, David Frankel) allowed Blunt to indulge Charlton’s excesses. “We all had scenery stuck in our teeth on that one. It was so fun to go back to playing that lunatic. My favorite scene was the funeral scene where she comes in and rants about Dolce and Gabbana. It was such a ludicrous outfit to be wearing to a funeral. Anne Hathaway is the most unstoppable force. And what a wide range of roles she has access to. I feel this moment in her life. She’s in this full wingspan of being able to harness everything she can do and everything she has to offer, and I can’t believe she had the year she just did, and she was pregnant!”.

Recent findings suggest that “Disclosure Day” (2026, Steven Spielberg) leaned on Blunt to carry the sci-fi thriller. “The four-and a-half minute oner in the beginning when she arrives at the news station. I’ve seen what Steven Spielberg can do visually, his visual prowess is rather unparalleled. So to be in a oner that he conjures up on the day, that happened spontaneously — he was planning on covering it. And I said, ‘what would help me so much is if you could let me whirlwind out of control in one take from the moment I pull up, going into the makeup room, coming out speaking Korean, she’s in this incoherent tailspin, and then you see her disintegrate over the course of it. And she gets up there to deliver the weather, and she starts to speak in the alien language. Can we just try it as a oner, just for me to see where I’ve got to get to?’ And he watched me do it. And by the time I got up there to do the weather, my legs were shaking. I was out of breath, beside myself, and he loved it. And he goes, ‘We’re going to do it as a oner.’ And we were done by 2 pm. because he planned to shoot it all day. It was Steven in his element of going, ‘Oh, I see it’ and not only was he intentional about creating the environment for me to be able to do that so he didn’t overcover it, he saw a cinematic advantage.”.

In a recent development, blunt plays several characters in one. “All the stuff in the childhood home was deeply moving because that also dealt with that moment where the character goes from crisis to serenity and the ability to then deploy these powers rather than be puppeteered by them. So I loved that shape-shift in the character, like playing two people throughout the course of this film. And the other moment that felt so human to me was the panic attack in the box car after the train sequence, and she’s at max capacity, bubbling over, overwhelmed, and a few people, including myself on set, had experienced panic attacks, and that felt like a real reaction to someone who was utterly overwhelmed. That also felt so Spielbergian: no one’s a slick elite action hero in Steven’s films. Everyone’s afraid. Everyone, including Indiana Jones, everyone’s scared. That hand that’s shaking on the way to Omaha Beach, that is trauma. He can relate to your vulnerabilities. Everyone’s a bit over their head, and in a different action movie, me and Josh O’Connor would have dropped in the boxcar and gone, ‘Whoa, that was crazy.’ And instead, she has a panic attack. I got them a lot in my early twenties, and Steven’s not immune, neither is Josh. All of us have experienced that. That moment where he takes my hands and he puts them on the piano and he goes, ‘This is real. This is real. Feel this. I’m here. You’re here. We’re here.’ I’ve done that. So it just was like, ‘Oh my God!’ You get to sublimate what you’ve experienced into this creative art form sometimes. That’s the great gift often on movies.”.

The languages were right in Blunt’s wheelhouse. She has always loved languages. She learned them two to three months before the start of the shoot. “I learned those scenes. The first thing I learned was the Russian and the Korean, because I wanted it to be spoken at such a velocity that it sounded as conversational as it does as me speaking to you right now, and she doesn’t know she’s speaking Russian,” she stated. “She thinks she’s speaking English. You have someone who is white-knuckling their way through most of this film, and these forms of mind control are unconscious to her in the beginning, it’s compulsive.”.

Next up: “Walk the Blue Fields” directed by John Crowley and co-starring Andrew Scott as another hot priest, Father Joe, presiding at a wedding. “It’s a short story that I bought the rights to about six years ago by Claire Keegan. If you’ve ever read any of her short stories, they’re like laser beams. They’re so wonderful. My sister Felicity is a book agent. She represents Claire, and she sent it to me. Story A is a wedding day, and story B is what led up to that wedding and why everything is starting to unravel on the wedding day. And it plays like a thriller,” she noted. “She’s coming back to Ireland to try to build a relationship with her Irish father [Ciaran Hinds] after they’ve been estranged for years, and it’s a story about identity and religion and love. Andrew Scott has to be one of the most beautiful actors I’ve ever shared a scene with.”.

It has been revealed that and, of course, John Krasinski’s upcoming “Quiet Place 3,” which co-stars Jack O’Connell, Cillian Murphy, Jason Clarke and Noah Jupe, is shrouded in secrecy. “I don’t want to blow John’s cover here,” she remarked. And “Sicario 3” is also moving forward with the original cast, a script by James Bond writer Steven Knight and director Padraic McKinley.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews latest releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Pokémon GO players have plenty to look forward to before the franchise wraps up its 30th anniversary celebrations. Between the introduction of upcoming Mega Evolutions in Pokémon Legends: Z-A and its Mega Dimension DLC, some Pokémon that haven't received much love in years are finally getting their moment. That includes a Ghost-type from the Sinnoh region and one of the more unusual Dragon-types introduced in Pokémon Sun and Moon.

It has been revealed that the winter months will also give Trainers another opportunity to add one of Unova’s most powerful Legendary Pokémon to their collection. Introduced in Pokémon Black and White, Kyurem became the mascot of both sequels thanks to its ability to fuse with Reshiram and Zekrom. Its return is especially exciting for Trainers still looking to collect its Shiny variant, and December’s encounter won’t require a paid pass.

Pokémon GO’s new season, Daydream Destinations, begins December 1, 2026, at 10 a.m. local time and runs through March 1, 2027. The season will introduce Mega Froslass and Mega Drampa through dedicated Raid Day events, alongside Max Battle Day events featuring Gigantamax Inteleon and Gigantamax Toxtricity. Meanwhile, the free December GO Pass features a guaranteed Kyurem encounter, with the possibility of encountering a Shiny. Players can progress through the pass until January 5.

December's GO Pass will also reward Trainers with Rare Candy XL, a Premium Battle Pass, and a Lucky Egg. Those who upgrade to the $7.99 GO Pass Deluxe can unlock a Timed Incubator at Rank 20, giving them an additional unlimited-use Incubator until January 12. That should come in handy once players reach Rank 75, which grants increased XP and Stardust from hatching Eggs. Other milestone bonuses include double Daily Adventure Incense duration at Rank 50 and increased Gift limits at Rank 25. Several Community Days have also been confirmed for the fresh season:.

The biggest event of the season, however, will take Trainers back to the Alola region. Pokémon GO Tour: Alola will take place in Los Angeles and Kaohsiung from February 19–21, followed by a global event on February 27–28. Inspired by the seventh generation of Pokémon games, the celebration will feature Alolan Pokémon and upcoming raid opportunities, with additional Special Research and increased Shiny encounter chances available through a paid global event ticket.

Pokémon GO: Daydream Destinations begins December 1, 2026.

Why David Fincher Is The Perfect Director For Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Sequel

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that one of the best movies of the 2010s was Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.
  • Tarantino isn’t particularly well known for making sequels to his work, which made the announcement that Brad Pitt’s character would be getting a solo film all the more surprising.
  • In a recent development, with Booth firmly the main character of his own adventure(s), it’s likely that audiences will get to see a more complete look at him this time around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of the best movies of the 2010s was Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. The film, which was written and directed by Quentin Tarantino, perfectly recaptured the late 1960s aesthetic of Hollywood and, more broadly, the entertainment industry that plays such a huge role in the area. Not only that, but the two leading characters, Rick Dalton and Cliff Booth, were some of the best that Tarantino has ever created.

Tarantino isn’t particularly well known for making sequels to his work, which made the announcement that Brad Pitt’s character would be getting a solo film all the more surprising. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, which Tarantino wrote and was directed by David Fincher, highlights the title character eight years after his last adventure, and, this time, gives him the spotlight as the film’s main character.

In a recent development, with Booth firmly the main character of his own adventure(s), it’s likely that audiences will get to see a more complete look at him this time around. In Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Booth’s backstory was teased a little bit, such as his service during the Second World War and the suspicious death of his wife (which he was, more likely than not, responsible for).

Sources indicate that tarantino and Fincher may be an odd combination for screenwriter and director, but it may actually work in favor of the new movie. After all, Fincher is known for telling dark, brooding, and moody stories, so he might just be the perfect filmmaker to explore the darker sides of Cliff Booth in Netflix’s new Oscar contender.

It has been revealed that once Upon a Time in Hollywood was firmly a double act. On one hand, there was Rick Dalton, an often misguided but well-meaning actor obsessed with getting his career back on track. Then there’s Cliff Booth, his trusty sidekick, someone who has a mysterious past before he joined the entertainment industry. Brad Pitt arguably had the meatier of the two roles in the film, even though Once Upon a Time in Hollywood only teased the full extent of his character.

Industry observers note that for example, Booth is portrayed as something of a killing machine, taking down several bad guys throughout the course of the film. Even when he isn’t killing people, Booth still demonstrates his fighting expertise. For example, he beat none other than Bruce Lee in hand-to-hand combat, and did so with relative ease, something that is mentioned repeatedly in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Sources indicate that booth also defeated the Manson family murderers at the end of Once Upon A Time in Hollywood, and did so with such calmness that he actually seemed he was having fun. All of this teased the character, but it didn’t show how he became this cool, calm, and collected killing machine. Now, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth looks set to explore that side of its title character.

Who better to bring out the dark side of Brad Pitt as an actor than David Fincher? After all, the two have worked together before, and done so with great success. Se7en, for example, has an incredibly dark and twisted story with Pitt’s character at the center of it. Then there’s Fight Club, which is an even bleaker tale, and also features Brad Pitt as one of the darkest characters he’s ever played.

Sources indicate that with Tarantino writing the script, plus David Fincher directing the movie, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth may be the perfect vessel to explore the true nature of this character, including his darker side. Plus, Brad Pitt has remarkable range as an actor, and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood featured one of his career-best performances.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth releases in theaters on November 25.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there are all sorts of magic worlds waiting to be discovered in the stop-motion epic “Wildwood,” but it’s a credit to the film that one of them is Portland, Oregon. Laika Studio’s Head of CG Animation Benoit Dubuc was involved early and often in order to determine what would be shot practically by the stop-motion animation team and what CG effects would be used to achieve. Even in the most mundane and ordinary moments of the film question of either/or. It was one of how the collaboration between different kinds of animation would work.

“We mostly shoot two or three puppets at a time, so any time that there’s background characters, they’re gonna be digital,” Dubuc remarked during IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable on visual effects. He pointed out that when Baby Mac gets kidnapped by a murder of crows under the command of the dread sorceress Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), the amount of work to achieve that moment fully through stop-motion would mean they’d probably still be animating it. Related Stories From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder.

In a recent development, “We’ll often get [animators] to produce some practical work to lead the visual effects work. We built a crow puppet to spec. We didn’t animate it in the film, but it informed the visual effects work. We try to stay away from simulations as much as possible, knowing that what we’re chasing is something that feels handmade and something that is slightly imperfect,” Dubuc mentioned.

According to recent reports, that goes for individual characters and for the vibrant backgrounds of “Wildwood” alike. “The audience would think that we built sets the size of an airport hangar with a hundred thousand practical puppets running downhill. It’s not possible,” Dubuc stated. The fact that it looks possible, in both the most intricate battle sequences and the ordinary chaos of biking past Powell’s Books, means that the VFX team has done its job. “ The portrayal of Portland that we were striving for is a beautiful, vibrant city,” Dubuc said.

#177224. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6
