Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • In a recent development, GTA 6 is absurdly large.
  • Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

In a recent development, GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

It has been revealed that file size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

It has been revealed that game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

Industry observers note that according to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

In a recent development, first, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

Industry observers note that the DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

Recent findings suggest that the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.
  • As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.
  • But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were announced Monday, November 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.

As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.

But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were announced Monday, November 23. IndieWire understands that the Academy’s Animation Branch Executive Committee determined “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not meet the Academy’s definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards. Related Stories The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments.

Here’s the full rule as written that the Academy felt “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not satisfy:.

An animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life by having movement created for them, by any human means. While the crucial movement of a live-action motion picture is captured at speed, animation is the craft of human creation and manipulation of images to produce a performance from inanimate objects. At least 75 percent of the motion picture’s running time, without opening or end credits, must include animation of the primary subject or subjects. An animated feature has a running time of more than 40 minutes. Upon submission, filmmakers must provide information supporting how the motion picture qualifies as an animated film.

In a recent development, edward Saatchi, a producer on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” with Fable Studios, told IndieWire he and director Zack London (a.k.a. Gossip Goblin) plan to appeal the animation branch’s decision and cited the example of Richard Linklater’s rotoscoped film “Apollo 10 1/2,” which was originally deemed ineligible but saw the branch reverse its decision upon appeal. Saatchi said that the film, in addition to submitting for Best Animated Feature, also submitted in other categories such as Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, VFX, and Sound. But if the film doesn’t fall under the animation branch today, he believes eventually AI movies will inevitably find a place somewhere within Academy rules, even if it ends up being a theoretical “Best AI Movie” category.

Recent findings suggest that “‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ is starting a big debate around where cinematic works of art made with AI fit. Is it time to consider a ‘Best AI Movie?’ Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the new VFX? It’s going to take the whole industry time to figure it out,” Saatchi said. “With traditional garlanded directors like Matthieu Kassovitz, Alex Proyas, and Doug Liman making heavily-AI films, it’s going to be a good debate of how to categorize. We think Best Animated is simplest, but it may be the Academy decides ultimately that a Best AI movie category will make the most sense with these films where everything you’re seeing is generative.”.

It has been revealed that of note, one of the films that did qualify for Best Animated Feature was “Coyote vs. Acme,” which is a hybrid animated and live-action film featuring the Looney Tunes alongside human actors in the real world. The Academy on Monday also revealed the eligible features in the Best Documentary Feature race and the Best International Feature race.

As part of the Academy’s most recent rules changes from earlier this year, only roles credited in the film’s legal billing that are demonstrably performed by humans with their consent are eligible for acting categories, and screenplays must be human-authored to be eligible. That rule changed followed on guidelines from last year ahead of the 98th Oscars in which the Academy specified, “[Gen-AI] tools neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination. The Academy and each branch will judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the case of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the film has a script written by London, and though all the characters in the film are generated with AI visually, it features real human actors doing the voice work for the characters. The film also features cameos of some real-life people playing parts resembling themselves, most notably the pop star Grimes. But the film has elaborate look books, visual reference points, and photo mashing that all went into the creation of these characters, something that clearly has human authorship and goes beyond a computer interpreting a single prompt.

Part of Gossip Goblin’s battle in legitimizing “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is in showing there was a human team, between 30-35 people, working for years on the film’s creation. Gossip Goblin also recently released a behind-the-scenes documentary that showcases the film’s composer, its foley artist, its voice actors, and more detailing the human effort that went into the project.

Discussion over AI in Oscar eligible films came to a head after several movies in the 2024 Oscar race were reported to have included AI in their post-production editing process, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Brutalist,” and “Emilia Pérez.” The examples were for traditional VFX, not for anything that enhanced or altered performances, but the Academy as a result now requires disclosure of AI if it is used in a film.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” begins its theatrical run on December 4, which will initially be an Oscar-qualifying run, and it will expand on January 22 alongside a rollout with the film’s international distributor AGC International.

Additional reporting by Marcus Jones.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday is usually a great time to grab a newly introduced e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a major discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is presently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

It has been revealed that the X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also notable to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

It has been revealed that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a storm brewing, chere, and it has nothing to do with the weird Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Herbie the Robot Dunkin Donuts ads that played like once a quarter during all the football games on Sunday.

Industry observers note that the final trailer was released ahead of Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” the mega-Sentinel, crossover-tastic 165-minute Russo Brothers opus out on December 18. And the response hasn’t been great — in part because Cyclops claims, “To me, my X-Men!” and there isn’t actually a Storm.

According to recent reports, way back in the salad days of 2012, Joss Whedon first did an “Assemble” shot that roved in a circle all of the original “Avengers” film, while an Alan Silvestri score bwaaamped the brassy “Avengers” theme. Say whatever you like about Whedon’s strengths and weaknesses when it comes to visual style, but the first time this happened, the shot’s continuous nature served a storytelling purpose. It was the cinematic way to finally bind these crazy kids together in superhero fellowship — through the timeless crucible of Latest York City getting shredded into CGI bits by alien-monster things. Related Stories AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch.

Industry observers note that but over the many, many Phases of the MCU, the Avengers Assemble shots have kept happening. And happening. And sure enough, the “Doomsday” trailer crescendos with a bunch of our heroes stuck in a gray-black wasteland void that looks like a glitched “Expedition 33” loading screen, with the camera straining to create that same sense of unity.

It doesn’t. At least not in the trailer. Which is why so much of the response to the finale “Doomsday” trailer has been focused on it.

In a recent development, as folks online have pointed out, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) looks like he’s standing in entirely different lighting from the people closest to him. There’s no sense of texture or proximity that suggests anybody was placed against the same green screen together, let alone acting together (a problem that has been pointed out about the filmmaking process for “Doomsday” already).

Recent findings suggest that no amount of money can make up for shooting for maximum flexibility — which so often can devolve into being indecisive — or for pursuing relentless revisions throughout the VFX pipeline. That is exactly what leads to shadowy, sloppily-framed environments like wherever the hell the Avengers are fighting Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) and his creations. And because the environment is so flattened and indistinct, only the barest hints of color survive. And really, only because Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) is still wearing a coat from a different movie.

In a recent development, now, what comes most naturally to Cyclops is shooting an optic blast from his eyes, and what comes most naturally to us is posting negative takes online. The trailer takes that shot out of context for nostalgia’s sake; its dramatic purpose within the film itself might be more complicated, or the setup for a twist in three different timelines’ worth of Avengers’ fortunes. But when it comes to all the cinematic crimes of artless visuals, repetitive plots, and overbearing lore that have contributed to superhero fatigue? The “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer doesn’t seem to be beating the charges.

Mike Flanagan's Carrie season 2 is coming together well.

Howell as the eponymous teenage outcast who grapples with the emotional rollercoaster of high school, all while developing telekinetic powers. Scoring largely positive reviews from critics and solid ratings on Prime Video, Carrie season 2 was officially confirmed to be in the works in late October 2026, just two weeks after its premiere.

It has been revealed that now, during a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Flanagan offered an update on Carrie season 2's development. The creator/showrunner confirmed that he is "back to work" on the next chapter of the Stephen King adaptation, revealing that the "writers room is firing on all cylinders" and that he has already hit a major writing milestone in having "turned in the first episode script" the morning of the interview.

Flanagan went on to share that he and his team had been "working on it unofficially for a while" in the hopes of Carrie season 2 getting the greenlight from Prime Video and wanting to "be prepared in case it did." The creator further expressed that the hope is to "go into production next year" if the writing remains on schedule, though didn't specify what the timeline would look like for its production:.

Mike Flanagan: The beautiful thing is that Carrie’s journey has always seemed to me to have a clear trajectory. And that was something, even though we were never taking for granted that it would happen, it was something that was always in the back of my mind. I know it was in conversations that I had with Summer about where she could go and with Steve too — King was very aware and excited about the potential for that. It’s always been in the room with us, but we didn’t really have permission to fully explore it until it was real because you don’t want to jinx it. But we are fully immersed in it.

It has been revealed that when asked about his previous comments about a three-season blueprint for Carrie, Flanagan confirmed the plan is still in place for the series, seeing a "very clean arc" going through seasons 2 and 3. However, he does confess that there is "danger in the temptation to do more," and confesses it's "very presumptuous" he'll get a third season, and therefore the writers room is still approaching it as "we only know we're doing [season] 2.".

In this newly introduced series adaptation of Stephen King's classic novel, Carrie White struggles through the daily torments of school life, her domineering mother, and a dormant  set of telekinetic powers.

Breaking: 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When John Hamburg worked on “Meet the Parents” as a writer over 25 years ago, it seemed like there were well-resourced comedies opening in theaters every week.
  • It has been revealed that to that end, Hamburg and cinematographer Barry Peterson decided to shoot widescreen for the first time in Focker history, eschewing the 1.85:1 frame established by director Jay Roach in the first film (and perpetuated in Roach’s “Meet the Rockers” in 2004 and Paul Weitz’s “Little Fockers” in 2010) in favor of a more expansive 2.40:1 aspect ratio.
  • For Hamburg, it’s all at the service of extracting the best possible work from his actors, whether it be “Meet the Parents” stalwarts like Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, and Blythe Danner or newcomers to the series like Skyler Gisondo (as Stiller’s son) or Ariana Grande (who fulfills the comic promise of her turn in “Wicked” with a hilarious performance as Gisondo’s fiancée).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When John Hamburg worked on “Meet the Parents” as a writer over 25 years ago, it seemed like there were well-resourced comedies opening in theaters every week. Returning to the series this year for the third sequel, “Focker In-Law,” which he directed as well as wrote, the filmmaker was fully aware that major screen comedies had become a rare treat. “We felt like it had been so long since this type of comedy had been in movie theaters that we wanted to do everything we could to make it feel theatrical,” Hamburg told IndieWire.

It has been revealed that to that end, Hamburg and cinematographer Barry Peterson decided to shoot widescreen for the first time in Focker history, eschewing the 1.85:1 frame established by director Jay Roach in the first film (and perpetuated in Roach’s “Meet the Rockers” in 2004 and Paul Weitz’s “Little Fockers” in 2010) in favor of a more expansive 2.40:1 aspect ratio. It’s a pivotal decision that not only gives “Focker In-Law” a visual elegance, but showcases the ensemble performances in compositions that make the most out of the subtle interchanges and reactions between characters, often registered with the subtlety that comes from allowing the comedy to play out within the frame rather than via emphatic cuts. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie.

For Hamburg, it’s all at the service of extracting the best possible work from his actors, whether it be “Meet the Parents” stalwarts like Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, and Blythe Danner or newcomers to the series like Skyler Gisondo (as Stiller’s son) or Ariana Grande (who fulfills the comic promise of her turn in “Wicked” with a hilarious performance as Gisondo’s fiancée). “I try to create a very loose, stress-free environment,” Hamburg said. “I’ve found that in these comedies, if the actors are laughing and enjoying each other’s manufacturer and having fun with the crew, and there’s no tension, they can do their best work.”.

Hamburg claims that his intention is to direct like he’s hosting a really fun dinner party, a process that begins with the table read. “You get to know the actors if you have the luxury of some rehearsal, which we did on this movie,” he said. “We do table reads, and then my version of rehearsing is the actors coming to my office, where we read the scenes and talk. Pretty swiftly you get a sense of how each actor approaches their work; there are actors who color code their character’s arc in the script and are very precise, and others who go by feel and instinct. You have to be part psychologist and figure out what all the actors need, which is not anything they ever teach you in film school, but it’s a big part of the job of being director.”.

Sources indicate that another part of the job is structuring the coverage to take maximum advantage of each actor’s strengths — no small task in a movie that often has over a half-dozen characters interacting in comic set-pieces. “There’s no science to it,” Hamburg mentioned. “It’s going with your gut and feeling it out and seeing, okay, this actor needs a little more time, so maybe we’ll start with the wide shots and wait on the close-ups until the actor has really found his or her rhythm.”.

It has been revealed that hamburg likens shooting the ensemble comedy scenes to conducting a symphony, only with actors instead of musicians. “ You have to make sure that you’re not losing sight of giving all of them their moments,” Hamburg stated. “There are a lot of angles, and a lot of eyelines. I need Ariana looking at Ben across the table, Ariana looking at Skyler, De Niro looking at Ben and looking at his wife … luckily I have a great script supervisor who sits next to me, and I can ask ‘Did we get that moment? Did we get that look?’ She makes sure that I’m not missing anything, because it’s too much for one person to keep in their head.”.

Industry observers note that although scenes like an early dinner involving nearly every major character in the film are a beast to shoot, Hamburg says he enjoys them. “Maybe it’s the masochist in me,” he remarked, adding that what he really likes are seeing the new options and possibilities the actors bring to his material. “ I’m very open with the writing. We work really hard on the script and make it as good as possible, and but then on the day, you want to be surprised. I want to start with the script and make sure we get that rhythm, but then let’s see what else happens.”.

The ability to pivot and incorporate latest material based on the actors’ interaction is why Hamburg likes the dual role of writer-director. “There’s so much magic that can happen on the set when you have the right actors and the right chemistry between them,” he stated. “That’s the thrill of being not just the screenwriter, but also being the director. It’s my favorite thing.”.

A Universal Pictures release, “Focker In-Law” opens in theaters on November 25.

Recent findings suggest that even with a dangling preposition (in a press release littered with errors), the claim felt like the more glaring mistake: Netflix is where fans go for discovery. They do? Still? Are you sure about that?

Recent findings suggest that but when it comes to Netflix’s core business — streaming television — the service is largely a preferred destination by default. Being an industry pioneer helped establish Netflix as a utility among TV fans, many of whom still turn to it when they want to see “what’s on,” but it’s hard to imagine why anyone would head there first when searching for their next favorite show.

Recent findings suggest that that would require the customer to trust Netflix — either as the service offering the most bang for their buck, the highlights everyone is talking about, or, most likely and simplest of all, the best series on TV. Can the streamer really stake a claim to any of those distinctions?

Industry observers note that not anymore. Not after this year.

Throughout 2026, Netflix has been plagued by problems and complaints. Viewership for returning seasons is dwindling, subscription prices are rising, hot fresh franchises are scarce, and high-quality programming — a subjective designation, to be sure — isn’t what it used to be. Netflix is no longer the most affordable SVOD service. It’s not the most award-winning, nor is it the buzziest.

It has been revealed that A sustainable hit could quiet things down, but those have been hard to come by. Netflix’s most popular newly introduced highlights this year were limited series (like “His & Hers” and “I Will Find You”), which only offer short-term juice. Promising first seasons (“The Boroughs”) faced quick cancellations that left fans fuming and analysts searching for answers. Even touted chart toppers (“Man on Fire”) don’t get a quick Season 2 renewal, let alone a quick turnaround between seasons.

It has been revealed that ignoring these very-online narratives, none of the aforementioned shows earned rave reviews, and the streamer’s awards output echoed what’s felt like a dearth in quality. Total Emmy wins were cut nearly in half this year, from 30 to 16, causing Netflix to fall to third place (behind HBO and Apple) for the first time since topping the town in 2021.

A month after Emmy night, all the criticism reached a crescendo when a plunging stock price and lack of hits forced mass layoffs, including the dismissal of chief content officer Bela Bajaria and other key executives. Peter Rice is at the helm now, and his new team is setting the table for changes in 2027 — much like Netflix did in 2022 after The Great Streaming Correction opened the door for an ad-tier and shut the door on password sharing.

While it would be foolish to believe fixing one aspect of a diverse business would make all its other problems go away, it would be equally foolish to pretend there’s not a TV problem at Netflix. A healthy TV slate only benefits engagement across the platform, and the streamer is still the major dog in SVOD — it’s just losing ground year by year. So what’s to be done?

Well, that depends on how much Netflix is willing to change. If it’s all on the table, there are a handful of reasonable shifts they could make to improve their reputation. If not, well, I’ve got an idea for that, too.

At the root of Netflix’s TV problem is that its demonstrates feel disposable. Sometimes that’s by design: Netflix makes a lot of programs that can be watched while scrolling, which can be OK. TV has long been a medium built for background entertainment, and it’s still nice to have an easily digestible distraction while doing dishes or folding laundry.

Recent findings suggest that but Netflix may have gone too far. Setting aside quality (for a moment), the streamer’s focus on “discovery” paired with its faith in the almighty algorithm to sort through its substantial monthly programming influx emphasizes new reveals above all else. There’s always another new series, new special, or new live event to watch, but there isn’t always more of the show you already love. Some original series take years between releasing new seasons. Some only dole out six or eight episodes every 18 months. Some get canceled after one or two seasons, and very few run more than three or four seasons in total.

According to recent reports, whether or not the approach works from a financial perspective, it fails to foster audience investment, and investment is where TV thrives. Just look at this year’s most-watched demonstrates on streaming, per Nielsen: “Stranger Things” holds down the No. 1 spot, but then it’s “Bluey,” “The Pitt,” “Grey’s Anatomy,” and “The Major Bang Theory.” Keep scrolling and it’s even easier to spot the dominant trend: Shows with huge libraries that first aired on network TV.

These are the kind of demonstrates that people keep up with for years, decades, or more. They like the characters, they like the structure, they like the setting — they like being in the show’s world, whether it’s a hospital filled with hot doctors or a nerd’s living room. Offering access on a regular basis encourages investment, which breeds loyalty, which creates longevity. Producing more episodes, more often — like broadcast TV has done all along — creates bigger libraries that fans will happily live in for years on end because they enjoy spending time with those characters and within those stories.

Sources indicate that streamers have been reluctant to adopt their predecessor’s production model (for reasons both valid and ridiculous that I’ll get into in the next section), but the success of long-running (and long-gone) broadcast series on streaming, paired with the recent popularity of “The Pitt,” makes it hard to argue against making longer seasons, consisting of more episodes, that are released on a regular basis. It’s what audiences want now, and it’s what they’ve shown they’ll want later.

Sources indicate that which brings us to the binge model. One of the reasons Netflix hasn’t experimented with more broadcast-style streaming shows (like “The Pitt”) is because it can’t. Its release model is different. The binge model requires everything be done before anything premieres, including timely post-production work like subtitles and dubbing, which Netflix needs to serve its global base. While episodes of most network series are still being written, shot, and edited as earlier, completed episodes roll out, episodes of a Netflix series drop all at once.

Luckily, Netflix already made the change. Or started to, at least.

Nowadays, Netflix’s most popular original series are often released in batches (or “parts”), including the last two seasons of “Stranger Things” and “Bridgerton.” Both highlights are among the most-watched programs on the planet, so the shift in release strategy hasn’t hurt their popularity. Other shows are already released weekly, like “The Great British Baking Show,” or close to weekly, like “Love Is Blind.”.

Sources indicate that moreover, the addition of live events has forced Netflix to implement fresh tactics to raise awareness for time-sensitive content (instead of just relying on the algorithm), which should limit fears over viewer confusion. (For seasons released in parts, the Netflix platform tends to list how many episodes will be released and when. You can even set reminders for upcoming programming, even if none of it is available yet — like, say, the NFL game on Thanksgiving Eve, which is a thing, I guess.).

Netflix decided long ago to break up the binge, now they just need to keep going. After all, the binge model was created to disrupt Hollywood. No one was releasing full seasons at once, and Netflix executives recognized how DVDs had primed viewers to marathon TV demonstrates. Instead of old favorites (like “The Office”), why not give them fresh ones to devour?

But Netflix isn’t a disruptor anymore. It’s the industry leader. It doesn’t need a gimmick to draw attention. It needs a strategy to help keep it.

A weekly release model could help. Netflix doesn’t need to enforce it on every series — let people binge “Ginny & Georgia” — but for shows that could benefit from the regular cycle of anticipation, fulfillment, dissection (repeat), the tried-and-true strategy could do wonders for audience investment. In the short-term, it could help prevent dips in engagement and help foster engagement with newly beloved series. In the long-term, it could help build franchises, libraries, and loyalty.

You can’t just make the next “Pitt.” You have to create the system to support it.

Speaking of support, it’s time to talk about quality. What constitutes a good show and a bad show will always, in the end, remain in the eye of the beholder, but a tech giant aiming to “replace all television” can’t rely on subjective interpretations to define its brand. Nor can it rely primarily on an algorithm to elevate the best options instead of the easiest ones. Otherwise, you risk a narrative like this year’s, where objective measurements like ratings (where the three most-watched new highlights average a 56 rating on Metacritic) and awards (where Netflix landed one more win than NBC and Peacock combined) create the impression of less-than-“gourmet” service.

Some such schemes are already underway with pre-show ads running before episodes and prominent brand campaigns helping connect viewers with their upcoming favorite programs. Hopefully, that signals more old-school advocacy efforts are coming. Eventize episodes, not just new seasons. Build channels for episodic programs to elevate their best moments. Add permanent subsections to Netflix’s genre listings.

This is not a fresh idea. At various times for various reasons, various experts have suggested Netflix launch a free subscription tier in order to promote its growing library to a wider audience. FAST (free, ad-supported streaming) platforms like Pluto, Tubi, and The Roku Channel are growing swiftly mainly by replicating the broadcast model for the streaming age, and Netflix could take a page out of their playbook to expand their business in any number of ways. But in terms of solving their TV problem, they should use it to distinguish their premium original programming from their recent obsession: YouTube slop.

Industry observers note that I’ll be honest: I don’t think of Netflix and YouTube as competitors, mainly because Netflix isn’t free. Sure, there’s YouTube Premium, but YouTube is instantly accessible, sans subscription, and that’s how most people get hooked. I don’t care how many more hours people spend watching YouTube than Netflix because the hours I spend watching movie trailers, how-to-videos, and late-night clips are not the same as the hours I spend watching “Little House on the Prairie,” “Long Story Short,” and “East of Eden.” One I’m willing to pay for, one I’m not. So the idea that Netflix, as a business, should be trying to surpass YouTube never made sense to me.

It still doesn’t, but I understand the market demands constant growth, and I understand why Netflix would want YouTube’s viewers, especially in the younger demographic. So Netflix has been busy signing content creators, adding podcasts, and filling the service with easy-listening videos (aka videos you don’t need to watch, but can play in the background without much disturbance). If that helps bring the next generation to Netflix so they can discover the glory of “BoJack Horseman,” great! But right now, BoJack is sitting side by side with random content like “Conspiracy Theories,” “Small Town Murder,” and “Bill Simmons.”.

That’s a problem. We shouldn’t equate those very distinct experiences, and Netflix shouldn’t suggest we do. At best, it builds a false equivalency that steadily lowers our artistic standards for visual entertainment. At worst, it leads to more fans of this “Bill Simmons.”.

So let’s create some tiers. Launch a free version of Netflix where all the podcasts, creator videos, and short-form content can live. Make money the old-fashioned way — from ads — while offering select TV shows to sample in the hopes viewers will get hooked and pay for an upgraded subscription. Keep original series, movies, and other top library offerings on the paid tiers, and structure those however you like. (Presently, there’s Standard with Ads, Standard, and Premium, each with their distinct perks.).

It has been revealed that is creating a FAST version of Netflix a whole lot of work to dispel the notion that Netflix makes too much disposable TV? Yup, and I won’t pretend to know how feasible it is, financially or otherwise. But Netflix needs to take a significant swing or two if it hopes to fix its reputation, which brings us to my last option.

According to recent reports, netflix is still the dominant streamer in Hollywood. Plentiful stats support its case, but why look any further than how many other streamers license content to their biggest competitor? Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+, and more all lend their once-exclusive series to their rival in the hope of getting the Netflix bump (or a quick influx of cash). Never did I think I’d see the day where HBO would be available anywhere else, and yet everything from “Sex and the City” to “Ballers” has graced Netflix in 2026.

With that in mind, Netflix may choose to stay the course. The once-and-future tech firm is notorious for sticking to certain brand tenets, like trusting the algorithm over traditional marketing and its binge model over traditional release strategies. Even when Hollywood pushes back, Netflix’s broader goals continue to evolve. Originally, it wanted to be the HBO of streaming. Then it wanted to replace cable. Then it wanted to replace all television.

Industry observers note that what it wants to be now isn’t so clear. Wall Street keeps forcing comparisons to YouTube, some of which are invited by Netflix’s pursuit of its content and podcast creators. Maybe Netflix executives believe they can raise their market cap with vertical videos and video game previews, with latest decision-makers and added theatrical grosses, with a few small tweaks here and a few surprise wins there. It has the leverage to wait out complaints and keep making TV exactly as it has been, if it so chooses.

Recent findings suggest that but because of its relative health, I hope Netflix sees its TV problem as more of a TV opportunity. Yes, it needs more hits. Yes, it needs to build back trust. But it also wants to grow, and the suggestions above are all about sustainable growth through better TV. Longer seasons, more episodes, weekly releases, stronger support, clearer delineations, a FAST service — none of these ideas are revolutionary. They’re not meant to be. They’re meant to give the people what they want.

If Netflix is going to be where fans go for discovery, it first needs to be a place they can trust to get what what they need.

Using the score as a way of transporting Alex back into his own memories, the film jumps around through 20+ years of his life and career and indicates Gilroy's ability to tell a story that spans any number of years within a character's life. To celebrate the film's release on December 4, Collider is thrilled to bring you an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at one of the most fascinating parts of the film: its composers.

Recent findings suggest that the film has nine unique composers bringing the world of Behemoth! to life, including the likes of Michael Giacchino, Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Alan Silvestri, Lukas Frank, James Newton Howard, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, and Brandon Roberts. In a recent development, not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a substantial "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be stated for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

It has been revealed that price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The problem isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

Industry observers note that the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

In a recent development, yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

It has been revealed that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Industry observers note that the sweeping World War I romance comes from the young Belgian filmmaker whose last film, Cannes winner “Close,” received a Best International Feature Oscar nomination. Per MUBI, “Surrounded by brutality but bound by tenderness, two World War I soldiers find a fragile sanctuary of love and art amid the shadows of the Belgian trenches. ‘Coward’ asks a profound question for a generation sent to war: when the world demands violence, is walking away the truest act of bravery?”.

More from IndieWire’s review: “Belgian filmmaker wrestles the tenderness and softness between soldiers from the brutality of the battlefield in his visually arresting if thematically by-the-book third feature, ‘Coward.’ Starring newcomers Valentin Campagne and Emmanuel Macchia as achingly beautiful soldiers of the Belgian front in World War I who fall in love and learn to discover that, in one of the most fascinatingly contradictory ideas of Dhont’s highly contradictory career, the violence of war is what both enables and protects their attraction, and allows them to be together at all.”.

It has been revealed that there’s more, as “in 1916, on the western front of World War I, the flamboyant Francis (Valentin Campagne) leads a not-so-merry band of rejects among his infantry, of soldiers whose job it is to entertain and raise the morale of their comrades. In this case, it’s forming a theater troupe of the soldiers in drag as they move from battle to battle, a role that’s become almost as instrumental in keeping spirits high as actual combat is to wearing them down. The withdrawn, ethereally beautiful Pierre (Emmanuel Macchia) becomes drawn into the world of the troupe, and he’s intrigued by the outré Francis’ ostentatious theatricality, and how comfortable he is in dresses and makeup. … Through an attraction that’s only allowed to flower because of and in context of their closeness to each other on Francis’ performances, he and Pierre become secret lovers.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:.

Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Industry observers note that as mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

In a recent development, yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

According to recent reports, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software patch for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following concern:.

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now indicates: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”.

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496.

8 Most Universally Loved Movies From 1995

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that though blockbusters had been around for a good 20 years by the time 1995 came around, that year took things to a latest level as the age of old-school practical filmmaking and the dawn of the digital revolution clashed together.
  • In a recent development, franchise movies like Batman Forever broke opening weekend records, but the year also produced notorious disasters.
  • Away from the bloated misfires, 1995 also delivered an extraordinary run of movies, including grounded dramas, mid-budget thrillers, and some technical marvels thrown in for good measure, and made it arguably one of the finest years for cinema of modern times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that though blockbusters had been around for a good 20 years by the time 1995 came around, that year took things to a latest level as the age of old-school practical filmmaking and the dawn of the digital revolution clashed together. Studios had begun throwing obscene amounts of money at massive spectacles, and though the box office returns weren't quite guaranteed for those gambles, things were hurtling towards the behemoth tentpole culture that we have today.

In a recent development, franchise movies like Batman Forever broke opening weekend records, but the year also produced notorious disasters. Waterworld became the most expensive movie ever made up to that point and was roundly laughed out of theaters, though, whisper it, it's actually pretty good when you rewatch it. Showgirls became instantly comically infamous, and Cutthroat Island basically made the entire pirate genre walk the plank until Johnny Depp sashayed over the horizon as Captain Jack Sparrow.

Away from the bloated misfires, 1995 also delivered an extraordinary run of movies, including grounded dramas, mid-budget thrillers, and some technical marvels thrown in for good measure, and made it arguably one of the finest years for cinema of modern times.

Recent findings suggest that michael Mann's LA crime epic had been sitting in the back of the director's head for years, just as its upcoming sequel has been. He actually filmed it as a TV pilot called LA Takedown in 1989, but we can all be thankful that it took another 6 years for it to come to the big screen, because what was delivered was a complete masterpiece.

According to recent reports, heat famously pulled off the ultimate casting coup, putting Al Pacino and Robert De Niro on screen together for the first time, though not for very long. The coffee shop confrontation between Detective Vince Hanna and master thief Neil McCauley absolutely lived up to the hype. Critics loved it on release, praising Mann's atmospheric direction, the rip-roaring tactical gunplay, and the complexity added to both sides of the law.

In a recent development, it made almost 190 million worldwide and was a fairly solid commercial hit, but its true cultural footprint grew from the point that it landed on home video and persists today. Audiences still consider Heat one of the greatest crime movies of all time, and rightly so. It's far more than just the union of Pacino and De Niro, with both Val Kilmer and Ashley Judd offering excellent supporting performances.

Recent findings suggest that it's incredible to think that before Se7en arrived in September 1995, David Fincher was essentially just a music video director who had taken a bit of a humbling with the misunderstood Alien 3. But the combination of the thriller master, as he's now recognized, with Andrew Kevin Walker's bleak script allowed for an instant career reinvention that also left an indelible mark on the modern thriller landscape.

The casting was incredible, pairing Morgan Freeman's world-weary detective Somerset, who is on the verge of retirement, with Brad Pitt's impulsive newcomer Mills, and, of course, Kevin Spacey's sociopathic, ice-cold serial killer, John Doe, focused on using the seven deadly sins as his murderous blueprint.

An uncompromisingly dark movie, it is inventive in its nastiness and beautifully shot, thanks to Darius Khondji, the cinematographer, with a brilliantly oppressive score by Howard Shore. Despite ending on one of the bleakest notes in the history of mainstream studio cinema, which both Fincher and Pitt famously had to fight to keep in there, audience word of mouth drove Se7en to an astonishing 327 million worldwide. And it's still utterly rewatchable, even when you know the awful sucker punch that comes.

Not content with making one untouchable gangster masterpiece in Goodfellas, Martin Scorsese got the band back together in '95 by reuniting screenwriter Nicholas Pileggi and stars Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci for an even more operatic story set in the 1970s and early '80s. Casino charts the rise and fall of Sam "Ace" Rothstein, a sports handicapper tapped by the Chicago outfit to run the Tangiers Casino in Las Vegas, alongside volatile enforcer Nicky Santoro and his self-destructive wife, Ginger.

Sources indicate that as with Goodfellas, Scorsese paints a perversely aspirational picture of criminal enterprise, and the two films share a lot of DNA, but Goodfellas leans a little more bleak towards its end. Since its release, critical and audience consensus has shifted to appreciate Casino even more. It's relentlessly fast, brilliantly violent, and it has a documentary-like fascination with how the mob operated, with the rise of Las Vegas. The entire cast is excellent, with Joe Pesci on particularly explosive form and Sharon Stone offering a career-best turn as the tragic Ginger.

Telling the story of a notorious historical event that everybody knew the outcome of and still managing to make it a white-knuckle thriller was no small achievement, but Ron Howard pulled it off in style, starring Tom Hanks as Commander Jim Lovell, alongside Kevin Bacon and Bill Paxton.

Apollo 13 dramatizes the true story of the doomed 1970 lunar mission that turned into a desperate fight for survival. The film was widely praised for its meticulous historical accuracy, including the genius use of zero gravity to shoot sequences, and it comes with another one of James Horner's brilliantly stirring scores. Audiences made it the third-highest-grossing movie of the year with just over 350 million, and it earned nine Academy Awards.

Beyond those glossy achievements, it is a deeply compelling, painfully human story that is universally beloved because it celebrates human ingenuity and teamwork while under the gravest of pressure.

Sources indicate that A wildly different movie than the rest of those collected here, on paper, Babe would just be a gentle live-action Australian family movie about a talking pig who becomes a sheepdog. And what could have been straight-to-video fodder in someone else's hands was a gloriously heartwarming gem, thanks to the brilliant minds of George Miller and Chris Noonan. With that creative marriage of writer and director, the movie turned the premise, which was based on the famous book "The Sheep Pig," into a soulful fable about kindness and defying expectations.

Before release, Babe's Best Picture nomination at the Oscars, along with six other nominations including for James Cromwell as the brilliantly understated farmer Hoggett, might have looked like a shock, but for anybody who watched it, it was very well-earned. It made a lot of money, but more importantly, decades later, Babe holds up because of its charming earnestness and because it tells a very sentimental story without ever becoming overly saccharine. It has genuine emotional weight, despite the fact that this is fundamentally a movie about a talking pig.

Industry observers note that when The Usual Suspects was released, the neo-Noir puzzle box was pushed by a tidal wave of positive word of mouth. And these days, it's all too easy to forget how great a movie it is, because of the weight of the shocking twist at the end.

Structured around the police interrogation of Roger "Verbal" Kint, the meek con man who survived a mass shootout and fire at a dock in San Pedro, the movie weaves an intricate tale of five colorful career criminals who are coerced into working for the mythical crime lord Keyser Söze. Made for just $6 million, it won screenwriter Chris MacQuarrie an Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay, and watching his snappy dialogue and the cast dynamic, it's not hard to see why.

Industry observers note that every one of the main stars is great, but particular enjoyment comes from Benicio Del Toro's mumbling Fred Fenster. It is, of course, a top-level water cooler phenomenon, thanks to the Keyser Söze twist, but crucially, The Usual Suspects holds up on repeat viewings despite that, because of the craft that goes into the storytelling up to that point. It doesn't even matter that you know the secret.

Bruce Willis could probably have made ten Die Hard movies where the iconic John McClane gets locked in a series of increasingly complex buildings and takes down gangs of long-haired European henchmen. We probably would have all enjoyed it, but the real genius of the original Die Hard trilogy is that it managed to shake up the formula so well after the somewhat confined setting of Die Hard 2.

It has been revealed that original director John McTiernan returned and opened up the doors, turning all of New York City into a ticking time bomb. He also brought in a second lead character alongside John McClane in the form of Samuel L. Jackson's reluctant Harlem shopkeeper, Zeus Carver.

In a recent development, die Hard with Vengeance makes John McClane feel more desperate and less in control than he was even when he was scuttling around in overhead vents. The chemistry between Willis and Jackson is incredible, and Jeremy Irons' menacing villain almost lived up to the brilliance of Alan Rickman's Hans Gruber.

The threequel was the highest-grossing movie of 1995, and even if you don't agree that it's better than the 1988 original, the fact that it pushes it so close at all is very impressive.

It's almost impossible to overstate just how much Toy Story changed the entertainment industry and blockbuster filmmaking when it arrived in November 1995. History has it as the first feature-length movie created entirely with computer-generated technology. Really, Pixar's debut could just be remembered as a technical novelty. Instead, the early Pixar team married the groundbreaking visuals with a deeply relatable story about jealousy and the fear of being replaced, with the irresistible hook of Tom Hanks and Tim Allen's performances as Woody and Buzz Lightyear.

In a recent development, toy Story is obviously the founding stone for the entire Pixar story, and even now that the visuals have aged, understandably, it hasn't lost any of its magic. It remains universally cherished because it does all the important, simple things, like the character work, the story, and the humor, so well. Really, the cutting-edge technology only mattered because of how well the story it was telling captivated us all. And still does.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps.
  • Sources indicate that the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027.
  • It has been revealed that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

Sources indicate that the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

It has been revealed that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

In a recent development, on the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly states it has no intends for a native Mac app.

In a recent development, you can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft intends to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Industry observers note that planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the tech giant.

Industry observers note that the June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:.

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team plans. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”.

  • Loosely based on Akira Kurosawa's samurai epic Seven Samurai, 1960's The Magnificent Seven centered around seven disparate outlaws and gunslingers (including Yul Brynner, Steve McQueen, and Charles Bronson) who are recruited to defend a small frontier town against an army of marauding bandits.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, joanne Froggatt is leaving the mean streets of London for the Wild West. The MobLand star has just finished filming MGM+'s new TV adaptation of the classic Western The Magnificent Seven, and she's excited for viewers to see it. She recently sat down with Collider's Therese Lacson while promoting MobLand's explosive second-season finale to discuss the upcoming series.

Loosely based on Akira Kurosawa's samurai epic Seven Samurai, 1960's The Magnificent Seven centered around seven disparate outlaws and gunslingers (including Yul Brynner, Steve McQueen, and Charles Bronson) who are recruited to defend a small frontier town against an army of marauding bandits. The film spawned several sequels, a TV series that ran from 1998 to 2000, and a 2016 Antoine Fuqua remake that starred Denzel Washington and Chris Pratt.

It has been revealed that now, it's coming to TV once more, courtesy of MGM+. The project was originally developed by True Detective's Nic Pizzolatto, but was turned over to Heroes' Tim Kring. It is set to star Matt Dillon in the role of Chris Adams, originally played by Brynner, as well as Will Patton, Michael Ealy, Danny Pino, Amy Forsyth, Joshua Close, and Ken Yamamura. It was Froggatt's first experience filming a Western, and it did not disappoint.

It has been revealed that "It was so much fun to film. We finished at the end of September, so we did four months in Alberta, and it was a wonderful experience. I’ve just seen a few little clips when I’ve been in to do ADR redoing the sound, and it looks incredible. It looks so exciting, and it’s like adventure, and drama, and it’s a Western. It’s got everything you want it to have, the horses and the locations are just stunning, the most amazing vistas, and I think it’s gonna look beautiful, and it’s gonna be wholly entertaining. So I’m super excited for people to watch it.".

Froggatt also teased another upcoming project, a dramatization of a murder case that shocked America and Britain in the late 1990s. In 1998, Matthew Eappen, an eight-month-old infant in the care of teenage au pair Louise Woodward, died of a fractured skull. Woodward, a British citizen, was put on trial for murder; the resulting twists and turns of the case dominated the headlines for months. The series will be directed by Oscar-winning Danish filmmaker Susanne Bier (In a Better World), and will star Froggatt, Meghann Fahy, Sagar Radia, and Catriona Chandler.

Sources indicate that "I’m now in Latest York doing a miniseries for HBO called The Trial of Louise Woodward, which is based on a true story, so that’s completely different. So it’s been an amazing year. I went from MobLand to Western — so that was two bucket list things — I got to play in the gangster genre and I got to play in a Western, which I’ve always wanted to do. And now I’m in New York playing a Brit in an adaptation of a true story, so it’s been a really fun, amazingly satisfying, creative year.".

Harry works alongside the Harrigans' son, Kevin (Paddy Considine), to prevent the conflicts between the Harrigans and the other crime families of the city from erupting into full-on gang wars. Froggatt stars as Jan, Harry's wife, who gets caught in the crossfire of gangland violence. The series' second season concluded last week, and it has been renewed for a third.

Jimmy Kimmel zeroed in on Jensen Huang on last night’s episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live, taking aim at Donald Trump‘s unabashed support of the Nvidia CEO.

According to recent reports, “Who doesn’t love a good comeback story?” Kimmel quipped of Huang, who was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia despite an ongoing investigation into multiple alleged affairs — including one with an accused Chinese spy and two with Nvidia subordinates. Trump took credit for the decision, telling CNBC that he personally called into an Nvidia board meeting and “convinced” it to give Huang, one of the president’s closest allies in tech, his job back.

In a recent development, “After 10 grueling days of forced unemployment, the board at Nvidia today voted to reinstate their former CEO, who, according to our president, did nothing wrong,” Kimmel recounted. “All this guy did was cheat on his wife with two employees and a Chinese spy. Who hasn’t done that?”.

Kimmel explained that the board issued a statement saying they have “every confidence” in Huang. “Which, of course, had nothing to do with the pressure from our Silicon Man in Chief, who has at least 62 million reasons why he wanted his pal in charge. After the board made it clear that they were unequivocally moving on, Trump called them personally to harangue them. And if you think that sounds fishy, it’s not. It’s called being a good friend.”.

In a recent development, he added, “There’s nothing unusual about a president who owns a huge amount of stock in a tech giant putting his little carrot thumb on the scale in a way that immediately boosts that company’s stock price. I’m sure it also didn’t hurt that Huang donated $25 million to the big stupid ballroom he’s building.”.

After sharing an AI image Trump posted of Huang holding up a red bra after an assassination attempt, Kimmel noted, “What a profoundly stupid time to be alive.”.

Huang resigned from his position as CEO and board member on Nov. 12, acknowledging multiple affairs, including with Chinese business executive Alice Huang (no relation), who is alleged by the U.S. government to be an asset of China’s foreign intelligence operations.

The shock decision to reinstate Huang came after Nvidia’s board previously dismissed public pressure campaigns to reinstate him. Trump seemed to know the decision was coming during another interview earlier Monday morning, telling PBS before the announcement that Huang is “back where he should be.” Nvidia’s stock skyrocketed after the announcement. Trump — who is perpetually obsessed with the stock market — has reportedly traded close to $100 million in Nvidia stock over the course of the last two years.

U2 have finally announced a North American leg for their “Greatest Show on Earth World Tour” in support of their new LP, Carnaval De Luz.

Industry observers note that the stadium tour is set to start Aug. 3 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami and wrap Oct. 18 at BC Place in Vancouver. During the first half of the tour, U2 will receive support from Stephen Wilson Jr., while the War on Drugs will open the second half of the tour. A full itinerary is below.

It has been revealed that U2 will spend much of 2027 on the road, marking their first major outing since the 2019 leg of their Joshua Tree anniversary tour. The Greatest Show on Earth Tour will kick off in February with a run of demonstrates in Mexico City, followed by dates in South America. A European and U.K. tour will launch in April and wrap in July.

U2 released Carnaval de Luz, their 16th studio album, earlier this month. It’s the band’s first album of all newly introduced material since 2017’s Songs of Experience, with their 2023 project, Songs of Surrender, featuring newly recorded versions and interpretations of older songs.
